In that case the offense of the cross has been removed. [^12^](javascript:void(0))I wish those who unsettle you would castrate themselves!

[^13^](javascript:void(0))For you were called to freedom, brothers and sisters;^b^ only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for selfindulgence,[^c^](javascript:void(0)) but through love become slaves to one another. [^14^](javascript:void(0))For the whole law is summed up in a single commandment, "You shall love your neighbor as yourself." [^15^](javascript:void(0))If, however, you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another.

[^16^](javascript:void(0))Live by the Spirit, I say, and do not gratify the desires of the flesh. [^17^](javascript:void(0))For what the flesh desires is opposed to the Spirit, and what the Spirit desires is opposed to the flesh; for these are opposed to each other, to prevent you from doing what you want. [^18^](javascript:void(0))But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not subject to the law. [^19^](javascript:void(0))Now the works of the flesh are obvious: fornication, impurity, licentiousness, [^20^](javascript:void(0))idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, [^21^](javascript:void(0))envy,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) drunkenness, carousing, and things like these. I am warning you, as I warned you before: those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

[^22^](javascript:void(0))By contrast, the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, [^23^](javascript:void(0))gentleness, and self-control. There is no law against such things. [^24^](javascript:void(0))And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. [^25^](javascript:void(0))If we live by the Spirit, let us also be guided by the Spirit. [^26^](javascript:void(0))Let us not become conceited, competing against one another, envying one another.

**[6](javascript:void(0))** My friends,[^b^](javascript:void(0)) if anyone is detected in a transgression, you who have received the Spirit should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness. Take care that you yourselves are not tempted. [^2^](javascript:void(0))Bear one another\'s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill[^c^](javascript:void(0)) the law of Christ. [^3^](javascript:void(0))For if those who are nothing think they are something, they deceive themselves. [^4^](javascript:void(0))All must test their own work; then that work, rather than their neighbor\'s work, will become a cause for pride. [^5^](javascript:void(0))For all must carry their own loads.

[^6^](javascript:void(0))Those who are taught the word must share in all good things with their teacher.

[^7^](javascript:void(0))Do not be deceived; God is not mocked, for you reap whatever you sow. [^8^](javascript:void(0))If you sow to your own flesh, you will reap corruption from the flesh; but if you sow to the Spirit, you will reap eternal life from the Spirit. [^9^](javascript:void(0))So let us not grow weary in doing what is right, for we will reap at harvest time, if we do not give up. [^10^](javascript:void(0))So then, whenever we have an opportunity, let us work for the good of all, and especially for those of the family of faith.

[^11^](javascript:void(0))See what large letters I make when I am writing in my own hand! [^12^](javascript:void(0))It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh that try to compel you to be circumcised---only that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ. [^13^](javascript:void(0))Even the circumcised do not themselves obey the law, but they want you to be circumcised so that they may boast about your flesh. [^14^](javascript:void(0))May I never boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which[^d^](javascript:void(0)) the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world. [^15^](javascript:void(0))For[^a^](javascript:void(0)) neither circumcision nor uncircumcision is anything; but a new creation is everything! [^16^](javascript:void(0))As for those who will follow this rule---peace be upon them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.

[^17^](javascript:void(0))From now on, let no one make trouble for me; for I carry the marks of Jesus branded on my body.

[^18^](javascript:void(0))May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers and sisters.[^b^](javascript:void(0)) Amen.

**[1.1](javascript:void(0))--[5](javascript:void(0)): The greeting.** **[1](javascript:void(0)):** *Apostle* or "messenger," lit., "one who is sent." Only later does this become a formal designation for a specific group of Jesus\'s first disciples. **[2](javascript:void(0)):** *Churches of Galatia* refers to "gatherings" or "assemblies" in the region. **[3](javascript:void(0)):** A common greeting formula found also in Rom 1.7; 1 Cor 1.3; 2 Cor 1.2. **[4](javascript:void(0)):** *For our sins*, Paul does not clearly construe Christ\'s death as an atoning sacrifice, as it later comes to be understood. The language here suggests that Christ is pivotal for establishing a new way of dealing with sin. *The present evil age* draws an antagonistic relationship with outsiders and alludes to the promise of a new age right on the horizon. Apocalyptic expectations about the imminent return of Christ and a time of judgment frame Paul\'s arguments here as in his other letters.

**[1.6](javascript:void(0))--[2.14](javascript:void(0)): A recapitulation of Paul\'s life and ministry.** The earliest and best historical source for the movement (or set of movements) that will later come to be known as "Christianity." Unlike Acts, which presents a picture of harmony and agreement among the early leaders, Paul suggests relatively prickly meetings with others that sometimes became openly hostile.

**[1.6](javascript:void(0))--[9](javascript:void(0)): Paul rebukes the Galatians.** **[6](javascript:void(0)):** Instead of the standard praise and thanksgiving to those addressed at the opening of the letter (cf. Rom 1.8--15; 1 Cor 1.4--9), Paul charges the Galatians with *deserting the one who called you*, that is, God (or God through Christ). Paul implies that they stand behind his teachings and guarantee their authenticity. *A different gospel*, the Galatians have accepted teachings that are not compatible with Paul\'s true and legitimate instruction. **[8](javascript:void(0))--[9](javascript:void(0)):** Even if *an angel from heaven* revealed another teaching, that angelic gospel would still be false. The idea that lesser deities (or angels) might act as mediators of divine teachings also appears in 3.19 and was common in folk religions of Asia Minor.

**[1.10](javascript:void(0))--[12](javascript:void(0)): Paul again defends his teachings as authoritative.** Paul states that his teaching was directly revealed to him by Jesus Christ, implying that other teachings are of lesser value because they are *of human origin.*

**[1.13](javascript:void(0))--[24](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s call, early work among the Gentiles, and conflicts with others.** **[13](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0)):** Cf. Phil 3.4--6. **[15](javascript:void(0))--[16](javascript:void(0)):** Paul recounts a divine intervention that reorients his understanding of God\'s plan for history and his own place within it. Language such as *set ... born* is similar to prophetic call-narratives; cf. Isa 49.1; Jer 1.5. *To me* (lit., "in me"), links the ideas that Christ is revealed to Paul with the gospel\'s proclamation to the Gentiles. **[17](javascript:void(0)):** *Arabia*, most likely the Nabatean kingdom in Transjordan, whose capital was Petra. The geographic details establish Paul\'s distance from Jerusalem. **[18](javascript:void(0)):** It is unclear whether the *three years* are to be counted from Paul\'s call or from his return to Damascus. *Cephas*, the Aramaic equivalent of "Peter" (Gk "Petros"; both names mean "rock") and the form of the name used by Paul. **[19](javascript:void(0)):** *James*, the brother of Jesus; see 1 Cor 15.7; Mk 6.3; Mt 13.55; Acts 13.55; 15.13; 21.18--19. **[21](javascript:void(0)):** *Syria*, a district in the northeast corner of the Mediterranean; its capital Antioch was one of the largest and wealthiest in the Roman Empire. It was combined into a single province with the neighboring territory of *Cilicia*, on the southeast coast of Asia Minor. The capital of *Cilicia* was Tarsus, reportedly Paul\'s hometown (Acts 9.11). **[22](javascript:void(0))--[24](javascript:void(0)):** Paul distances himself from the Judean communities despite claiming to be their equal as an apostle (cf. 1 Cor 15.8--11).

**[2.1](javascript:void(0))--[10](javascript:void(0)): Paul meets with the Jerusalem leaders.** The relationship of this visit with that described in Acts 15.1--29 is uncertain. **[1](javascript:void(0))--[2](javascript:void(0)):** This second visit is instigated by divine revelation, again suggesting Paul\'s independence as an apostle. Whether the *fourteen years* are to be counted from his call or his first Jerusalem visit (1.18--19) is unclear. Two co-workers are named: *Barnabas* (also in 2.9) and *Titus*, an uncircumcised Gentile (see 2 Cor 2.13; 7.6,13,14; 8.6,16,23; 12.18). **[3](javascript:void(0))--[5](javascript:void(0)):** Hinting at future conflicts, Paul charges that *false believers* surreptitiously disrupted the meeting by challenging his teachings. The remark about Titus\'s uncircumcision and the later conflict at Antioch (vv. 11--14) suggest that the status of Gentiles was a matter of dispute. **[6](javascript:void(0))--[9](javascript:void(0)):** Paul seems to hedge on the authority of the Jerusalem leaders but portrays their interactions as conciliatory. *Uncircumcised ... circumcised*, Gentiles and Jews (or Judeans). Paul asserts that the Jerusalem leaders agree with him in distinguishing between their outreach to the Jews and his to the Gentiles, thus supporting his decisions concerning Gentile believers. **[10](javascript:void(0)):** *The poor* could allude to impoverished members of the movement. Josephus (*Ant.* 20.51) mentions a famine in 46/48 ce. It could also refer to some subgroup needing financial support. Paul elsewhere collects money to be sent to Jerusalem (Rom 15.25--29; 2 Cor 8.1--9.15); 1 Cor 16.1--3 mentions Galatia specifically.

**[2.11](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0)): Paul reports a confrontation with Peter at Antioch.** The issue of table-fellowship raised questions about the status of Gentiles and Jews. Sharing, or not sharing, a meal typically indicated acceptance or nonacceptance. Jewish writers sometimes stereotyped Gentiles as immoral, especially sexually (see Rom 1.18--32; 1 Thess 4.5), emphasizing their alienation from the true God and their worship of idols or false gods. Many also maintain that, in spite of this alienation, the Gentiles will eventually join in worshiping the true God, though they do not agree on precisely when or how this might happen. Paul\'s statements throughout Galatians suggest disagreement on these points, particularly the issue of whether Gentiles should be circumcised or have a second-class status within the movement. **[12](javascript:void(0)):** *The people ... from James*, presumably messengers from the Jerusalem apostles who insist that Gentile Christ-followers have a lesser status. Paul will portray this division as a matter of keeping or not keeping "the law" (2.16), but it is unclear why he construes eating with Gentiles in this way. Some texts show a concern with violating dietary laws (Dan 1.8--16; Tob 1.10--13; Jdt 10.5; *Letter of Aristeas* 142), but there are no explicit prohibitions against eating with Gentiles in the extant literature. **[14](javascript:void(0)):** Paul charges Peter with hypocritical behavior and here casts the issue as living "like Jews" instead of "like Gentiles."

**[2.15](javascript:void(0))--[21](javascript:void(0)): Jews and Gentiles are both justified through Christ.** These verses fit within a larger set of arguments about the status of Gentiles and Jews in God\'s unfolding plan for human and cosmic history. Later interpreters see terms such as "works," "law," "justification," and "faith" as signs pointing to major theological issues, but it remains unclear why Paul distinguishes between works of the law and justification by faith here. **[15](javascript:void(0)):** *Jews by birth*, Paul identifies himself with Peter, insisting that they are Jewish by birth and that they agree on what God demands of both Jews and Gentiles in the new era that has dawned with Christ. *Gentile sinners*, see 2.11--14n. **[16](javascript:void(0)):** By *works* Paul probably means Jewish practices that his rivals are insisting that Gentiles must observe. Whatever they are precisely, he deems them irrelevant to the larger issue of finding favor with God. Paul emphasizes Jesus\'s faithfulness and the radical transformation made possible by Christ\'s "pneuma." *Faith in Jesus Christ*, better "the faithfulness of Jesus Christ." This translation frames the issue in terms of the remarkable things that Christ has done (2.20; 3.22; Rom 3.22,26; Phil 3.9), not the convictions of individual believers. Christ\'s faithfulness alludes to Christ\'s trusting obedience to God, even to the point of death (1.4; Rom 5.18--19; Phil 2.8). **[17](javascript:void(0)):** Paul suggests an ironic objection to his view. **[18](javascript:void(0)):** *Things that I once tore down* (i.e., observance of the law) as the only path for Gentiles. **[19](javascript:void(0)):** *Through the law I died to the law*, it is unclear how Paul understands the different roles played by "law" here, but he stresses a new, radical kind of transformation that reorients him around a singular good (see also Phil 3.7--11). *Crucified with Christ*, the death and resurrection of Christ serve as an analogy for Paul\'s own transformation (see also Phil 3.8); this is applied to Christ-followers in 5.24; 6.14; Rom 6.5--11; cf. 2 Cor 4.10--12. **[20](javascript:void(0)):** *Christ who lives in me*, suggests a material transformation that Paul elsewhere connects with the "pneuma" ("Spirit") of Christ; see 4.5--6; Rom 8.9--11; 1 Cor 2.13--16; 15.20--29,35--54; 2 Cor 1.22. *Gave himself for me*, see 1.4n.

**[3.1](javascript:void(0))--[5](javascript:void(0)): Paul again addresses his Gentile audience.** Paul asks the Galatians whether they received the gift of the "Spirit" (Gk "pneuma"; see 2.20n.) through following practices of the Jewish law, or through accepting the gospel proclaimed by Paul. **[1](javascript:void(0)):** *Jesus Christ was publicly exhibited as crucified*, most likely a reference to Paul\'s graphic description of Jesus\'s crucifixion. **[3](javascript:void(0)):** *Ending with the flesh*, an oblique reference to circumcision. Paul often opposes "pneuma" to "flesh" (e.g., 4.29; 5.16--25; 6.8; Rom 8.1--12; 3.1; 1 Cor 15.35--55; Phil 3.2--6). He typically associates the "pneuma" of Christ with heavenly, divine, and eternal things while the flesh is associated with mortal bodies and with passions and desires that cause immorality and vice (see especially 5.16--6.10; Rom 1.26,28; 7.5). **[5](javascript:void(0)):** *Miracles* are associated with Paul\'s teaching activity and with the presence of the "pneuma" among his followers (Rom 15.19; 1 Cor 12.10; 2 Cor 12.12).

**[3.6](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0)): Abraham as a model of trusting obedience.** Paul portrays Abraham\'s faithful obedience as a model for Gentiles. The promises to Abraham also link together God\'s plan for human history with the Gentile Christ-followers who can now inherit the promises. Abraham also appears as a model in Rom 4. **[6](javascript:void(0)):** Paul appropriates Gen 15.6 here and in Rom 4.3. Those who share this trusting loyalty (*believe*) are now deemed children of Abraham. **[8](javascript:void(0)):** The blessings promised to Abraham (Gen 12.3; 18.18; 22.18) are now realized among Paul\'s Gentiles **[10](javascript:void(0)):** Paul\'s statements about the "curse" of the law draw on Deut 27.26. In Paul\'s time the general Jewish view was that perfect fulfillment of the law was not a requirement of belonging to God\'s covenant people, but observance of the law expressed faithfulness to God\'s covenant. It sounds strange for Paul to suggest that the law demands perfect obedience. **[11](javascript:void(0))--[12](javascript:void(0)):** Quoting Hab 2.4 (as in Rom 1.17), Paul again makes faithful obedience and loyalty the key to divine reward. By contrast, the law appears ill-suited for this purpose. **[13](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0)):** Paul again draws connections between keeping the law and being under a curse, this time quoting Deut 21.23 to envision the crucifixion as a curse. Christ\'s death clears the way so that the promises to Abraham can be realized among the Gentiles. As elsewhere, Paul suggests that this new situation involves the gifts of Christ\'s "pneuma" (*Spirit*) and trusting loyalty (Gk "pistis," *faith*).

**[3.15](javascript:void(0))--[18](javascript:void(0)): The inheritance of Abraham.** Paul insists that Christ is the singular heir of Abraham\'s promises and that these promises have priority over the law, which came centuries later (cf. Rom 5.13--14). **[15](javascript:void(0)):** *Will*, the Gk means "covenant" as well as a person\'s document of bequest (see textual note *b*). **[16](javascript:void(0)):** *Offspring*, lit., "seed" (see textual notes *c* and *d*). Paul uses the same Greek word as the Septuagint (LXX) text of Genesis where God makes promises to Abraham (Gen 12.7; 15.5; 17.8; 22.17). Paul contrasts the singular "seed" with the common (and in his view mistaken) interpretation of it as a plural, "seeds." In Rom 4.16, by contrast, he interprets the "seed" as plural (NRSV "descendants"). **[17](javascript:void(0))--[18](javascript:void(0)):** Paul distinguishes the promises from the giving of the law and connects the inheritance of the Gentiles with the former. His time frame of *four hundred thirty years* from Abraham to the giving of the law follows the LXX of Ex 12.40.

**[3.19](javascript:void(0))--[25](javascript:void(0)): The purpose of the law of Moses.** The law does not replace God\'s promise to Abraham but is a temporary means of discipline for God\'s people. **[19](javascript:void(0)):** *Added because of transgressions* allows several interpretations: It can mean to make aware of sin (Rom 3.20; 7.7); it can also carry the sense of restraining transgressions (vv. 23--25); and it can also signify that the law provoked sin (Rom 5.20; 7.7--12). *Ordained through angels* some Jewish traditions claim that the Sinai law was delivered by divine mediators, not directly by God; see Deut 33.2 (LXX); *Jub.* 1.26--2.1; Josephus, *Ant*. 15.136; cf. Acts 7.38,53; Heb 2.2. *A mediator*, Moses (see Lev 26.46; Num 36.13). **[20](javascript:void(0)):** An obscure verse that seems to play the mediator figure off against the idea of one, unique God; it perhaps implies that the new situation with Christ allows for more direct, unmediated access to God. **[21](javascript:void(0))--[22](javascript:void(0)):** Paul raises the possible objection that the law is at odds with the promises (see 2.19--20; Rom 3.31), only to dismiss it. The promises which come through Christ are life-giving, perhaps alluding to the immortal destiny of the Christ-elect. **[22](javascript:void(0)):** *Imprisoned ... under the power of sin*, lit., "the scripture confined all things under sin." This role of the law has negative connotations, but Paul construed this as a necessary prelude to the coming of Christ. *Faith in Jesus Christ*, better "faith of Jesus Christ" (see textual note *e*), emphasizes Jesus\'s faith or trusting loyalty as that basis for the promise; this promise of sonship accrues to the elect who believe, trust, and are loyal; see 2.16n. **[24](javascript:void(0))--[25](javascript:void(0)):** The law is construed as a disciplinarian, necessary only during early phases of life. *Disciplinarian*, a slave who accompanied a boy to school and who often punished him for bad behavior.

**[3.26](javascript:void(0))--[29](javascript:void(0)): Baptism into Christ.** Through a ritual washing, the Christ-elect come to participate "in Christ" and are made into offspring of Abraham, thus fulfilling the promises. Paul may be recalling a formula used during baptism in vv. 26--28. **[26](javascript:void(0)):** The Christ-elect become children of God and therefore coheirs with Christ (see also Rom 8.14--17). **[27](javascript:void(0)):** This ritual produces a radical transformation (Rom 6.3--11). *Clothed ... with Christ*, an analogy for the changed physical or social-psychological reality of the baptized; see also Rom 13.14. **[28](javascript:void(0)):** Paul here insists that participation "in Christ" obviates common social classifications: Jew/Greek, slave/free, and male/female. It is unclear how this relates practically to social distinctions among the Christ-elect, whether in the present or in an imagined future. A similar erasure of social distinctions appears in 1 Cor 12.13 (cf. Col 3.9--11) without the phrase *male and female* that is taken from Gen 1.27. **[29](javascript:void(0)):** Christ alone is *Abraham\'s offspring* or "seed" (see 3.16n.), but now Paul\'s elect can be united with him through ritual washing.

**[4.1](javascript:void(0))--[7](javascript:void(0)): The elect become children of God through Christ.** **[1](javascript:void(0))--[2](javascript:void(0)):** Paul uses the analogy of a *guardian* (typically a slave) to explain the role of the law. During their earlier, immature phase God\'s elect had the law as a guardian until the appropriate time arrived for a transition of relationships. This analogy suggests that the earlier slave-like submission to the law was necessary and inevitable. **[3](javascript:void(0)):** *Elemental spirits of the world*, lit., "elements (Gk "stoicheia") of the cosmos." "Stoicheia" can refer to the four elements (earth, water, air, and fire) as well as components or parts of some broader system or whole. Many scholars construe these as malevolent lesser beings (as suggested by the NRSV "elemental spirits"), but this is unlikely. Taking these "stoicheia" as parts of the cosmos that the Gentiles (mistakenly) worship fits with other polemics against idolatry (see v. 8; cf. Rom 1.23,25; Wis 13.3; Philo, *Opif*. 7; *De spec. leg.* 2.55). **[4](javascript:void(0)):** Paul stresses Jesus\'s human birth and responsibility to the law, as if it connects to his mission to rescue others. **[6](javascript:void(0))--[7](javascript:void(0)):** *Abba*, see textual note *d*; Rom 8.15. The Christ-elect receive the "pneuma" (*Spirit*) inside their bodies and are adopted as sons of God.

**[4.8](javascript:void(0))--[10](javascript:void(0)): The Galatians risk returning to their former slave status.** Paul construes keeping the law (at least in the ways his rivals would have them do) in this new, changed situation as equivalent to returning to their old ways, which involved enslavement and submission to weak and illegitimate gods. **[9](javascript:void(0)):** *Elemental spirits*, see 4.3n. **[10](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0)):** *Days, months, and seasons* suggests that the Galatians may be observing Jewish or other festivals.

**[4.12](javascript:void(0))--[20](javascript:void(0)): Paul reminds the Galatians of their close relationship.** **[12](javascript:void(0)):** Paul uses common friendship tropes to create a picture of warm, mutual relationships between himself and the Galatians. The language of imitation appears elsewhere in his letters (1 Thess 1.6; 1 Cor 4.16; 11.1; Phil 3.17) but without the emphasis on mutuality here (but see 1 Cor 9.21). **[13](javascript:void(0))--[15](javascript:void(0)):** Paul may be alluding to earlier visits to Galatia. The precise nature of the *infirmity* is not known (see 6.17; 2 Cor 11.23--27; 12.7--10), but it exemplifies the care and self-sacrifice that formerly characterized their relationship. **[16](javascript:void(0))--[17](javascript:void(0)):** Paul shifts to a tone of sharp rebuke, defends his own truth-telling, and launches another high-pitched attack on his alleged competitors and opponents. **[17](javascript:void(0)):** *They*, i.e., Paul\'s rivals, are depicted as self-interested, insincere, and aiming to exclude Paul\'s Christ-elect in some way. **[19](javascript:void(0)):** The birth imagery suggests that the Christ-elect of Galatia remain immature and unformed. Paul elsewhere uses parent/ child analogies to characterize his addressees as in need of his instruction (1 Cor 4.14; 2 Cor 6.13; 1 Thess 2.11).

**[4.21](javascript:void(0))--[5.1](javascript:void(0)): The allegory of Hagar and Sarah.** A polemically charged allegory that seems to cast non-Christfollowing Jews in a harshly negative light. **[21](javascript:void(0)):** *The law*, construed here as the entire Pentateuch/Torah. **[22](javascript:void(0))--[23](javascript:void(0)):** Summarizes key points of the story in Gen 16.1--4,15; 21.1--7. **[24](javascript:void(0))--[26](javascript:void(0)):** *Allegory*, lit., "these things are spoken allegorically." Paul is familiar with traditions of allegorical interpretation, which treat texts as having nonliteral meanings that can be known by those with special learning and skill. Here the women stand for two types of covenants and, upending the story told in Genesis, Hagar stands for the old covenant associated with Sinai and with Jerusalem, while Sarah represents the heavenly covenant and the true Jerusalem above. **[25](javascript:void(0)):** *Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia* (see textual note *a*). Paul is unique in identifying Hagar directly with Mount Sinai, where the law was given to Israel. This negative identification probably targets Jews who are not part of the Christ-movement; Paul aims to associate his rivals with them in some way. **[26](javascript:void(0)):** *The Jerusalem above ... our mother*, images of a heavenly Jerusalem appear in some later texts, but Paul often imagines the heavens as the true home of his Christ-elect (1 Thess 4.15--17; 1 Cor 15.12--57; 2 Cor 4.16--5.5; Phil 3.14--21) **[27](javascript:void(0)):** Paul uses language from Isa 54.1 to celebrate the Christ-elect as the true children of Sarah; see also Isa 51.2--3. **[29](javascript:void(0))--[30](javascript:void(0)):** Gen 21.9--10 does not explicitly describe Ishmael persecuting Isaac; for Paul, however, this conflict becomes the basis for an attack on his rivals. [**5:1**](javascript:void(0)) The allegory leads to exhortations about *slavery* versus *freedom*, flesh versus spirit (see 4.29).

**[5.2](javascript:void(0))--[12](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s case against circumcision.** A Gentile who accepts circumcision is seeking righteousness in the wrong way. **[2](javascript:void(0))--[5](javascript:void(0)):** Paul states unequivocally that circumcision will exclude Gentiles from the Christ-community and tie them to the demands of the law, which they cannot keep (see 2.16; 3.10--12). **[6](javascript:void(0)):** *Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision*, seeming to contradict the position stated in vv. 2--5, circumcision now appears to be a matter of indifference, a point that is repeated again in 6.15 (see also 1 Cor 7.19). Among the elect, the main thing is "faith made effective through love" (see textual note *a*). This gives trusting obedience (Gk "pistis," *faith*) a passive sense because it is instigated through love, presumably God\'s love. **[7](javascript:void(0))--[8](javascript:void(0)):** The Galatians are deserting the true teachings of Paul. His rivals attempt to pervert the truth, which comes from *The one who calls you*, God through Christ. **[9](javascript:void(0)):** Paul uses the same saying in 1 Cor 5.6. **[10](javascript:void(0)):** Paul continues to drive a wedge between his Galatian followers and the rivals and competitors who actively seek to harm them. **[11](javascript:void(0)):** *If I am still preaching circumcision*, raises a possible objection that Paul\'s teachings about circumcision have been inconsistent. It is unclear what role the *offense of the cross* plays in this subargument, but it suggests Paul\'s alienation and persecution by others (see 1 Cor 1.18--25). **[12](javascript:void(0)):** Paul\'s polemic about his competitors comes to an apex of bitter sarcasm: his opponents should castrate themselves rather than seek to mutilate the genitals of others; see also Phil 3.2.

**[5.13](javascript:void(0))--[6.10](javascript:void(0)): Ethics among the Christ-elect.** In a shift of topic and tone, Paul presents a series of moral teachings that center on mutuality and solidarity.

**[5.13](javascript:void(0))--[26](javascript:void(0)): The constraints on freedom among the elect.** **[13](javascript:void(0)):** Paul again uses freedom/slavery analogies. *Self-indulgence*, lit., "the flesh," which Paul associates negatively with self-directed desires. The alternative is enslavement to one another for the sake of love; its opposite is strife and conflict (see v. 15). Love, mutuality, and solidarity are common ethical ideals in Stoic traditions, but Paul confines them to the elect here and in Phil 2.2--4; Rom 13.8--10; 14.7--23. **[14](javascript:void(0)):** Returning to the *law*, Paul insists that the Christ-elect fulfill the law through this ethic of solidarity, here construed in terms of the command to love one\'s neighbor, quoting Lev 19.18 (also in Rom 13.8--10). **[16](javascript:void(0))--[17](javascript:void(0)):** The life of the "pneuma" (*Spirit*) requires alienation from *the desires of the flesh* (v. 13n.; 3.3; Rom 8.1--17; cf. Rom 7.14--24), which are antithetical to the "pneuma." Greek moral philosophy considered passions and desires the root cause of immorality. Platonic discussions of self-mastery associate these irrational (bad) desires with the flesh and body, as Paul does here; see also Rom 1.24,26; 6.12--13; 7.5; 13.13--14; 1 Cor 9.24--27. **[18](javascript:void(0)):** *Not subject to the law*, although v. 14 suggests that they may fulfill it in some way. **[19](javascript:void(0))--[23](javascript:void(0)):** Catalogues of vices and virtues were commonly used in Greco-Roman ethical instruction and were adapted by early Christian writers; see Rom 1.29--31; 1 Cor 6.9--10; 2 Cor 6.6--7; 12.20--21; in other early Christian literature, see Col 3.5--14; Mk 7.21--23; Mt 15.19; 1 Tim 1.9--10; 6.11; 2 Tim 3.2--5; 1 Pet 2.1; 4.3; 2 Pet 1.5--7; Rev 21.8; 22.15. Paul\'s virtue and vice lists are relatively conventional but he adds language about idolatry, the kingdom of God, the law, the "pneuma" ("Spirit"), and belonging to Christ. **[24](javascript:void(0)):** The use of crucifixion as an analogy for controlling the passions is distinctive. Paul elsewhere uses death metaphors to convey domination and control (7.7--25), as does Philo (e.g., *De spec. leg.* 1.105--107; 2.78; *Posterity* 73).

**[6.1](javascript:void(0))--[10](javascript:void(0)): Paul exhorts the Galatians about ethical conduct.** **[1](javascript:void(0)):** The stress is on mutuality and care for others who share the "pneuma" (*Spirit*) of Christ; see also Rom 15.1--7. **[2](javascript:void(0)):** Here the Gentiles seem to fulfill the law in some way; see also 5.14; 1 Cor 9.21; Rom 8.2. **[3](javascript:void(0))--[5](javascript:void(0)):** Paul again warns that self-directed behavior will lead to a bad outcome at the impending judgment. **[6](javascript:void(0)):** Cf. 1 Cor 9.14. **[7](javascript:void(0))--[9](javascript:void(0)):** Paul again warns about the ways of the *flesh* versus "pneuma" (*Spirit*), here emphasizing the possible reward of *eternal life* (see also Rom 8.5--8). **[9](javascript:void(0)):** *Not grow weary*, see 2 Thess 3.13; in 2 Cor 4.1,16; Eph 3.13, the same verb is translated as "not lose heart." **[10](javascript:void(0)):** *The family of faith*, lit., "members of the household of faithfulness."

**[6.11](javascript:void(0))--[18](javascript:void(0)): Final warning about the dangers of rival teachers.** A return to the polemical tone characteristic of the letter. **[11](javascript:void(0)):** *What large letters I make*, Paul had dictated this letter to a secretary but writes the conclusion in his *own hand*; see 1 Cor 16.21; 2 Thess 3.17. **[12](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0)):** Paul paints an antagonistic picture of his rivals as boastful, as he does elsewhere (see Phil 3.2--4; Rom 2.17--24; 3.27; 4.2; 1 Cor 4.7; 2 Cor 11.12--13,18). He charges that their interest in circumcising the Gentiles stems from self-interested motives: *to make a good showing in the flesh* and to avoid persecution. They are also portrayed as hypocritical, as they do not obey the law themselves. Paul sums up his own teachings as *boasting ...* in *the cross*; positive use of boasting language also appears in Rom 5.2--3,11; 1 Cor 1.29--31; 2.2 **[15](javascript:void(0)):** See 5.6. *New creation*, the new mode of being that is made possible by the "pneuma" ("Spirit"), given to those who are "in Christ"; cf. 2 Cor 5.17; Rom 8.19--23. **[16](javascript:void(0))--[18](javascript:void(0)):** A two-part blessing. Verse 16 has the form of a traditional Jewish blessing and is conditional, bestowed on those who follow Paul\'s teaching; it is the counterpart to the curse in 1.8. The address *brothers and sisters* in v. 18 does not appear in the final blessing of Paul\'s other letters and expresses the hope that the former warm relationship between the apostle and the community will be restored. **[16](javascript:void(0)):** *This rule* is the teaching that Paul has advocated throughout the letter. *Israel of God*, a phrase unique to this verse, equivalent to the "true Israel," i.e., those who follow Paul\'s *rule* and not the teachings of his alleged rivals and opponents. **[17](javascript:void(0)):** *Marks of Jesus*, perhaps the scars from injuries inflicted on Paul during his work as an apostle (2 Cor 6.4--5; 11.23--25). Paul may also be suggesting that his scars identify him as belonging to Christ like the brand marks on a slave. **[18](javascript:void(0)):** Cf. Phil 4.23; Philem 25.

#### 1 Corinthians c. 53--54 CE

The First Letter of Paul to The Corinthians

**Name and Authorship**

The letter is named for its recipients, the community of believers in Christ in the Greek city of Corinth (see [map 14](javascript:void(0)) in the color map section at the end of the volume). Scholars agree that Paul was its author.

**Historical Context**

First Corinthians affords an unparalleled glimpse into the life of an early Christian community in a Greco-Roman city. This portrait both reflects the ethical challenges faced by converts rooted in Greco-Roman polytheism and signals intense experimentation with their new social identity discovered in Messiah Jesus.

Paul\'s Corinth was a Roman city, refounded by order of Julius Caesar in 44 bce after its brutal destruction by Mummius in 146 bce. Caesar populated the colony with numerous freedmen, but the ethnic mix was more diverse a century later, including Syrians and Egyptians, along with Greeks who had immigrated from surrounding cities. The first-century ce Jewish philosopher Philo speaks of a sizeable Jewish community in Corinth; see also [Acts 18.4](javascript:void(0)), [7](javascript:void(0)). Corinth rapidly regained its ancient prosperity owing to its favorable location, on the Isthmus. By 27 bce, Corinth was already the capital of the senatorial province of Achaia and the judicial seat of the Roman proconsul (see [Acts 18.12](javascript:void(0))). Sharp contrasts between rich and poor were apparent in this flourishing commercial center. But opportunities for social advancement also existed: even freedmen held civic office (see [Rom 16.23b](javascript:void(0))), something uncommon elsewhere. The Isthmian Games, hosted by Corinth every two years, drew large crowds. The theater, rehabilitated by the emperor Augustus in the late first century bce, held more than fifteen thousand spectators. The Roman-style amphitheater was one of the earliest built in the Greek world, probably dating to just after the foundation of the colony; the gladiatorial games held there during the imperial cult festivals were emulated by other Greek cities, such as Athens. The city was sacred to the goddess Aphrodite, whose famous sanctuary stood on the Acrocorinth. The temple of Asclepius, the god of healing, had extensive dining facilities. Inscriptions and dedications attest to the importance of the worship of the Roman emperor. Paul\'s choice of this bustling cosmopolis as one of the principal centers of his missionary activity reveals the scope of his missionary ambition.

The date of Paul\'s arrival in Corinth is debated by scholars. The majority place the beginning of Paul\'s Corinthian mission in 50 ce, correlating the account of Paul\'s trial before Gallio, the Roman proconsul of Achaia, in [Acts 18.12](javascript:void(0))--[17](javascript:void(0)) with an inscribed letter of the emperor Claudius to Delphi, in which Gallio\'s name is mentioned. A minority of scholars propose that Paul first visited Corinth in 41 ce, correlating the edict of Claudius on the Jews, as reported by Suetonius and Cassius Dio, with the account in [Acts 18.1](javascript:void(0))--[2](javascript:void(0)) that Aquila and Priscilla had relocated from Italy to Corinth, "because Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome." The account of Paul\'s activity in Corinth in [Acts 18.1](javascript:void(0))--[18](javascript:void(0)) is incomplete and anecdotal, but can be supplemented by information from Paul\'s letters. Upon arrival in Corinth, Paul found lodging with Aquila and his wife Priscilla, both Jews and of the same trade as Paul. Paul preached in the synagogue every sabbath; Greeks were among those whom Paul tried to persuade. In response to opposition from some Jews, Paul withdrew from the synagogue and began preaching in the house of a "godfearer" named Titius Justus. Paul names Stephanas and his household as the first coverts of the Roman province of Achaia in southern Greece ([1 Cor 16.15](javascript:void(0)); [1.16](javascript:void(0))). The author of Acts attributes sensational importance to the conversion of the synagogue president Crispus: "Many of the Corinthians believed and had themselves baptized when they heard \[of it\]"---that is, of the conversion of Crispus ([Acts 18.8](javascript:void(0))). As Paul represents it, most of his converts were lower class, lacking in education, wealth, and birth ([1 Cor 1.26](javascript:void(0))--[28](javascript:void(0))). But Paul also baptized a few wealthy persons, such as Gaius ([1.14](javascript:void(0))), who eventually became the "host ... of the whole church" ([Rom 16.23](javascript:void(0))). After Paul left Corinth, confusion arose among the new converts regarding boundaries between the church and the larger society, prompting Paul to write the letter on association with "immoral" persons and "idolaters," to which reference is made in [1 Cor 5.9](javascript:void(0))--[10](javascript:void(0)). While Paul was in Ephesus, the Corinthians sent him a letter, seeking his advice on several issues, including marriage, food sacrificed to idols, spiritual gifts, and other matters ([7.1](javascript:void(0)); [8.1](javascript:void(0)); [12.1](javascript:void(0)); [16.1](javascript:void(0)),[12](javascript:void(0))). At some point after Paul\'s founding visit, another Christian teacher visited Corinth, an Alexandrian Jew named Apollos, "an eloquent man, powerful in the \[exposition of\] scriptures" ([Acts 18.24](javascript:void(0))). Apollos made a strong impression on the Corinthians, especially upon the elite who valued proficiency in philosophy and rhetoric. Factions formed within the church, with members declaring support for one teacher or another ([1 Cor 1.10](javascript:void(0))--[12](javascript:void(0)); [3.4](javascript:void(0))).

**Literary History**

Most scholars view the writing known as 1 Corinthians as a single, unified composition. But its abrupt transitions, frequent changes of theme, and generally loose construction have raised questions about its integrity. Assigning portions of 1 Corinthians to separate letters would be justified only if the passages in question presupposed different situations. This appears to be the case in three instances: Paul\'s attitude toward the factions (contrast [11.18](javascript:void(0))--[19](javascript:void(0)) with [1.10](javascript:void(0))--[12](javascript:void(0))), Paul\'s advice on food sacrificed to idols (contrast [10.1](javascript:void(0))--[11.1](javascript:void(0)) with [8.1](javascript:void(0))--[13](javascript:void(0))), and Paul\'s announcement of his travel plans (contrast [16.5](javascript:void(0))--[9](javascript:void(0)) with [4.17](javascript:void(0))--[21](javascript:void(0))). Hence, some scholars have divided 1 Corinthians into three letters, composed in the following order: Letter A, On Association with the Immoral and Idolaters ([10.1](javascript:void(0))--[22](javascript:void(0)); [6.12](javascript:void(0))--[20](javascript:void(0)); [10.23](javascript:void(0))--[11.34](javascript:void(0))); Letter B, In Response to the Corinthians' Questions ([7](javascript:void(0))--[9](javascript:void(0)); [12](javascript:void(0))--[16](javascript:void(0))); Letter C, Counsel of Concord ([1.1](javascript:void(0))--[6.11](javascript:void(0))).

The strongest argument for the unity of the present text derives from rhetorical analysis, which identifies 1 Corinthians as a deliberative appeal for concord ([1.1](javascript:void(0))--[4.21](javascript:void(0))), with advice on divisive issues organized under subheadings ([5.1](javascript:void(0))--[16.24](javascript:void(0))). Yet a single letter may not be consistent with the several occasions and sources of information evident in the text: an anonymous report ([11.18](javascript:void(0))), the Corinthians' letter ([7.1](javascript:void(0))), a visit by Stephanas ([16.17](javascript:void(0))), and a report from "Chloe\'s people" ([1.11](javascript:void(0))). Whether 1 Corinthians is one letter or several, the place of composition was western Asia Minor ([1 Cor. 16.19](javascript:void(0))), probably Ephesus. According to the traditional chronology of Paul\'s life, the date of composition would be in the mid-50s ce.

**Interpretation**

In 1 Corinthians Paul shows remarkable familiarity with the culture of his converts and with its forms of discourse: for example, [ch 7](javascript:void(0)) shows Paul conversant with Cynic-Stoic views of marriage (like those of Musonius and Epictetus); [9.24](javascript:void(0))--[27](javascript:void(0)) employs an athletic metaphor from the Isthmian Games; [ch 13](javascript:void(0)) praises *agape* ("love"), a Christian counterpart to the praise of *eros* ("sexual love") in Plato\'s *Symposium*; [ch 15](javascript:void(0)) offers a reasoned proof of the resurrection of the body, analogous to philosophical arguments for the immortality of the soul in Plato and Cicero; [chs 1](javascript:void(0))--[4](javascript:void(0)) evoke the language of Corinth\'s colonial charter, in seeking to establish a constitution for the *ekklesia* ("church, assembly"; see 1.2n.) of Christ-believers. In several passages, Paul addresses a group whose opinions on a variety of subjects---eating meat sacrificed to idols, financial support of missionaries, speaking in tongues, the resurrection of the dead, going to court before unbelievers---diverge sharply from his own. The attitudes of this group ("the strong") correlate with those typically held by persons of high social status and education.

First Corinthians demonstrates Paul\'s capacity to think through the social and ethical implications of the new being "in Christ": for example, his exhortation to share with "the have-nots" at the communal meal, so as to "discern the body" of Christ ([11.17](javascript:void(0))--[34](javascript:void(0))); and his insight into the paradoxical power of "the word of the cross" ([1.18](javascript:void(0))) to call, redeem, and sanctify the low and despised of this world, "the nothings and nobodies."

*Laurence L. Welborn*

[**1**](javascript:void(0)) Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes,

[^2^](javascript:void(0))To the church of God that is in Corinth, to those who are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, together with all those who in every place call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both their Lord[^a^](javascript:void(0)) and ours:

[^3^](javascript:void(0))Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

[^4^](javascript:void(0))I give thanks to my[^b^](javascript:void(0)) God always for you because of the grace of God that has been given you in Christ Jesus, [^5^](javascript:void(0))for in every way you have been enriched in him, in speech and knowledge of every kind---[^6^](javascript:void(0))just as the testimony of[^c^](javascript:void(0)) Christ has been strengthened among you---[^7^](javascript:void(0))so that you are not lacking in any spiritual gift as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ. [^8^](javascript:void(0))He will also strengthen you to the end, so that you may be blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. [^9^](javascript:void(0))God is faithful; by him you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

[^10^](javascript:void(0))Now I appeal to you, brothers and sisters,[^d^](javascript:void(0)) by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you be in agreement and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same purpose. [^11^](javascript:void(0))For it has been reported to me by Chloe\'s people that there are quarrels among you, my brothers and sisters.[^e^](javascript:void(0)) [^12^](javascript:void(0))What I mean is that each of you says, "I belong to Paul," or "I belong to Apollos," or "I belong to Cephas," or "I belong to Christ." [^13^](javascript:void(0))Has Christ been divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul? [^14^](javascript:void(0))I thank God[^a^](javascript:void(0)) that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, [^15^](javascript:void(0))so that no one can say that you were baptized in my name. [^16^](javascript:void(0))(I did baptize also the household of Stephanas; beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.) [^17^](javascript:void(0))For Christ did not send me to baptize but to proclaim the gospel, and not with eloquent wisdom, so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied of its power.

[^18^](javascript:void(0))For the message about the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.

[^19^](javascript:void(0))For it is written, "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise,

  and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart."

[^20^](javascript:void(0))Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? [^21^](javascript:void(0))For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, God decided, through the foolishness of our proclamation, to save those who believe. [^22^](javascript:void(0))For Jews demand signs and Greeks desire wisdom, [^23^](javascript:void(0))but we proclaim Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, [^24^](javascript:void(0))but to those who are the called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. [^25^](javascript:void(0))For God\'s foolishness is wiser than human wisdom, and God\'s weakness is stronger than human strength.

[^26^](javascript:void(0))Consider your own call, brothers and sisters:[^b^](javascript:void(0)) not many of you were wise by human standards,[^c^](javascript:void(0)) not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. [^27^](javascript:void(0))But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong; [^28^](javascript:void(0))God chose what is low and despised in the world, things that are not, to reduce to nothing things that are, [^29^](javascript:void(0))so that no one[^d^](javascript:void(0)) might boast in the presence of God. [^30^](javascript:void(0))He is the source of your life in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption, [^31^](javascript:void(0))in order that, as it is written, "Let the one who boasts, boast in[^a^](javascript:void(0)) the Lord."

[**2**](javascript:void(0)) When I came to you, brothers and sisters,[^b^](javascript:void(0)) I did not come proclaiming the mystery[^c^](javascript:void(0)) of God to you in lofty words or wisdom. [^2^](javascript:void(0))For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. [^3^](javascript:void(0))And I came to you in weakness and in fear and in much trembling. [^4^](javascript:void(0))My speech and my proclamation were not with plausible words of wisdom,[^d^](javascript:void(0)) but with a demonstration of the Spirit and of power, [^5^](javascript:void(0))so that your faith might rest not on human wisdom but on the power of God.

[^6^](javascript:void(0))Yet among the mature we do speak wisdom, though it is not a wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are doomed to perish. [^7^](javascript:void(0))But we speak God\'s wisdom, secret and hidden, which God decreed before the ages for our glory. [^8^](javascript:void(0))None of the rulers of this age understood this; for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. [^9^](javascript:void(0))But, as it is written, "What no eye has seen, nor ear heard,

  nor the human heart conceived,

what God has prepared for those who love him"---

[^10^](javascript:void(0))these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit; for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. [^11^](javascript:void(0))For what human being knows what is truly human except the human spirit that is within? So also no one comprehends what is truly God\'s except the Spirit of God. [^12^](javascript:void(0))Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit that is from God, so that we may understand the gifts bestowed on us by God. [^13^](javascript:void(0))And we speak of these things in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual things to those who are spiritual.[^e^](javascript:void(0))

[^14^](javascript:void(0))Those who are unspiritual[^f^](javascript:void(0)) do not receive the gifts of God\'s Spirit, for they are foolishness to them, and they are unable to understand them because they are spiritually discerned. [^15^](javascript:void(0))Those who are spiritual discern all things, and they are themselves subject to no one else\'s scrutiny.

[^16^](javascript:void(0))"For who has known the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him?"

But we have the mind of Christ.

[**3**](javascript:void(0)) And so, brothers and sisters,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but rather as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ. [^2^](javascript:void(0))I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not ready for solid food. Even now you are still not ready, [^3^](javascript:void(0))for you are still of the flesh. For as long as there is jealousy and quarreling among you, are you not of the flesh, and behaving according to human inclinations? [^4^](javascript:void(0))For when one says, "I belong to Paul," and another, "I belong to Apollos," are you not merely human?

[^5^](javascript:void(0))What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you came to believe, as the Lord assigned to each. [^6^](javascript:void(0))I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. [^7^](javascript:void(0))So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth. [^8^](javascript:void(0))The one who plants and the one who waters have a common purpose, and each will receive wages according to the labor of each. [^9^](javascript:void(0))For we are God\'s servants, working together; you are God\'s field, God\'s building.

[^10^](javascript:void(0))According to the grace of God given to me, like a skilled master builder I laid a foundation, and someone else is building on it. Each builder must choose with care how to build on it. [^11^](javascript:void(0))For no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid; that foundation is Jesus Christ. [^12^](javascript:void(0))Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw---[^13^](javascript:void(0))the work of each builder will become visible, for the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed with fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each has done. [^14^](javascript:void(0))If what has been built on the foundation survives, the builder will receive a reward. [^15^](javascript:void(0))If the work is burned up, the builder will suffer loss; the builder will be saved, but only as through fire.

[^16^](javascript:void(0))Do you not know that you are God\'s temple and that God\'s Spirit dwells in you?[^b^](javascript:void(0)) [^17^](javascript:void(0))If anyone destroys God\'s temple, God will destroy that person. For God\'s temple is holy, and you are that temple.

[^18^](javascript:void(0))Do not deceive yourselves. If you think that you are wise in this age, you should become fools so that you may become wise. [^19^](javascript:void(0))For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written,

"He catches the wise in their craftiness," [^20^](javascript:void(0))and again,

"The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile."

[^21^](javascript:void(0))So let no one boast about human leaders. For all things are yours, [^22^](javascript:void(0))whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future---all belong to you, [^23^](javascript:void(0))and you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.

[**4**](javascript:void(0)) Think of us in this way, as servants of Christ and stewards of God\'s mysteries. [^2^](javascript:void(0))Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found trustworthy. [^3^](javascript:void(0))But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court. I do not even judge myself. [^4^](javascript:void(0))I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me. [^5^](javascript:void(0))Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart. Then each one will receive commendation from God.

[^6^](javascript:void(0))I have applied all this to Apollos and myself for your benefit, brothers and sisters,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) so that you may learn through us the meaning of the saying, "Nothing beyond what is written," so that none of you will be puffed up in favor of one against another. [^7^](javascript:void(0))For who sees anything different in you?[^b^](javascript:void(0)) What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if it were not a gift?

[^8^](javascript:void(0))Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! Quite apart from us you have become kings! Indeed, I wish that you had become kings, so that we might be kings with you! [^9^](javascript:void(0))For I think that God has exhibited us apostles as last of all, as though sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels and to mortals. [^10^](javascript:void(0))We are fools for the sake of Christ, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are held in honor, but we in disrepute. [^11^](javascript:void(0))To the present hour we are hungry and thirsty, we are poorly clothed and beaten and homeless, [^12^](javascript:void(0))and we grow weary from the work of our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; [^13^](javascript:void(0))when slandered, we speak kindly. We have become like the rubbish of the world, the dregs of all things, to this very day.

[^14^](javascript:void(0))I am not writing this to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children. [^15^](javascript:void(0))For though you might have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers. Indeed, in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel. [^16^](javascript:void(0))I appeal to you, then, be imitators of me. [^17^](javascript:void(0))For this reason I sent[^c^](javascript:void(0)) you Timothy, who is my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, to remind you of my ways in Christ Jesus, as I teach them everywhere in every church. [^18^](javascript:void(0))But some of you, thinking that I am not coming to you, have become arrogant. [^19^](javascript:void(0))But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power. [^20^](javascript:void(0))For the kingdom of God depends not on talk but on power. [^21^](javascript:void(0))What would you prefer? Am I to come to you with a stick, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?

[**5**](javascript:void(0)) It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not found even among pagans; for a man is living with his father\'s wife. [^2^](javascript:void(0))And you are arrogant! Should you not rather have mourned, so that he who has done this would have been removed from among you?

[^3^](javascript:void(0))For though absent in body, I am present in spirit; and as if present I have already pronounced judgment [^4^](javascript:void(0))in the name of the Lord Jesus on the man who has done such a thing.[^a^](javascript:void(0)) When you are assembled, and my spirit is present with the power of our Lord Jesus, [^5^](javascript:void(0))you are to hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.[^b^](javascript:void(0))

[^6^](javascript:void(0))Your boasting is not a good thing. Do you not know that a little yeast leavens the whole batch of dough? [^7^](javascript:void(0))Clean out the old yeast so that you may be a new batch, as you really are unleavened. For our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed. [^8^](javascript:void(0))Therefore, let us celebrate the festival, not with the old yeast, the yeast of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

[^9^](javascript:void(0))I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral persons---[^10^](javascript:void(0))not at all meaning the immoral of this world, or the greedy and robbers, or idolaters, since you would then need to go out of the world. [^11^](javascript:void(0))But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother or sister[^c^](javascript:void(0)) who is sexually immoral or greedy, or is an idolater, reviler, drunkard, or robber. Do not even eat with such a one. [^12^](javascript:void(0))For what have I to do with judging those outside? Is it not those who are inside that you are to judge? [^13^](javascript:void(0))God will judge those outside. "Drive out the wicked person from among you."

[**6**](javascript:void(0)) When any of you has a grievance against another, do you dare to take it to court before the unrighteous, instead of taking it before the saints? [^2^](javascript:void(0))Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you incompetent to try trivial cases? [^3^](javascript:void(0))Do you not know that we are to judge angels---to say nothing of ordinary matters? [^4^](javascript:void(0))If you have ordinary cases, then, do you appoint as judges those who have no standing in the church? [^5^](javascript:void(0))I say this to your shame. Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to decide between one believer[^a^](javascript:void(0)) and another, [^6^](javascript:void(0))but a believer^a^ goes to court against a believer^a^---and before unbelievers at that?

[^7^](javascript:void(0))In fact, to have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded? [^8^](javascript:void(0))But you yourselves wrong and defraud---and believers[^b^](javascript:void(0)) at that.

[^9^](javascript:void(0))Do you not know that wrongdoers will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived! Fornicators, idolaters, adulterers, male prostitutes, sodomites, [^10^](javascript:void(0))thieves, the greedy, drunkards, revilers, robbers---none of these will inherit the kingdom of God. [^11^](javascript:void(0))And this is what some of you used to be. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God.

[^12^](javascript:void(0))"All things are lawful for me," but not all things are beneficial. "All things are lawful for me," but I will not be dominated by anything. [^13^](javascript:void(0))"Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food,"[^c^](javascript:void(0)) and God will destroy both one and the other. The body is meant not for fornication but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. [^14^](javascript:void(0))And God raised the Lord and will also raise us by his power. [^15^](javascript:void(0))Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Should I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Never! [^16^](javascript:void(0))Do you not know that whoever is united to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For it is said, "The two shall be one flesh." [^17^](javascript:void(0))But anyone united to the Lord becomes one spirit with him. [^18^](javascript:void(0))Shun fornication! Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the fornicator sins against the body itself. [^19^](javascript:void(0))Or do you not know that your body is a temple[^d^](javascript:void(0)) of the Holy Spirit within you, which you have from God, and that you are not your own? [^20^](javascript:void(0))For you were bought with a price; therefore glorify God in your body.

[**7**](javascript:void(0)) Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: "It is well for a man not to touch a woman." [^2^](javascript:void(0))But because of cases of sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband. [^3^](javascript:void(0))The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband. [^4^](javascript:void(0))For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. [^5^](javascript:void(0))Do not deprive one another except perhaps by agreement for a set time, to devote yourselves to prayer, and then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control. [^6^](javascript:void(0))This I say by way of concession, not of command. [^7^](javascript:void(0))I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has a particular gift from God, one having one kind and another a different kind.

[^8^](javascript:void(0))To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is well for them to remain unmarried as I am. [^9^](javascript:void(0))But if they are not practicing self-control, they should marry. For it is better to marry than to be aflame with passion.

[^10^](javascript:void(0))To the married I give this command---not I but the Lord---that the wife should not separate from her husband [^11^](javascript:void(0))(but if she does separate, let her remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband), and that the husband should not divorce his wife.

[^12^](javascript:void(0))To the rest I say---I and not the Lord---that if any believer[^a^](javascript:void(0)) has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. [^13^](javascript:void(0))And if any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him. [^14^](javascript:void(0))For the unbelieving husband is made holy through his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy through her husband. Otherwise, your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy. [^15^](javascript:void(0))But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so; in such a case the brother or sister is not bound. It is to peace that God has called you.[^b^](javascript:void(0)) [^16^](javascript:void(0))Wife, for all you know, you might save your husband. Husband, for all you know, you might save your wife.

[^17^](javascript:void(0))However that may be, let each of you lead the life that the Lord has assigned, to which God called you. This is my rule in all the churches. [^18^](javascript:void(0))Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision. [^19^](javascript:void(0))Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing; but obeying the commandments of God is everything. [^20^](javascript:void(0))Let each of you remain in the condition in which you were called.

[^21^](javascript:void(0))Were you a slave when called? Do not be concerned about it. Even if you can gain your freedom, make use of your present condition now more than ever.[^a^](javascript:void(0)) [^22^](javascript:void(0))For whoever was called in the Lord as a slave is a freed person belonging to the Lord, just as whoever was free when called is a slave of Christ. [^23^](javascript:void(0))You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human masters. [^24^](javascript:void(0))In whatever condition you were called, brothers and sisters,[^b^](javascript:void(0)) there remain with God.

[^25^](javascript:void(0))Now concerning virgins, I have no command of the Lord, but I give my opinion as one who by the Lord\'s mercy is trustworthy. [^26^](javascript:void(0))I think that, in view of the impending[^c^](javascript:void(0)) crisis, it is well for you to remain as you are. [^27^](javascript:void(0))Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife. [^28^](javascript:void(0))But if you marry, you do not sin, and if a virgin marries, she does not sin. Yet those who marry will experience distress in this life,[^d^](javascript:void(0)) and I would spare you that. [^29^](javascript:void(0))I mean, brothers and sisters,^b^ the appointed time has grown short; from now on, let even those who have wives be as though they had none, [^30^](javascript:void(0))and those who mourn as though they were not mourning, and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, and those who buy as though they had no possessions, [^31^](javascript:void(0))and those who deal with the world as though they had no dealings with it. For the present form of this world is passing away.

[^32^](javascript:void(0))I want you to be free from anxieties. The unmarried man is anxious about the affairs of the Lord, how to please the Lord; [^33^](javascript:void(0))but the married man is anxious about the affairs of the world, how to please his wife, [^34^](javascript:void(0))and his interests are divided. And the unmarried woman and the virgin are anxious about the affairs of the Lord, so that they may be holy in body and spirit; but the married woman is anxious about the affairs of the world, how to please her husband. [^35^](javascript:void(0))I say this for your own benefit, not to put any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and unhindered devotion to the Lord.

[^36^](javascript:void(0))If anyone thinks that he is not behaving properly toward his fiancée,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) if his passions are strong, and so it has to be, let him marry as he wishes; it is no sin. Let them marry. [^37^](javascript:void(0))But if someone stands firm in his resolve, being under no necessity but having his own desire under control, and has determined in his own mind to keep her as his fiancée,^a^ he will do well. [^38^](javascript:void(0))So then, he who marries his fiancée^a^ does well; and he who refrains from marriage will do better.

[^39^](javascript:void(0))A wife is bound as long as her husband lives. But if the husband dies,[^b^](javascript:void(0)) she is free to marry anyone she wishes, only in the Lord. [^40^](javascript:void(0))But in my judgment she is more blessed if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.

[**8**](javascript:void(0)) Now concerning food sacrificed to idols: we know that "all of us possess knowledge." Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. [^2^](javascript:void(0))Anyone who claims to know something does not yet have the necessary knowledge; [^3^](javascript:void(0))but anyone who loves God is known by him.

[^4^](javascript:void(0))Hence, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that "no idol in the world really exists," and that "there is no God but one." [^5^](javascript:void(0))Indeed, even though there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth---as in fact there are many gods and many lords---[^6^](javascript:void(0))yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.

[^7^](javascript:void(0))It is not everyone, however, who has this knowledge. Since some have become so accustomed to idols until now, they still think of the food they eat as food offered to an idol; and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. [^8^](javascript:void(0))"Food will not bring us close to God."[^a^](javascript:void(0)) We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do. [^9^](javascript:void(0))But take care that this liberty of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak. [^10^](javascript:void(0))For if others see you, who possess knowledge, eating in the temple of an idol, might they not, since their conscience is weak, be encouraged to the point of eating food sacrificed to idols? [^11^](javascript:void(0))So by your knowledge those weak believers for whom Christ died are destroyed.[^b^](javascript:void(0)) [^12^](javascript:void(0))But when you thus sin against members of your family,[^c^](javascript:void(0)) and wound their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ. [^13^](javascript:void(0))Therefore, if food is a cause of their falling,[^d^](javascript:void(0)) I will never eat meat, so that I may not cause one of them[^e^](javascript:void(0)) to fall.

[**9**](javascript:void(0)) Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord? [^2^](javascript:void(0))If I am not an apostle to others, at least I am to you; for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.

[^3^](javascript:void(0))This is my defense to those who would examine me. [^4^](javascript:void(0))Do we not have the right to our food and drink? [^5^](javascript:void(0))Do we not have the right to be accompanied by a believing wife,[^f^](javascript:void(0)) as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? [^6^](javascript:void(0))Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living? [^7^](javascript:void(0))Who at any time pays the expenses for doing military service? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat any of its fruit? Or who tends a flock and does not get any of its milk?

[^8^](javascript:void(0))Do I say this on human authority? Does not the law also say the same? [^9^](javascript:void(0))For it is written in the law of Moses, "You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain." Is it for oxen that God is concerned? [^10^](javascript:void(0))Or does he not speak entirely for our sake? It was indeed written for our sake, for whoever plows should plow in hope and whoever threshes should thresh in hope of a share in the crop. [^11^](javascript:void(0))If we have sown spiritual good among you, is it too much if we reap your material benefits? [^12^](javascript:void(0))If others share this rightful claim on you, do not we still more?

Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right, but we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ. [^13^](javascript:void(0))Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple, and those who serve at the altar share in what is sacrificed on the altar? [^14^](javascript:void(0))In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel.

[^15^](javascript:void(0))But I have made no use of any of these rights, nor am I writing this so that they may be applied in my case. Indeed, I would rather die than that---no one will deprive me of my ground for boasting! [^16^](javascript:void(0))If I proclaim the gospel, this gives me no ground for boasting, for an obligation is laid on me, and woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel! [^17^](javascript:void(0))For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward; but if not of my own will, I am entrusted with a commission. [^18^](javascript:void(0))What then is my reward? Just this: that in my proclamation I may make the gospel free of charge, so as not to make full use of my rights in the gospel.

[^19^](javascript:void(0))For though I am free with respect to all, I have made myself a slave to all, so that I might win more of them. [^20^](javascript:void(0))To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews. To those under the law I became as one under the law (though I myself am not under the law) so that I might win those under the law. [^21^](javascript:void(0))To those outside the law I became as one outside the law (though I am not free from God\'s law but am under Christ\'s law) so that I might win those outside the law. [^22^](javascript:void(0))To the weak I became weak, so that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that I might by all means save some. [^23^](javascript:void(0))I do it all for the sake of the gospel, so that I may share in its blessings.

[^24^](javascript:void(0))Do you not know that in a race the runners all compete, but only one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you may win it. [^25^](javascript:void(0))Athletes exercise self-control in all things; they do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable one. [^26^](javascript:void(0))So I do not run aimlessly, nor do I box as though beating the air; [^27^](javascript:void(0))but I punish my body and enslave it, so that after proclaiming to others I myself should not be disqualified.

[**10**](javascript:void(0)) I do not want you to be unaware, brothers and sisters,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) that our ancestors were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, [^2^](javascript:void(0))and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, [^3^](javascript:void(0))and all ate the same spiritual food, [^4^](javascript:void(0))and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ. [^5^](javascript:void(0))Nevertheless, God was not pleased with most of them, and they were struck down in the wilderness.

[^6^](javascript:void(0))Now these things occurred as examples for us, so that we might not desire evil as they did. [^7^](javascript:void(0))Do not become idolaters as some of them did; as it is written, "The people sat down to eat and drink, and they rose up to play." [^8^](javascript:void(0))We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day. [^9^](javascript:void(0))We must not put Christ[^b^](javascript:void(0)) to the test, as some of them did, and were destroyed by serpents. [^10^](javascript:void(0))And do not complain as some of them did, and were destroyed by the destroyer. [^11^](javascript:void(0))These things happened to them to serve as an example, and they were written down to instruct us, on whom the ends of the ages have come. [^12^](javascript:void(0))So if you think you are standing, watch out that you do not fall. [^13^](javascript:void(0))No testing has overtaken you that is not common to everyone. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tested beyond your strength, but with the testing he will also provide the way out so that you may be able to endure it.

[^14^](javascript:void(0))Therefore, my dear friends,[^c^](javascript:void(0)) flee from the worship of idols. [^15^](javascript:void(0))I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say. [^16^](javascript:void(0))The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ? [^17^](javascript:void(0))Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread. [^18^](javascript:void(0))Consider the people of Israel;[^a^](javascript:void(0)) are not those who eat the sacrifices partners in the altar? [^19^](javascript:void(0))What do I imply then? That food sacrificed to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything? [^20^](javascript:void(0))No, I imply that what pagans sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. I do not want you to be partners with demons. [^21^](javascript:void(0))You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons. [^22^](javascript:void(0))Or are we provoking the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?

[^23^](javascript:void(0))"All things are lawful," but not all things are beneficial. "All things are lawful," but not all things build up. [^24^](javascript:void(0))Do not seek your own advantage, but that of the other. [^25^](javascript:void(0))Eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising any question on the ground of conscience, [^26^](javascript:void(0))for "the earth and its fullness are the Lord\'s." [^27^](javascript:void(0))If an unbeliever invites you to a meal and you are disposed to go, eat whatever is set before you without raising any question on the ground of conscience. [^28^](javascript:void(0))But if someone says to you, "This has been offered in sacrifice," then do not eat it, out of consideration for the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience---[^29^](javascript:void(0))I mean the other\'s conscience, not your own. For why should my liberty be subject to the judgment of someone else\'s conscience? [^30^](javascript:void(0))If I partake with thankfulness, why should I be denounced because of that for which I give thanks?

[^31^](javascript:void(0))So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.
