[^32^](javascript:void(0))Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God, [^33^](javascript:void(0))just as I try to please everyone in everything I do, not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, so that they may be saved.

[**11**](javascript:void(0)) Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.

[^2^](javascript:void(0))I commend you because you remember me in everything and maintain the traditions just as I handed them on to you. [^3^](javascript:void(0))But I want you to understand that Christ is the head of every man, and the husband[^b^](javascript:void(0)) is the head of his wife,[^c^](javascript:void(0)) and God is the head of Christ. [^4^](javascript:void(0))Any man who prays or prophesies with something on his head disgraces his head, [^5^](javascript:void(0))but any woman who prays or prophesies with her head unveiled disgraces her head---it is one and the same thing as having her head shaved. [^6^](javascript:void(0))For if a woman will not veil herself, then she should cut off her hair; but if it is disgraceful for a woman to have her hair cut off or to be shaved, she should wear a veil. [^7^](javascript:void(0))For a man ought not to have his head veiled, since he is the image and reflection[^a^](javascript:void(0)) of God; but woman is the reflection^a^ of man. [^8^](javascript:void(0))Indeed, man was not made from woman, but woman from man. [^9^](javascript:void(0))Neither was man created for the sake of woman, but woman for the sake of man. [^10^](javascript:void(0))For this reason a woman ought to have a symbol of[^b^](javascript:void(0)) authority on her head,[^c^](javascript:void(0)) because of the angels. [^11^](javascript:void(0))Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man or man independent of woman. [^12^](javascript:void(0))For just as woman came from man, so man comes through woman; but all things come from God. [^13^](javascript:void(0))Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a woman to pray to God with her head unveiled? [^14^](javascript:void(0))Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair, it is degrading to him, [^15^](javascript:void(0))but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For her hair is given to her for a covering. [^16^](javascript:void(0))But if anyone is disposed to be contentious---we have no such custom, nor do the churches of God.

[^17^](javascript:void(0))Now in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse. [^18^](javascript:void(0))For, to begin with, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you; and to some extent I believe it. [^19^](javascript:void(0))Indeed, there have to be factions among you, for only so will it become clear who among you are genuine. [^20^](javascript:void(0))When you come together, it is not really to eat the Lord\'s supper. [^21^](javascript:void(0))For when the time comes to eat, each of you goes ahead with your own supper, and one goes hungry and another becomes drunk. [^22^](javascript:void(0))What! Do you not have homes to eat and drink in? Or do you show contempt for the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What should I say to you? Should I commend you? In this matter I do not commend you! [^23^](javascript:void(0))For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took a loaf of bread, [^24^](javascript:void(0))and when he had given thanks, he broke it and said, "This is my body that is for[^d^](javascript:void(0)) you. Do this in remembrance of me." [^25^](javascript:void(0))In the same way he took the cup also, after supper, saying, "This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me." [^26^](javascript:void(0))For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord\'s death until he comes.

[^27^](javascript:void(0))Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be answerable for the body and blood of the Lord. [^28^](javascript:void(0))Examine yourselves, and only then eat of the bread and drink of the cup. [^29^](javascript:void(0))For all who eat and drink[^a^](javascript:void(0)) without discerning the body,[^b^](javascript:void(0)) eat and drink judgment against themselves. [^30^](javascript:void(0))For this reason many of you are weak and ill, and some have died.[^c^](javascript:void(0)) [^31^](javascript:void(0))But if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged. [^32^](javascript:void(0))But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined[^d^](javascript:void(0)) so that we may not be condemned along with the world.

[^33^](javascript:void(0))So then, my brothers and sisters,[^e^](javascript:void(0)) when you come together to eat, wait for one another. [^34^](javascript:void(0))If you are hungry, eat at home, so that when you come together, it will not be for your condemnation. About the other things I will give instructions when I come.

[**12**](javascript:void(0)) Now concerning spiritual gifts,[^f^](javascript:void(0)) brothers and sisters,^e^ I do not want you to be uninformed. [^2^](javascript:void(0))You know that when you were pagans, you were enticed and led astray to idols that could not speak. [^3^](javascript:void(0))Therefore I want you to understand that no one speaking by the Spirit of God ever says "Let Jesus be cursed!" and no one can say "Jesus is Lord" except by the Holy Spirit.

[^4^](javascript:void(0))Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; [^5^](javascript:void(0))and there are varieties of services, but the same Lord; [^6^](javascript:void(0))and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who activates all of them in everyone. [^7^](javascript:void(0))To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. [^8^](javascript:void(0))To one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, [^9^](javascript:void(0))to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit, [^10^](javascript:void(0))to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues. [^11^](javascript:void(0))All these are activated by one and the same Spirit, who allots to each one individually just as the Spirit chooses.

[^12^](javascript:void(0))For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ. [^13^](javascript:void(0))For in the one Spirit we were all baptized into one body---Jews or Greeks, slaves or free---and we were all made to drink of one Spirit.

[^14^](javascript:void(0))Indeed, the body does not consist of one member but of many. [^15^](javascript:void(0))If the foot would say, "Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body," that would not make it any less a part of the body. [^16^](javascript:void(0))And if the ear would say, "Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body," that would not make it any less a part of the body. [^17^](javascript:void(0))If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole body were hearing, where would the sense of smell be? [^18^](javascript:void(0))But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose. [^19^](javascript:void(0))If all were a single member, where would the body be? [^20^](javascript:void(0))As it is, there are many members, yet one body. [^21^](javascript:void(0))The eye cannot say to the hand, "I have no need of you," nor again the head to the feet, "I have no need of you." [^22^](javascript:void(0))On the contrary, the members of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, [^23^](javascript:void(0))and those members of the body that we think less honorable we clothe with greater honor, and our less respectable members are treated with greater respect; [^24^](javascript:void(0))whereas our more respectable members do not need this. But God has so arranged the body, giving the greater honor to the inferior member, [^25^](javascript:void(0))that there may be no dissension within the body, but the members may have the same care for one another. [^26^](javascript:void(0))If one member suffers, all suffer together with it; if one member is honored, all rejoice together with it.

[^27^](javascript:void(0))Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it. [^28^](javascript:void(0))And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers; then deeds of power, then gifts of healing, forms of assistance, forms of leadership, various kinds of tongues. [^29^](javascript:void(0))Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? [^30^](javascript:void(0))Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret? [^31^](javascript:void(0))But strive for the greater gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way.

[**13**](javascript:void(0)) If I speak in the tongues of mortals and of angels, but do not have love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. [^2^](javascript:void(0))And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. [^3^](javascript:void(0))If I give away all my possessions, and if I hand over my body so that I may boast,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) but do not have love, I gain nothing.

[^4^](javascript:void(0))Love is patient; love is kind; love is not envious or boastful or arrogant [^5^](javascript:void(0))or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful; [^6^](javascript:void(0))it does not rejoice in wrongdoing, but rejoices in the truth. [^7^](javascript:void(0))It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

[^8^](javascript:void(0))Love never ends. But as for prophecies, they will come to an end; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will come to an end. [^9^](javascript:void(0))For we know only in part, and we prophesy only in part; [^10^](javascript:void(0))but when the complete comes, the partial will come to an end. [^11^](javascript:void(0))When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child; when I became an adult, I put an end to childish ways. [^12^](javascript:void(0))For now we see in a mirror, dimly,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) but then we will see face to face. Now I know only in part; then I will know fully, even as I have been fully known. [^13^](javascript:void(0))And now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; and the greatest of these is love.

[**14**](javascript:void(0)) Pursue love and strive for the spiritual gifts, and especially that you may prophesy. [^2^](javascript:void(0))For those who speak in a tongue do not speak to other people but to God; for nobody understands them, since they are speaking mysteries in the Spirit. [^3^](javascript:void(0))On the other hand, those who prophesy speak to other people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation. [^4^](javascript:void(0))Those who speak in a tongue build up themselves, but those who prophesy build up the church. [^5^](javascript:void(0))Now I would like all of you to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy. One who prophesies is greater than one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets, so that the church may be built up.

[^6^](javascript:void(0))Now, brothers and sisters,[^b^](javascript:void(0)) if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I speak to you in some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching? [^7^](javascript:void(0))It is the same way with lifeless instruments that produce sound, such as the flute or the harp. If they do not give distinct notes, how will anyone know what is being played? [^8^](javascript:void(0))And if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle? [^9^](javascript:void(0))So with yourselves; if in a tongue you utter speech that is not intelligible, how will anyone know what is being said? For you will be speaking into the air. [^10^](javascript:void(0))There are doubtless many different kinds of sounds in the world, and nothing is without sound. [^11^](javascript:void(0))If then I do not know the meaning of a sound, I will be a foreigner to the speaker and the speaker a foreigner to me. [^12^](javascript:void(0))So with yourselves; since you are eager for spiritual gifts, strive to excel in them for building up the church.

[^13^](javascript:void(0))Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray for the power to interpret. [^14^](javascript:void(0))For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unproductive. [^15^](javascript:void(0))What should I do then? I will pray with the spirit, but I will pray with the mind also; I will sing praise with the spirit, but I will sing praise with the mind also. [^16^](javascript:void(0))Otherwise, if you say a blessing with the spirit, how can anyone in the position of an outsider say the "Amen" to your thanksgiving, since the outsider does not know what you are saying? [^17^](javascript:void(0))For you may give thanks well enough, but the other person is not built up. [^18^](javascript:void(0))I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you; [^19^](javascript:void(0))nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind, in order to instruct others also, than ten thousand words in a tongue.

[^20^](javascript:void(0))Brothers and sisters,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) do not be children in your thinking; rather, be infants in evil, but in thinking be adults. [^21^](javascript:void(0))In the law it is written,

"By people of strange tongues

  and by the lips of foreigners

I will speak to this people;

  yet even then they will not listen to me,"

says the Lord. [^22^](javascript:void(0))Tongues, then, are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, while prophecy is not for unbelievers but for believers. [^23^](javascript:void(0))If, therefore, the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your mind? [^24^](javascript:void(0))But if all prophesy, an unbeliever or outsider who enters is reproved by all and called to account by all. [^25^](javascript:void(0))After the secrets of the unbeliever\'s heart are disclosed, that person will bow down before God and worship him, declaring, "God is really among you."

[^26^](javascript:void(0))What should be done then, my friends?^a^ When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up. [^27^](javascript:void(0))If anyone speaks in a tongue, let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn; and let one interpret. [^28^](javascript:void(0))But if there is no one to interpret, let them be silent in church and speak to themselves and to God. [^29^](javascript:void(0))Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said. [^30^](javascript:void(0))If a revelation is made to someone else sitting nearby, let the first person be silent. [^31^](javascript:void(0))For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged. [^32^](javascript:void(0))And the spirits of prophets are subject to the prophets, [^33^](javascript:void(0))for God is a God not of disorder but of peace.

(As in all the churches of the saints, [^34^](javascript:void(0))women should be silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be subordinate, as the law also says. [^35^](javascript:void(0))If there is anything they desire to know, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.[^b^](javascript:void(0)) [^36^](javascript:void(0))Or did the word of God originate with you? Or are you the only ones it has reached?)

[^37^](javascript:void(0))Anyone who claims to be a prophet, or to have spiritual powers, must acknowledge that what I am writing to you is a command of the Lord. [^38^](javascript:void(0))Anyone who does not recognize this is not to be recognized. [^39^](javascript:void(0))So, my friends,[^c^](javascript:void(0)) be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues; [^40^](javascript:void(0))but all things should be done decently and in order.

[**15**](javascript:void(0)) Now I would remind you, brothers and sisters,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) of the good news[^b^](javascript:void(0)) that I proclaimed to you, which you in turn received, in which also you stand, [^2^](javascript:void(0))through which also you are being saved, if you hold firmly to the message that I proclaimed to you---unless you have come to believe in vain.

[^3^](javascript:void(0))For I handed on to you as of first importance what I in turn had received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures, [^4^](javascript:void(0))and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the scriptures, [^5^](javascript:void(0))and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. [^6^](javascript:void(0))Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers and sisters^a^ at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have died.[^c^](javascript:void(0)) [^7^](javascript:void(0))Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles. [^8^](javascript:void(0))Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. [^9^](javascript:void(0))For I am the least of the apostles, unfit to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. [^10^](javascript:void(0))But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me has not been in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them---though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me. [^11^](javascript:void(0))Whether then it was I or they, so we proclaim and so you have come to believe.

[^12^](javascript:void(0))Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say there is no resurrection of the dead? [^13^](javascript:void(0))If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised; [^14^](javascript:void(0))and if Christ has not been raised, then our proclamation has been in vain and your faith has been in vain. [^15^](javascript:void(0))We are even found to be misrepresenting God, because we testified of God that he raised Christ---whom he did not raise if it is true that the dead are not raised. [^16^](javascript:void(0))For if the dead are not raised, then Christ has not been raised. [^17^](javascript:void(0))If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins. [^18^](javascript:void(0))Then those also who have died^c^ in Christ have perished. [^19^](javascript:void(0))If for this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are of all people most to be pitied.

[^20^](javascript:void(0))But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who have died.^c^ [^21^](javascript:void(0))For since death came through a human being, the resurrection of the dead has also come through a human being; [^22^](javascript:void(0))for as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ. [^23^](javascript:void(0))But each in his own order: Christ the first fruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ. [^24^](javascript:void(0))Then comes the end,[^d^](javascript:void(0)) when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, after he has destroyed every ruler and every authority and power. [^25^](javascript:void(0))For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. [^26^](javascript:void(0))The last enemy to be destroyed is death. [^27^](javascript:void(0))For "God[^a^](javascript:void(0)) has put all things in subjection under his feet." But when it says, "All things are put in subjection," it is plain that this does not include the one who put all things in subjection under him. [^28^](javascript:void(0))When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who put all things in subjection under him, so that God may be all in all.

[^29^](javascript:void(0))Otherwise, what will those people do who receive baptism on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf?

[^30^](javascript:void(0))And why are we putting ourselves in danger every hour? [^31^](javascript:void(0))I die every day! That is as certain, brothers and sisters,[^b^](javascript:void(0)) as my boasting of you---a boast that I make in Christ Jesus our Lord. [^32^](javascript:void(0))If with merely human hopes I fought with wild animals at Ephesus, what would I have gained by it? If the dead are not raised,

"Let us eat and drink,

  for tomorrow we die."

[^33^](javascript:void(0))Do not be deceived:

"Bad company ruins good morals."

[^34^](javascript:void(0))Come to a sober and right mind, and sin no more; for some people have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.

[^35^](javascript:void(0))But someone will ask, "How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?" [^36^](javascript:void(0))Fool! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies. [^37^](javascript:void(0))And as for what you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare seed, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain. [^38^](javascript:void(0))But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body. [^39^](javascript:void(0))Not all flesh is alike, but there is one flesh for human beings, another for animals, another for birds, and another for fish. [^40^](javascript:void(0))There are both heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is one thing, and that of the earthly is another. [^41^](javascript:void(0))There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; indeed, star differs from star in glory.

[^42^](javascript:void(0))So it is with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable, what is raised is imperishable. [^43^](javascript:void(0))It is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness, it is raised in power. [^44^](javascript:void(0))It is sown a physical body, it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a physical body, there is also a spiritual body. [^45^](javascript:void(0))Thus it is written, "The first man, Adam, became a living being"; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. [^46^](javascript:void(0))But it is not the spiritual that is first, but the physical, and then the spiritual. [^47^](javascript:void(0))The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is[^c^](javascript:void(0)) from heaven. [^48^](javascript:void(0))As was the man of dust, so are those who are of the dust; and as is the man of heaven, so are those who are of heaven. [^49^](javascript:void(0))Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we will[^d^](javascript:void(0)) also bear the image of the man of heaven.

[^50^](javascript:void(0))What I am saying, brothers and sisters,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) is this: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. [^51^](javascript:void(0))Listen, I will tell you a mystery! We will not all die,[^b^](javascript:void(0)) but we will all be changed, [^52^](javascript:void(0))in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed. [^53^](javascript:void(0))For this perishable body must put on imperishability, and this mortal body must put on immortality. [^54^](javascript:void(0))When this perishable body puts on imperishability, and this mortal body puts on immortality, then the saying that is written will be fulfilled:

"Death has been swallowed up in victory."

[^55^](javascript:void(0))"Where, O death, is your victory?

   Where, O death, is your sting?"

[^56^](javascript:void(0))The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. [^57^](javascript:void(0))But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

[^58^](javascript:void(0))Therefore, my beloved,[^c^](javascript:void(0)) be steadfast, immovable, always excelling in the work of the Lord, because you know that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.

[**16**](javascript:void(0)) Now concerning the collection for the saints: you should follow the directions I gave to the churches of Galatia. [^2^](javascript:void(0))On the first day of every week, each of you is to put aside and save whatever extra you earn, so that collections need not be taken when I come. [^3^](javascript:void(0))And when I arrive, I will send any whom you approve with letters to take your gift to Jerusalem. [^4^](javascript:void(0))If it seems advisable that I should go also, they will accompany me.

[^5^](javascript:void(0))I will visit you after passing through Macedonia---for I intend to pass through Macedonia---[^6^](javascript:void(0))and perhaps I will stay with you or even spend the winter, so that you may send me on my way, wherever I go. [^7^](javascript:void(0))I do not want to see you now just in passing, for I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits. [^8^](javascript:void(0))But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, [^9^](javascript:void(0))for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.

[^10^](javascript:void(0))If Timothy comes, see that he has nothing to fear among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord just as I am; [^11^](javascript:void(0))therefore let no one despise him. Send him on his way in peace, so that he may come to me; for I am expecting him with the brothers.

[^12^](javascript:void(0))Now concerning our brother Apollos, I strongly urged him to visit you with the other brothers, but he was not at all willing[^d^](javascript:void(0)) to come now. He will come when he has the opportunity.

[^13^](javascript:void(0))Keep alert, stand firm in your faith, be courageous, be strong. [^14^](javascript:void(0))Let all that you do be done in love.

[^15^](javascript:void(0))Now, brothers and sisters,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) you know that members of the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia, and they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints; [^16^](javascript:void(0))I urge you to put yourselves at the service of such people, and of everyone who works and toils with them. [^17^](javascript:void(0))I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus, because they have made up for your absence; [^18^](javascript:void(0))for they refreshed my spirit as well as yours. So give recognition to such persons.

[^19^](javascript:void(0))The churches of Asia send greetings. Aquila and Prisca, together with the church in their house, greet you warmly in the Lord. [^20^](javascript:void(0))All the brothers and sisters^a^ send greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss.

[^21^](javascript:void(0))I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. [^22^](javascript:void(0))Let anyone be accursed who has no love for the Lord. Our Lord, come\![^b^](javascript:void(0)) [^23^](javascript:void(0))The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. [^24^](javascript:void(0))My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus.[^c^](javascript:void(0))

[1.1](javascript:void(0))--[3](javascript:void(0)): Prescript and Greeting. The prescript of Paul\'s letters has the same form found in many papyrus letters of antiquity: the names of the sender and the addressees, with a short greeting. [1](javascript:void(0)): "Paulos" is the Greek form of a Latin cognomen ("Paulus"), meaning "small, of little significance," perhaps a self-deprecatory nickname expressing the apostle\'s sense of humility. Paul\'s sense of being *called* as *an apostle* is vividly described in Gal 1.15--16. *Christ* is not part of the proper name of *Jesus*, but is the Gk translation of Heb *mashiaḥ*, "the anointed," that is, the Messiah; Paul is the emissary of Messiah Jesus. It is not certain whether *Sosthenes* named here as a Christian *brother* is the same person as the synagogue president of Acts 18.17. [2](javascript:void(0)): *Church of God* (Gk "ekklesia theou") may be a translation of Heb *qahal Yahweh* ("assembly of Yahweh") expressing a sense of divine election; but "ekklesia" was the designation of the city "assembly" of Corinth, so that *church of God* may have evoked a sense of belonging to an alternative community. [2b](javascript:void(0)): This phrase is likely a gloss added to the prescript in order to make Paul\'s advice applicable to *all those who in every place call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ*, an indication that the original letter has been edited. [3](javascript:void(0)): The greeting *grace and peace* derives from older Jewish formulas (see *Apoc. Bar.* 78.2), but embodies the essence of Paul\'s own experience of God in Christ.

[1.4](javascript:void(0))--[9](javascript:void(0)): Thanksgiving. The thanksgiving is a standard feature of the prescripts of Paul\'s letters, comparable to the assurance of prayer for the addressees of other ancient letters. [4](javascript:void(0)): Paul gives thanks for the *grace of God ... given* to the Corinthians, not for their "labor of love" as in 1 Thess 1.3. [5](javascript:void(0)): Because *speech* and *knowledge* are attainments of which the Corinthians are proud (1.17; 8.1--2; 13.1--2), Paul\'s selective mention of these gifts has an ironic quality, enhanced by the hyperbolic phrases, *in every way ... of every kind.* [8](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s assurance that God *will ... strengthen* the Corinthians contains a mild reproach of their instability. *The day of our Lord* is an apocalyptic term for the day of judgment; see 3.13; 4.5.

[1.10](javascript:void(0))--[17](javascript:void(0)): Divisions in the church. Paul describes the situation in the church of Corinth in terms also used by political orators to characterize conflicts within city-states: *divisions* and *quarrels* are synonyms for discord, and Paul\'s appeal to *be in agreement* and *be united in the same mind and the same purpose* echoes the language of speeches on concord. [11](javascript:void(0)): Mention of *Chloe* without introduction indicates that she and her *people* (probably slaves) were known to the Corinthians and that she probably lived in Corinth. [12](javascript:void(0)): Paul caricatures the Corinthians' partisanship using slogans like those shouted by fans of star performers in the amphitheater. *Apollos*, from Alexandria in Egypt, was an eloquent early Christian preacher according to Acts 18.24--28; see also 1 Cor 3.4--6; 4.6; 16.12. *Cephas*, the Aramaic form of Peter\'s name. The climactic slogan, *I belong to Christ*, is added for ironic effect, and does not indicate the existence of a "Christ-party." [13](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s rhetorical question, *Has Christ been divided?* uses a verb related to a common Greek term for "party": "Has the body of Christ been split into parties?" [14](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s thanksgiving that he *baptized none ... except Crispus and Gaius* has a note of irony which suggests that Crispus and Gaius may have been involved in forming factions. *Crispus* is the former synagogue president (Acts 18.8), while *Gaius* is described as "the host ... to the whole church" (Rom 16.23); both are evidently of high social standing. [16](javascript:void(0)): Paul employs the device of a feigned lapse of memory to separate *Stephanas*, his strongest supporter (see 16.15--18), from Crispus and Gaius. [17](javascript:void(0)): Paul formulates his commission as an apostle antithetically: *not to baptize but to proclaim*. The negative definition of the style and content of Paul\'s preaching (*not with eloquent wisdom*) suggests that the Corinthians have found Paul\'s proclamation deficient.

[1.18](javascript:void(0))--[2.5](javascript:void(0)): The folly of the message about the cross. Paul acknowledges that his preaching is *foolishness* to the educated elite, but asserts that God has confounded the *wisdom* of this world. [18](javascript:void(0)): Paul provocatively reduces the content of the gospel to a single, shameful event---*the cross*. Greek "moria" (*foolishness*) has a social stigma that does not attach to English "folly": better, "a vulgar joke." *The message about the cross*, lit. "the word of the cross." [19](javascript:void(0)): Isa 29.14 (LXX). This text is particularly apt, since it critiques those who take pride in wisdom and foretells the creation of a new order in which the deaf will hear and the blind will see. [20](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s rhetorical questions mock the educated elite by means of culturally specific titles of dignity: the Jewish *scribe* is not merely a skilled copyist but an expert in the scriptures; the *debater* is a philosophical researcher highly esteemed in the Hellenic world. [21](javascript:void(0)): Paul shapes a playful contrast between two types of *wisdom*: on the one hand, a divine attribute; on the other, a human attainment (cf. Sir 1.9--10; Wis 7; 8). [22](javascript:void(0)): The *desire* for *wisdom* among the *Greeks* was proverbial: see Herodotus 4.77.1. [23](javascript:void(0)): The first-century bce orator Cicero attests the constraint upon discourse about the cross among persons of higher social class: "The mere mention of the word 'cross' is shameful to a Roman citizen and a free man" (*Pro Rabirio* 5.16). [24](javascript:void(0))--[25](javascript:void(0)): In formulating the paradox of the *crucified Christ* as *the power* and *wisdom of God*, Paul employs phrases that sound positively blasphemous---*God\'s foolishness ... God\'s weakness*. [26](javascript:void(0))--[31](javascript:void(0)): Paul expounds the social consequences of the divine reversal of wisdom and foolishness. [26](javascript:void(0))--[28](javascript:void(0)): The terms used by Paul to describe the makeup of the community are those employed by Greek writers to designate the major class divisions in civil strife: *wise, powerful*, and *of noble birth* are euphemisms for "the rich," while "the poor" are the *foolish, weak*, and *low* (born). Paul offers a radical explanation of why the majority of those who have been "called" by the gospel of the crucified are persons lacking in education, wealth, and birth: *God chose* (repeated three times for emphasis). [31](javascript:void(0)): Jer 9.23. [2.1](javascript:void(0))--[5](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s concession that he did not preach *in lofty words or wisdom* is a rejoinder to an anticipated objection against his assertion that the *crucified Christ* is the wisdom of God: "But little wisdom or eloquence was apparent when you came preaching among us!" Paul adopts the persona of the befuddled orator from comedy and mime in order to establish that, despite his stammering *weakness*, the message about Christ is *the power of God*. Paul\'s choice of terms belonging to the technical vocabulary of Hellenistic rhetoric (*lofty words, plausible words, demonstration, power*) marks a contrast between his proclamation and that of missionary rivals who have made use of the art of rhetoric. [2](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s use of the perfect participle, *crucified*, to describe more precisely the Christ whom he proclaims is a provocation to the elite: Paul insists that the present significance of Christ, even after his resurrection, consists in nothing other than that he is the crucified.

[2.6](javascript:void(0))--[16](javascript:void(0)): The wisdom Paul teaches. Paul\'s claim that he speaks *wisdom among the mature* is perplexing, in light of his previous assertion that he preaches the gospel without eloquent wisdom (1.17; 2.1,4). The seeming contradiction is resolved if 2.6--16 is regarded as Paul\'s self-parody as a teacher imparting *secret wisdom* to initiates. The brilliance of this strategy is that, by mocking himself and his proclamation, Paul undermines the idea that an apostle is a wise man as defined by the elite, while simultaneously asserting the existence of a paradoxical wisdom capable of transforming those who receive it, despite the ineptitude of its communicators. **[6](javascript:void(0)):** *Mature* (Gk "teleios") is a technical term in the mystery religions, designating one who has been fully initiated. *The rulers of this age* may be spiritual, demonic powers, but more likely are political authorities. **[9](javascript:void(0)):** The source of this citation is uncertain, but may come from the *Apocalypse of Elijah* (thus the second-century ce exegete Origen), cited here as scripture. **[16](javascript:void(0)):** Isa 40.13.

**[3.1](javascript:void(0))--[4.21](javascript:void(0)): Apostles as servants of the Lord.** **[3.1](javascript:void(0))--[4](javascript:void(0)):** Paul chides the Corinthians in a derisive manner for their spiritual immaturity. **[1](javascript:void(0)):** Paul\'s description of the Corinthians as *infants* uses a metaphor from political rhetoric, comparing the factious with quarrelsome children. **[4](javascript:void(0)):** The reduction in the number of slogans from the four of 1.12 to two, *"I belong to Paul," "I ... to Apollos,"* suggests that Apollos is the focus of the Corinthians' partisanship.

**[3.5](javascript:void(0))--[4.5](javascript:void(0)):** In a series of well-constructed metaphors, Paul portrays himself and Apollos as farm workers (3.6--9), construction laborers (3.9--15), and household stewards (4.1--5), in order to emphasize collegiality against partisanship, and to diminish the importance attributed to them. **[3.5](javascript:void(0)):** Both Paul and Apollos have been *assigned* positions as *servants* by *the Lord*. **[6](javascript:void(0)):** The one who *planted* has priority over the one who has *watered*, and a greater claim upon the produce. **[10](javascript:void(0)):** Paul is a *skilled master builder* (Gk "sophos architekton," a technical term of construction work) who has laid the *foundation* of the community, while Apollos is, figuratively, one of the anonymous workers (*someone*) who has added something to the structure. **[13](javascript:void(0)):** *The Day*, the day of judgment; see 1.8n.**[15](javascript:void(0)):** The expression *as through fire* is a common Greek idiom describing a narrow escape from danger: as the fire ignites, the workers escape from the legal penalty to be imposed upon their shoddy construction by running through the walls of the burning building. **[19](javascript:void(0)):** Job 5.12--13. **[20](javascript:void(0)):** Ps 94.11. **[22](javascript:void(0)):** *Paul ... Apollos ... Cephas*, see 1.12n. **[4.3](javascript:void(0)):** Paul\'s indifference to the possibility that he may be *judged* by the Corinthians employs a Greek verb ("anakrinein") with a technical usage for the preliminary examination of political leaders to establish their qualifications, suggesting that the Corinthians plan to "examine" Paul\'s apostolic credentials. **[5](javascript:void(0)):** *Before the Lord comes*, see 1.8n.; 3.13.

**[4.6](javascript:void(0))--[13](javascript:void(0)): Application.** **[6](javascript:void(0)):** Paul makes clear that he has been teaching with the aid of figures of speech *applied* to himself and Apollos (see 1.12n.). *"Nothing beyond what is written"* is a maxim of uncertain origin whose meaning must be pertinent to the following clause, *so that none of you will be puffed up.* **[7](javascript:void(0))--[8](javascript:void(0)):** With mounting sarcasm, Paul mocks the pretensions of leading figures in the Corinthian church (*king* was the client\'s term for a rich patron). Paul ironically reminds these patrons that everything they *have* (spiritually) they have *received* as a *gift*; they have nothing of which to *boast*. **[9](javascript:void(0))--[13](javascript:void(0)):** Paul expounds the consequences of the message about the cross for himself and his colleagues, who have conformed their lives to the fate of the crucified Christ: they are *fools* (Gk "moroi") in a *spectacle* (Gk "theatron") *exhibited* by God. Paul\'s vocabulary is explicitly theatrical: like the poor fools in the mime, Paul and his colleagues are *weak, hungry, poorly clothed, beaten* (literally, "given the knuckle-sandwich"), etc. **[13](javascript:void(0)):** *Rubbish* and *dregs* were the worst terms of abuse in Greek, originally applied to those unfortunate persons, mostly paupers and the deformed, who were put to death for the purification of the city.

**[4.14](javascript:void(0))--[21](javascript:void(0)): Admonition.** Paul portrays himself as a solicitous *father*, the Corinthians as unruly *children*, and other ministers of the gospel as *guardians* (Gk "paidagogoi"). That Paul is not altogether pleased with the performance of the guardians is suggested by his hyperbolic reference to their number, *ten thousand*, and by the need for parental intervention. If the Corinthians will not accept instruction from *faithful Timothy* (see Acts 18.5), Paul will come with his *stick* (Gk "rabdos"), standard equipment of the fool in the mime. Paul\'s warning to the Corinthians is imbued with an ironic consciousness of the possibility of his own discomfiture.

**[5.1](javascript:void(0))--[13](javascript:void(0)): Sexual immorality in the community.** **[1](javascript:void(0)):** The expression *father\'s wife* is an idiom for "stepmother." Paul accurately reports that sexual relations with one\'s stepmother were prohibited by biblical law (Lev 18.7--8; 20.11; Deut 22.30) as well as by Roman law; according to the *Institutes of Gaius*, "neither can I marry her who has previously been my mother-in-law ... or stepmother" (1.63) **[2](javascript:void(0)):** That the church had taken no disciplinary action suggests that the sinner was a person of high social status. **[3](javascript:void(0))--[5](javascript:void(0)):** While it is not clear precisely what was involved in the execution of this sentence, Paul\'s language (*hand this man over to Satan*) indicates a punishment that was drastic and permanent, such as excommunication. **[5](javascript:void(0)):** *Flesh* for Paul does not refer to the human body but to an instinct toward sin, a way of life unredeemed by the spirit and oriented toward worldly advantages. *The day of the Lord*, see 1.8n. **[6](javascript:void(0))--[8](javascript:void(0)):** Paul\'s metaphor compares immorality in the community with *old yeast* which must be cleansed from the house in preparation for the Jewish festival of Passover, when only *unleavened* bread was to be eaten (Ex 12.15--20). **[7](javascript:void(0)):** Paul nowhere else describes *Christ* as *our paschal lamb*; but cf. Jn 1.29; 19.36; Rev 5.12. **[9](javascript:void(0))--[13](javascript:void(0)): Clarifying a misunderstanding**. **[9](javascript:void(0)):** Defenders of the unity of 1 Corinthians assume that the *letter* to which Paul refers has been lost. But would the Corinthians have treated one of Paul\'s letters with such disregard? Alternatively, the letter may be preserved in 1 Cor 10.1--22; 6.12--20; 10.23--11.34, passages which discuss association with the immoral and idolaters; see further Introduction, pp. [1637--38](javascript:void(0)). **[13](javascript:void(0)):** *Drive out the wicked person*, following the instructions of Deut 13.5; 17.7; etc.

**[6.1](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0)): Lawsuits between believers.** Someone *dares* to do what should be unthinkable for a Christian: *to take another* Christian *to court before the unrighteous*. **[1](javascript:void(0)):** The phrase *has a grievance against another* employs a technical expression of legal proceedings frequently attested in Greek sources. In general, only persons of more than moderate wealth had access to the courts. **[2](javascript:void(0)):** For the idea that *the saints* (the believers) *will judge the world*, see Dan 7.22 (LXX); Wis 3.8; Rev 3.21; 20.4. **[3](javascript:void(0)):** That the angels themselves are subject to judgment, see Jude 6; 2 Pet 2.4. **[4](javascript:void(0)):** The lawsuits in question seem to have been *ordinary* civil *cases*, concerned with money or property. **[7](javascript:void(0)):** Paul\'s advice resembles that of Jesus in Mt 5.39--40; Lk 6.28--30: nonresistance. **[9](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0)):** Catalogues of vices and virtues are known from Jewish and Greek writers, especially the Stoic philosophers. **[9](javascript:void(0)):** *Male prostitutes* (Gk "malakoi," lit., "soft men") were boys and men sodomized by other males, while *sodomites* (Gk "arsenokoitai," lit., "men who bed males"; a word first found here and based on LXX Lev 18.22; 20.13) were men who exercised the dominant role, pederasts.

[6.12](javascript:void(0))--[20](javascript:void(0)): Christians going to prostitutes. The abrupt beginning of 6.12, and differences of tone and content with 5.1--6.11, suggest that this paragraph originally belonged not here but possibly between 10.22 and 10.23, with which 6.12--20 has much in common: in both passages, the temptation to immorality is strong and Christians are urged to "flee" (6.18; 10.8,14); in both passages, Paul quotes the Corinthian slogan, *"All things are lawful for me"* (6.12; 10.23). [12](javascript:void(0)): Paul quotes a slogan of the Corinthians, a proud boast of freedom, asserting liberation from cultural taboos. Paul counters by insisting upon the mutually *beneficial* as the criterion of moral judgment. [13](javascript:void(0)): Another slogan of the Corinthians, with a background in Cynic philosophy. Paul counters by affirming God\'s power over the body. [14](javascript:void(0)): The resurrection of Jesus signals that the body is not meant for corruption but for ongoing life. [15](javascript:void(0)): Paul appeals to his characteristic idea of the church as the body of Christ (see 12.12--14,27) in order to exclude the possibility of contact with a dangerous polluting agent, the *prostitute*. [16](javascript:void(0)): Gen. 2.24. [18](javascript:void(0)): Cf. 10.14 (5.9). That *the fornicator sins against* himself, against his own person (reflected in his *body*), is an idea with Stoic parallels. [19](javascript:void(0)): Like the community as a whole (cf. 3.16), each believer is *a temple of the Holy Spirit*. [20](javascript:void(0)): Paul draws upon the custom of sacred manumission: the slave whose freedom was *bought with a price* with money previously deposited in the temple treasury was regarded as the property of the god.

[7.1](javascript:void(0))--[40](javascript:void(0)): Marriage and sexual relations. In response to the Corinthians' questions, Paul rethinks the most basic relationships, with the result that marriage as well as other marks of social status are relativized in importance by the eschatological "calling" from the Lord. [1](javascript:void(0)): *Now concerning*, a formula introducing the first of several topics about which the Corinthians had queried Paul in their letter; see also 7.25; 8.1; 12.1; 16.1; 16.12. The words *"It is well for a man not to touch a woman"* are a quotation from the Corinthians' letter. *Touch* is an idiom for "have sex with." The quotation may be an expression of extreme asceticism, or may represent an ironic retort by those who claimed freedom from conventional morality (6.12n.) to Paul\'s warning against immorality in his previous letter. [2](javascript:void(0)): Against the temptation to immorality, Paul counsels monogamy and fidelity in marriage; cf. 1 Thess 4.3--5. [3](javascript:void(0)): *Conjugal rights*, lit., "debt," used here in a technical and euphemistic sense, to denote the obligation of spouses to each other. [4](javascript:void(0)): That the partnership of marriage includes the bodies of the husband and wife was also affirmed by the Stoic philosopher Musonius. [5](javascript:void(0)): Paul warns rather strongly (*deprive* is literally "defraud") against withholding conjugal relations and allows for exceptions only within limits---*by* harmonious *agreement*, for a season, *to devote* oneself *to prayer* (cf. *T*. *Naph*. 8). [6](javascript:void(0)): To avoid the impression that he commands sexual relations within marriage, Paul clarifies the point of his previous statement: he has spoken *by way of concession*, to prevent temptation on account of *lack of self-control*. [7](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s *wish* is that all were as he is---unmarried (v. 8) yet self-controlled, a state which he regards as a *gift from God*; yet Paul acknowledges that others have different gifts. [8](javascript:void(0))--[9](javascript:void(0)): Paul counsels celibacy *to the unmarried and widows*, unless they are "out of control." Greek writers describe *passion* as an internal burning; love spells in magical papyri send desire into the body of the beloved as "heat." [10](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0)): The *command* of *the Lord* appears to refer to sayings about divorce like those attributed to Jesus in Mk 10.2--12; Mt 5.31--32; 19:3--9. Paul has formulated the command of Jesus in accordance with Roman law under which *the wife* could *divorce her husband*; according to biblical law, divorce was initiated only by the husband (Deut 24.1). To *separate* is a technical term for divorce in Greek sources. [12](javascript:void(0))--[16](javascript:void(0)): Paul offers advice to Christ-believers in mixed marriages. The advice is naturally offered on Paul\'s own authority, because such marriages were not envisioned by Jesus. If the non-Christian is sympathetically disposed to live with the believer, there should be no divorce. [14](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s statement rests upon the notion that "holiness," like "uncleanness," is a quality transferable within relationships; cf. *1 Clem* 46.2. [15](javascript:void(0)): For *peace* as the goal of Christian life, see 2 Cor 13.11; Rom 14.17. [16](javascript:void(0)): The term *save* is used here in the sense of conversion; cf. 1 Pet 3.1--2. [17](javascript:void(0))--[24](javascript:void(0)): Paul inserts a paragraph enunciating his general *rule in all the churches*, of which the preceding advice on marriage has been a special application: the *call* of God does not remove a Christian from his or her situation in society, but intensifies obedience to God in the midst of life. [18](javascript:void(0)): Paul envisions cases of a Jewish convert who might *seek to remove the marks of circumcision*, and of a Gentile convert who might *seek circumcision*, motivated by a desire for social acceptance in either group. [19](javascript:void(0)): Paul insists that *circumcision* and *uncircumcision* amount to *nothing*; what matters is keeping *the commandments of God*; cf. Gal 5.6; 6.15; Rom 2.25--26. [20](javascript:void(0)): Paul plays provocatively with the word "calling" to indicate that something has been added to every *condition*, by virtue of which the Christian can *remain* in his or her calling, yet with a higher vocation. [21](javascript:void(0)): A *slave* should *not be concerned* about his condition. But what if he is able to become free? Paul\'s advice has puzzled interpreters; the Greek literally reads "rather make use of" (the words "your present condition now more than ever" have been supplied by the NRSV translators), with the verb lacking an object in the Greek text, and either "slavery" or "freedom" must be supplied to complete the meaning. The context argues for the latter: if the slave can somehow become free, he or she should *make use* of freedom. [22](javascript:void(0)): The calling *in the Lord* results in a status reversal: the Christian *slave* has become a *freed person* of Christ, while the free man has become *a slave of Christ*. Paul\'s thought moves beyond the Stoic consolation of "inner freedom" and implies changes in social relationship and behavior; see Philem 16. [23](javascript:void(0)): *You were bought with a price* evokes the readers' experience of the large Roman slave market at Corinth. As was the custom in sacred manumission, where the god was imagined to be the purchaser, so Christ has *bought* the Corinthians *with a price*, whether slave or free, so that they should no longer enslave themselves to *human masters*. [25](javascript:void(0))--[38](javascript:void(0)): Whether *virgins* should *marry* must have been a question raised in the Corinthians' letter to Paul, as indicated by the recurrence of the formula *now concerning* (see 7.1n.). [25](javascript:void(0)): Paul acknowledges that the advice that follows is his own *opinion*, since he has *no command of the Lord*; cf. 7.10,12. [26](javascript:void(0)): *The impending crisis* refers to the tribulations expected to occur in the last days before the judgment; see also vv. 29,31. [27](javascript:void(0)): What kind of "bond" is envisioned? Not, evidently, the bond of marriage, but a pledge to preserve the virginity of the young woman, to which the man addressed by Paul has committed himself. [28](javascript:void(0)): Paul reassures the man and his betrothed that the decision to *marry* is no *sin*, should they prove incapable of keeping their pledge to virginity. [29](javascript:void(0))--[31](javascript:void(0)): Paul shares his belief about the foreshortening of time as justification for urging an adjustment in social, emotional, and economic relations. The participle that Paul chooses (*grown short*) to describe what has happened to *time* in the Christ-event is from a verb used elsewhere in Greek literature of the furling of a ship\'s sails, of the folding of a bird\'s wings, of curtains gathered together. An apocalyptic parallel to Paul\'s account of life according to the principle of *as though ... not* is found in 2 Esd 16.41b--44: "Let the one who buys be like the one who will lose; ... those who marry, like those who will have no children." But there are important differences: for Paul, the eschatological rupture occurs in the present, and is immanent to every action, whereas 2 Esdras distinguishes present from future, and distributes the crisis across different actions. [32](javascript:void(0))--[35](javascript:void(0)): Paul wants his converts to be *free from anxieties*. Epictetus counselled the ideal Cynic to avoid the distractions of marriage; but the goal of Paul\'s advice is not philosophical self-mastery but *unhindered devotion to the Lord*. [36](javascript:void(0))--[38](javascript:void(0)): Paul gives particular consideration to a situation which posed a special danger: when the desires of those who have pledged themselves to celibacy threaten to get out of control. In advising marriage in this case, Paul is not compromising his preference for the unmarried state. In Paul\'s hierarchy of virtue, marriage is good, but celibacy is better. [39](javascript:void(0))--[40](javascript:void(0)): The freedom of a Christ-believing widow to remarry is affirmed, with one proviso: that she marry a fellow Christ-believer. Yet Paul judges a widow to be *more blessed* who *remains* unmarried.

[8.1](javascript:void(0))--[13](javascript:void(0)): Eating food offered to idols. [1](javascript:void(0)): The formula *now concerning* (see 7.1n.) indicates that this matter had been raised in the Corinthians' letter to Paul. The background was apparently this: Paul\'s advice in a previous letter (cf. 1 Cor 5.9) to shun the worship of idols (see 1 Cor 10.14--22) proved confusing and difficult for some to follow. What if one were invited to dine in the banquet hall of a sacred precinct? To decline such invitations would be socially disadvantageous (cf. 1 Cor 5.10). In reply, Paul quotes repeatedly from the Corinthians' letter (8.1,4,8), permitting a detailed reconstruction of the social location and religious beliefs of the disputants. *"All of us possess knowledge"* is a quotation from the Corinthians' letter. The content of their knowledge is quoted in 8.4: *"No idol ... really exists."* As a consequence, eating idol meat is a matter of indifference: *"We are no worse off,"* etc. (8.8; but also see further, below). Perhaps the "strong" represented it as their duty to build up the conscience of the "weak," so that they would not cling to superstitious scruples (8.10). In seeking to identify the "strong" and the "weak," one should bear in mind that the poor seldom had meat as part of their diet, except when it was distributed at public religious festivals, whereas the rich could afford to buy meat in the market, and would have received invitations to dine in temples, owing to their social status. [1](javascript:void(0)): Paul counters the emphasis upon religious *knowledge* by exposing its tendency to self-inflation; *love* (Gk "agape") is the constructive force of Christian community, praised in ch 13. [3](javascript:void(0)): Cf. Rom 8.28--30; Gal 4.9; 1 Cor 13.12. [4](javascript:void(0)): The Corinthians' knowledge that *"no idol in the world really exists"* is grounded in the monotheistic faith to which they have been converted; cf. Deut 4.35; 6.4; Wis 7.17; 13.1; 15.2--3. [5](javascript:void(0)): Paul acknowledges not that *many gods* exist, but that they are worshiped as such by others. [6](javascript:void(0)): Paul quotes an early confession; cf. Rom 11.36; Col 1.15--16. [7](javascript:void(0)): Paul confronts the "strong" with the reality that some do not share their enlightened attitude toward the gods. Those who have been *accustomed to idols until now* must be Gentiles rather than Jews. The Greek word translated *conscience* does not correspond to the modern conception of an internal guide to moral conduct in the future, but denotes a past misdeed which causes pain. The "strong" have asserted that their consumption of idol meat did not convict them of any wrongdoing, and have alleged that the *conscience* of other Christians is *weak* for harboring such scruples. Paul appropriates the term *conscience* from the "strong" and uses it to express his own true concern that someone for whom the *so-called gods* (v. 5) have existence might be *defiled* by eating *food offered to an idol*. [8](javascript:void(0)): The entire verse is another quotation from the Corinthians' letter, despite the NRSV\'s punctuation. [9](javascript:void(0)): The Greek word translated *liberty* has a meaning closer to "authority" or "right," as in 9.4--6,12,18. [10](javascript:void(0)): The situation envisioned here is illustrated by the temple of Asclepius at Corinth, which had three dining rooms on the east side of the courtyard. [11](javascript:void(0))--[12](javascript:void(0)): Paul formulates a radical conclusion regarding the relationship between *knowledge* and love: the proper object of religious concern is not an abstract truth about God, but *those weak believers for whom Christ died*. [13](javascript:void(0)): Paul formulates a general principle of Christian ethics: self-limiting regard for others.

[9.1](javascript:void(0))--[27](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s defense of his means of subsistence, with implications for his legitimacy as an apostle. As if to illustrate the principle of renunciation articulated in 8.13, Paul launches into a spirited defense of his decision not to accept financial support from some at Corinth. The background of the controversy was as follows: while Paul was resident in Corinth, he provided for his own needs by working with his hands (Acts 18.1--3). When other apostles and evangelists subsequently arrived, they accepted patronage from wealthy persons. In retrospect, Paul\'s refusal of support appeared questionable. Did Paul know he was not entitled to support because he was not really an apostle? Moreover, labor of the sort by which Paul sustained himself was viewed as degrading by persons of high social status. These doubts must have found expression in the Corinthians' letter to Paul. [1](javascript:void(0)): *Am I not free?* Paul responds to the insinuation that he is not "free" to evangelize because he is a "slave" of his labor. *An apostle ... seen Jesus*; cf. 15.8; Gal 1.1,11--17. [3](javascript:void(0)): *Defense* (Gk "apologia"), a speech of defense before a court. On plans to *examine* Paul, see the allusion in 4.3--4. [5](javascript:void(0)): *The brothers of the Lord* are Jesus\'s brothers; cf. Mk 6.3; Gal 1.19. *Cephas*, the Aramaic form of Peter\'s name. [6](javascript:void(0)): *Barnabas* was Paul\'s first colleague in mission; see Gal.2.1--10; Acts 9.27; 11.25--26; 13--14. [7](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0)): Why does Paul multiply examples of the exercise of a privilege (by the soldier, the planter, the herder, the priest) about which the Corinthians are in agreement, when it is not his exercise of the privilege which is in dispute, but his renunciation of it? For the key to Paul\'s argumentative strategy, see the following note on vv. 12b--14. [9](javascript:void(0)): Deut. 25.4. [12b](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0)): Paul cleverly reinterprets *the Lord\'s command* as a *right* of which he has *not made use*. Paul\'s critics may have pointed out that, by working as a craftsman, Paul had violated the norms of Christian mission---*that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel*. [14](javascript:void(0)): What *the Lord commanded* refers to a saying like that attributed to Jesus in Lk 10.7. [15](javascript:void(0)): Against those who find his occupation shameful, Paul asserts that it has provided him with *ground for boasting*; see also 2 Cor 11.7--10. [16](javascript:void(0)): Paul represents his preaching as an *obligation* (lit., "necessity"), not a choice; cf. Rom 1.14--15. **[17](javascript:void(0))--[18](javascript:void(0)):** By means of a series of well-chosen economic terms, Paul reverses the values of the Corinthian patrons: *reward* is literally "wages"; *commission* (Gk "oikonomia") is "the work of a household-manager"; *free of charge* is a characteristic of benefactors. Paul\'s point is that evangelists who accept financial support are mere hirelings, whereas he is the true benefactor of the community. **[19](javascript:void(0))--[23](javascript:void(0)):** Paul portrays himself as a populist leader who identifies with the interests of the common people. Paul justifies his self-lowering action *for the sake of the gospel*: by making himself *a slave to all*, he hopes to *save some*. Paul\'s upper-class critics may have regarded him as a demagogue, but the poor and weak would have found his self-presentation appealing. **[24](javascript:void(0))--[27](javascript:void(0)):** In an extended metaphor, Paul compares himself to an athlete in training for the games. His renunciation of financial support should be understood as a form of discipline, an exercise of *self-control*. **[25](javascript:void(0)):** The *perishable wreath* may allude specifically to the winner\'s crown of the Isthmian Games, which was made of pine.

**[10.1](javascript:void(0))--[22](javascript:void(0)): Warning against participation in the worship of idols.** Paul\'s demand for a complete break with polytheistic sacrificial rituals is significantly more rigorous than his advice on food offered to idols in ch 8, suggesting that this passage belonged (with 6.12--20) to the letter on association with the immoral and idolaters mentioned in 5.9--10. Paul\'s admonition takes the form of a typological interpretation of Israel\'s Exodus and wilderness traditions, encouraging the Corinthians to see the danger to their community through the prism of Israel\'s calamitous idolatry. **[1](javascript:void(0)):** The expression *our ancestors* reckons Gentile Christians as belonging to Israel. For Israel *under the cloud*, see Ps 105.39; Wis 10.17; 19.7; on passage *through the sea*, cf. Ex 14.21--22. **[2](javascript:void(0)):** Paul typologically constructs Israel\'s Exodus experience as prefiguring Christian baptism. **[3](javascript:void(0))--[4](javascript:void(0)):** *Spiritual food* refers to the "manna" of Ex 16.15; cf. Ps 78.24--25; *spiritual drink* is the water struck from the rock by Moses in Ex 17.6; Num 20.7--11; cf. Ps 78.15--16. The tradition that the *rock followed* Israel through the wilderness is found in *Tg. Ps.-J.* on Num 20.19. In a stunning typological substitution, Paul explains that *the rock was Christ.* Using a similar hermeneutical maneuver, the first-century ce Jewish interpreter Philo equates the "rock" with "wisdom" and "manna" with the divine "logos" (*Quod deterius* 115--18). **[5](javascript:void(0)):** For the divine punishment of the wilderness generation, see Num 14.29--30; Jude 5; Heb 3.17. **[6](javascript:void(0)):** Paul suggests that *evil desire* is the root of idolatry and immorality; for the background, see Num 11.4--6; Ps 106.14--15. **[7](javascript:void(0)):** Paul quotes Ex 32.6, the only scripture cited explicitly in ch 10, because it epitomizes Paul\'s concern with idolatry and immorality among the Corinthians. **[8](javascript:void(0)):** For the close connection of idolatry with sexual immorality, see *T. Reuben* 4. On the *twenty-three thousand* who died by the plague, cf. Num 25.1--9. **[9](javascript:void(0)):** That Israel *put* God *to the test*, see Ps 78.18; for *destroyed by serpents*, see Num 21.6. **[10](javascript:void(0)):** Num. 16.41,49. **[11](javascript:void(0)):** Paul discerns a deeper "typological" purpose in the *things* that *happened* to Israel. Paul\'s capacity to grasp such correspondences depends upon his eschatological perspective. **[12](javascript:void(0))--[13](javascript:void(0)):** Paul reassures the Corinthians that God *will provide the way out* of the temptation to participate in polytheistic rituals. **[14](javascript:void(0)):** Paul formulates the point of the preceding typological interpretation as an urgent injunction; cf. the similarly formulated warning in 6.18. **[15](javascript:void(0))--[22](javascript:void(0)):** To dissuade the Corinthians from participating in polytheistic rituals, Paul develops an argument that he hopes will appeal to the *sensible*. The argument rests upon the assumption that religious "fellowship" (Gk "koinonia") is mutually exclusive. **[16](javascript:void(0)):** The elasticity of the Greek phrase translated *sharing in* allows both for the social concept "fellowship with" and for the sacramental idea of "participation in" *the blood ... the body of Christ*. **[17](javascript:void(0)):** More than an act of communal sharing, Christ-believers become *one body* through partaking of the *one bread*; cf. 12.13. **[20](javascript:void(0)):** Cf. Deut 32.17. **[21](javascript:void(0)):** Greek papyri furnish examples of invitations to dine upon the "couch" of deities such as lord Sarapis. **[22](javascript:void(0)):** Cf. Deut 32.19,21.

**[10.23](javascript:void(0))--[11.1](javascript:void(0)): Limits upon religious exclusivity.** Paul anticipates objections to his advice to shun idolatry and deals with two ambiguous cases; on the meaning of "conscience," see 8.7n. **[23](javascript:void(0)):** As in 6.12, Paul quotes a Corinthian slogan and counters with consideration of what is *beneficial* and edifying. **[25](javascript:void(0)):** Should all meat *sold in the market* be regarded as idol meat? The question was relevant, because meat markets were often located in the vicinity of temples. **[27](javascript:void(0)):** The *meal* is presumably in the private home of an unbeliever. **[29b](javascript:void(0))--[30](javascript:void(0)):** Because these questions stand in tension with what precedes and follows, some interpreters regard them as the objections of an imaginary interlocutor, while others suggest that they originated as a marginal gloss by one of the "strong" who read Paul\'s letter. **[31](javascript:void(0))--[33](javascript:void(0)):** Paul foregoes consideration of further cases and formulates a general rule of conduct.

**[11.2](javascript:void(0))--[16](javascript:void(0)): Hairstyles in the assembly.** The point at issue is difficult to determine. Paul seems to insist that charismatic women leaders wear the veil, in accordance with Jewish custom. But v. 15 allows that women have their *hair* as a *covering*. Hence, some interpreters construe *unveiled* (vv. 5,13) more generally as "uncovered," in reference to the loose, disheveled hair of women in the ecstatic worship of Dionysus and Cybele. But there is little support for this connection in the text. More interesting than what Paul argues for is what he does not argue against---the Spirit-filled leadership of women. It is assumed that women will *pray* and *prophesy* in the worship assembly (v. 5). **[2](javascript:void(0)):** A problematic beginning: How will Paul *maintain the traditions* in the face of the new social identity given in Christ (cf. Gal 3.28)? **[3](javascript:void(0))--[7](javascript:void(0)):** Paul argues on the basis of a hierarchy of being: *God, Christ, man, woman*. **[4](javascript:void(0)):** Jewish men in the first century did not wear a head-covering; see *Gen. Rab.* 17.8. **[5](javascript:void(0))--[6](javascript:void(0)):** On the potential disgrace of a *woman unveiled* in public, see the comment of Plutarch on Roman custom: "It is more usual for women to go forth in public with their heads covered and men with their heads uncovered" (*Quaestiones Romanae* 267a). For Paul\'s assumption that *it is disgraceful for a woman to have her hair cut* short, it may be relevant that Roman portraiture generally depicts women with long hair braided and wound up around their heads. **[7](javascript:void(0)):** See Gen 1.27. **[8](javascript:void(0))--[9](javascript:void(0)):** An argument from the order of creation; see Gen 2.18--23. **[10](javascript:void(0)):** *The angels* are probably the "sons of God" in Gen 6.2 who had intercourse with mortal women and fathered a race of giants. Like other Jewish writers of the period (e.g., *T. Reuben* 5.6), Paul evidently fears that the angels will be aroused to lust by the sight of exposed women. **[11](javascript:void(0))--[12](javascript:void(0)):** *Nevertheless* indicates that Paul breaks off the preceding argument and moves on to emphasize what is important: *in the Lord* there is mutuality and reciprocity between *woman* and *man*. **[13](javascript:void(0))--[16](javascript:void(0)):** Paul\'s argument having collapsed, he hands the decision over to the Corinthians, invoking a Stoic argument from *nature* and finally appealing to *custom*.

[11.17](javascript:void(0))--[34](javascript:void(0)): Divisions at the Lord\'s Supper. A gulf between the "haves" and the "have-nots" emerged at the very place where the Corinthians should have been most capable of discerning the unity of the body of Christ--- at the Lord\'s Supper. According to the conventions of Greco-Roman dinner parties, the host apportioned the fare according to the status of his guests, reserving the best food and wine for his social equals and intimate friends. [18](javascript:void(0)): The phrase *come together as a church* designates the weekly assembly of all the Christians of Corinth (cf. 14.23; 16.2), a larger gathering of the several subgroups, or "house churches," for the purpose of eating the Lord\'s Supper. The whole church evidently met in the home of Gaius (Rom 16.23). [19](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s assertion that *there have to be factions* may reflect an apocalyptic belief about the tribulation expected in the last days, but also may be meant ironically. [20](javascript:void(0))--[21](javascript:void(0)): The contrast between *the Lord\'s supper* and "the private supper" (NRSV: *your own supper*) makes clear how Paul sees the problem: the privatization of a meal intended for the community. The Greek verb translated *goes ahead* is ambiguous: it may suggest that some (the leisure class) began to eat before others (slaves, laborers) had arrived, but also that some selfishly ate their food while others looked on. In any case, the result is that *one goes hungry and another becomes drunk*. [22](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s question *Do you not have homes?* is heavy with irony against the proprietary class. [23](javascript:void(0))--[26](javascript:void(0)): Paul reminds the Corinthians of the act of self-giving, which established the basis of their fellowship, on the basis of early tradition; cf. Mk 14.12--25. [25](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s reference to *the cup, after supper* presupposes that a meal was served between the bread and the wine. [26](javascript:void(0)): *Until he comes*, see 1.8n. [29](javascript:void(0)): What is meant by *discerning the body*? Probably the gathered church as Christ\'s body. [33](javascript:void(0))--[34](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s counsel that the Corinthians *wait for one another* implies sharing, so as to alleviate the hunger and humiliation of those who have nothing (vv. 21--22).

[12](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0)): On spiritual gifts. Paul counters an overemphasis upon glossolalia (speaking in tongues). Judging from the amount of space devoted to the subject, the gift of tongues must have been highly prized among the Corinthians. Not everyone in the church spoke in tongues (12.30); those who had the gift may have looked down upon those who did not. Paul does not deny the power of speaking in tongues, but interprets that power by ordering the gifts from the greatest (love) to the least (tongues), while affirming that all are necessary for the body of Christ. [12.1](javascript:void(0)): The formula *now concerning* (see 7.1n.) indicates that a question about *spiritual gifts* had been raised in the Corinthians' letter. [3](javascript:void(0)): Paul establishes criteria to determine whether a person is *speaking by the Spirit of God*. Did someone in the church at Corinth actually say *"Jesus be cursed!"* in an ecstatic trance? Did the Corinthians hesitate to expel this person because of an overvaluation of spiritual gifts? [4](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0)): Paul affirms the diversity of *gifts* within unity. [7](javascript:void(0)): The guiding principle should be *the common good*. [8](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0)): The nine named gifts are ranked: first *wisdom*, last *tongues*. [12](javascript:void(0))--[26](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s metaphor of the church as a *body* is derived from Greco-Roman political discourse, where the figure functioned to urge concord. In the well-known fable of Menenius Agrippa, the Roman senator compared a strike by the common people to a revolt of the hands, mouth, and teeth against the belly, resulting in the death of the body. In ancient politics, the body analogy was essentially conservative, portraying the established order as "natural." Paul uses the metaphor subversively to question conventional assumptions about status and honor. [13](javascript:void(0)): Paul alludes to an early baptismal formula; cf. Gal 3.27--28. [14](javascript:void(0))--[21](javascript:void(0)): Ancient philosophers and orators referred to the *hands* and *feet*, the *eyes* and *ears* in elaborating the society-as-body metaphor, but Paul emphasizes mutuality rather than hierarchy. [22](javascript:void(0))--[26](javascript:void(0)): Paul reverses the values of ancient political rhetoric, which figured the parts of the body representing the ruling class, such as the head and the belly, as most honorable and indispensable. Paul claims, scandalously, that the weaker parts are actually more *indispensable* and *honorable*, that we acknowledge this fact when *we clothe* these private parts, and that *God has so arranged the body* in this paradoxical manner, *giving the greater honor to the inferior member*. [27](javascript:void(0)): Paul summarizes the argument and applies it to *the body of Christ* metaphor. [28](javascript:void(0))--[30](javascript:void(0)): Because God has established the diversity of gifts in the body, one should not succumb to the ambition to have others' gifts, or to the tendency to privilege one gift over others.

[13.1](javascript:void(0))--[13](javascript:void(0)): Praise of love. In the context of chs 12--14, Paul\'s encomium of love serves to devalue the gift of tongues by showing the Corinthians a "more excellent way." Yet, ch 13 is self-contained, and the transitions from 12.31 to 13.1 and from 13.13 to 14.1 are weak, so that some scholars conjecture that ch 13 was conceived and written earlier and independently (possibly as an essay for Paul\'s school in Ephesus; cf. Acts 19.9) and reused here because of its relevance. With Paul\'s speech in praise of love, cf. Plato *Symp.* 197c--e. [1](javascript:void(0))--[3](javascript:void(0)): The gifts are *nothing* without *love*. [1](javascript:void(0)): *Tongues of mortals* refers to human speech; *tongues of angels* refers to glossolalia; cf. *T. Job* 48--52; 2 Cor 12.4. Paul\'s comparative terms, *noisy gong* and *clanging cymbal*, are derived from ancient religious rituals; such sounds lack the warmth of love. [3](javascript:void(0)): If the alternative reading *my body to be burned* (textual note *a*) is adopted, Paul is probably referring to the notorious Indian philosophers ("gymnosophists") who immolated themselves to demonstrate their contempt of death. [4](javascript:void(0))--[7](javascript:void(0)): The qualities of love: *patient*, cf. 1 Thess 5.14; Gal 5.22; *kind*, cf. Rom 2.4; *not envious*, cf. 3.3; not *arrogant*, cf. 4.18--19. [5](javascript:void(0)): Cf. 10.33. [8](javascript:void(0))--[13](javascript:void(0)): Paul emphasizes the imperishability of *love*, in contrast to the limitations of *prophecies*, *tongues*, and *knowledge*, which the Corinthians have overvalued. [8](javascript:void(0)): The Greek verb translated *ends* is used elsewhere in reference to the wind: love is like a wind that never "subsides." [12](javascript:void(0)): *In a mirror, dimly*: that is, one does not see the thing itself but only its reflected image. [13](javascript:void(0)): For the triad *faith, hope, and love*, cf. 1 Thess 1.3; 5.8; Col 1.4--5.

[14.1](javascript:void(0))--[40](javascript:void(0)): Prophecy is more edifying than tongues-speaking. [1](javascript:void(0)): *Prophesy*, not in the sense of "predict the future" but "edify" the church, as in v. 3. [2](javascript:void(0)): Paul shares with Plato, Philo, and others the belief in a higher form of Spirit-inspired speech directed to the divine, but incomprehensible to normal human intelligence. [5](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s concession, *I would like all of you to speak in tongues*, reveals the high value that was set upon this gift, and how many Corinthians earnestly strove for it. By declaring that *one who prophesies is greater than one who speaks in tongues*, Paul reverses the hierarchy of speech-types assumed by the elite, elevating the comprehensible above the esoteric. The new criterion of value is whether the community is edified. [6](javascript:void(0))--[12](javascript:void(0)): Paul devalues the esoteric speech of tongues by comparison with the sounds produced *by lifeless instruments*. [13](javascript:void(0))--[19](javascript:void(0)): In praying, singing, and other acts of worship, Paul counsels cooperation between *spirit* and *mind*.
