[16](javascript:void(0)): The word translated *outsider* (Gk "idiotes") means someone untrained, i.e., not adept at understanding those speaking in tongues. [18](javascript:void(0))--[19](javascript:void(0)): As in the case of food (cf. 8.13), Paul adopts the ethical principle of self-limiting regard for others. [20](javascript:void(0))--[25](javascript:void(0)): The Corinthians have been naïve in failing to consider the effects of speaking in tongues upon nonadept believers as well as unbelievers. [21](javascript:void(0)): The point of the citation (not found *in the law*, as Paul says, but in Isa 28.11--12) is that the word of the Lord foretold not only the phenomenon of speaking in tongues but also its failure to convince. [22](javascript:void(0))--[23](javascript:void(0)): For unbelievers, *tongues* are a *sign* opposed and spoken against, leading outsiders to the conclusion that Christ-believers are *out of their minds*. [26](javascript:void(0))--[33a](javascript:void(0)): Paul gives instructions for an orderly procedure involving tongues and prophecy in the worship assembly. [33b](javascript:void(0))--[36](javascript:void(0)): Many scholars regard this passage as a later non-Pauline addition, because it disrupts the flow of the argument from v. 33a to v. 37; it contradicts the assumption of 11.5 that women will pray and prophesy in the assembly; it resembles the viewpoint of the Deutero-Pauline letters (see 1 Tim 2.9--15); it exhibits non-Pauline sentiments, e.g., v. 34b, *as the law also says*; and vv. 34--35 appear after 14.40 in some manuscripts. [37](javascript:void(0))--[40](javascript:void(0)): Assertion of authority and summary of the argument of ch 14.

[15.1](javascript:void(0))--[58](javascript:void(0)): A reasoned proof of the resurrection of the dead. The issue that evokes this argument is identified in v. 12: some of the Corinthians have said, "*There is no resurrection of the dead*." Those Greeks and Romans who were not skeptics about life beyond death tended to believe in the separation of the soul from the body, a belief sanctioned by the oracle at Delphi and popular philosophers. Enlightened persons found the idea of the resurrection of the body laughable; cf. Acts 17.32. Paul constructs an argument for the resurrection of the body on the analogy of the philosophical proof of the immortality of the soul in Plato *Phaedr.* 245c--257d; Cicero *Tusculan Disputations* bk. 1; Plutarch *On the Soul*; etc. The major divisions of Paul\'s discourse are easily recognized and correspond to his philosophical models: 15.1--34, proof of the fact of the resurrection, established by reasoned arguments; and 15.35--58, discussion of the manner of the resurrection and the nature of the resurrection body, culminating in a "mythological hymn." [15.1](javascript:void(0))--[2](javascript:void(0)): Paul reminds the Corinthians that the resurrection faith belongs to the foundation of Christian tradition. [3](javascript:void(0))--[4](javascript:void(0)): Paul quotes an early creed; cf. Rom 4.24--25; 10.9--10; 1 Thess 5.10. The phrase, *he was buried*, is unique to this instance of the creed and may have been added by Paul for the context here. [5](javascript:void(0))--[7](javascript:void(0)): Within the argument of ch 15, the list of witnesses to Christ\'s resurrection, which belonged to the tradition that Paul had received, provides the evidential basis for what follows. [5](javascript:void(0)): *Cephas* is the Aramaic form of Peter\'s name. [8](javascript:void(0)): Paul adds his own witness to the tradition. The term translated *one untimely born* refers to an abortion or miscarriage. Paul may be taking up an insult hurled at him by his opponents. [9](javascript:void(0)): See 9.4--5; 22.4--5; Gal 1.13. [12](javascript:void(0))--[34](javascript:void(0)): The reality of the resurrection of the dead. [13](javascript:void(0))--[19](javascript:void(0)): Paul employs a series of rhetorical syllogisms (*if ... then*) to refute the denial of the resurrection by some at Corinth. [18](javascript:void(0))--[19](javascript:void(0)): Cf. 1 Thess 4.13. [20](javascript:void(0))--[28](javascript:void(0)): Paul argues positively for the resurrection based upon an *order* established by God. [20](javascript:void(0)): *The first fruits* guarantee the harvest to come. [21](javascript:void(0))--[23](javascript:void(0)): For the *Adam--Christ* typology, see also vv. 45--49; Rom 5.12--21. [23](javascript:void(0)): Cf. 1 Thess 4.16. [24](javascript:void(0))--[25](javascript:void(0)): On the apocalyptic scenario envisioned here, cf. 2 Esd 7.29; Rev 20.4--6; *Pirke Eliezer* 11. [24](javascript:void(0)): Cf. Rom 5.17. [25](javascript:void(0)): See Ps 110.1. [26](javascript:void(0)): For the personification of death, see vv. 54--55; 2 Esd 8.55. [27](javascript:void(0)): Ps 8.6. [29](javascript:void(0))--[34](javascript:void(0)): A personal attack on his opponents, appealing to practice, experience, and generally accepted wisdom. [29](javascript:void(0)): It is not clear what was involved in the Corinthian practice of *baptism on behalf of the dead*. Paul appeals to the practice to suggest to the Corinthians that they have an implicit faith in the resurrection. [32](javascript:void(0)): Paul speaks metaphorically, comparing the mortal danger to which he is daily exposed in his apostolic calling with a "beast fight" in the arena of Ephesus, the city from which Paul is writing. The quotation is from Isa 22.13. [33](javascript:void(0)): Paul cites a proverb from a play by the Greek comic writer Menander (third century bce ). [35](javascript:void(0))--[50](javascript:void(0)): The nature of the resurrection body. Through analogies, Paul seeks to show that there can be types of *bodies* other than bodies of *flesh*. [36](javascript:void(0))--[38](javascript:void(0)): The first analogy is drawn from a *seed*; the same analogy is used in Jn 12.24. [39](javascript:void(0)): The second analogy references the different kinds of *flesh* of lower beings. [40](javascript:void(0))--[41](javascript:void(0)): The third analogy points to the difference between *heavenly bodies* and *earthly bodies*, and references the various types of *glory* among celestial bodies. [42](javascript:void(0))--[44](javascript:void(0)): By means of four antitheses, Paul contrasts the resurrected *body* with the present, mortal body. [45](javascript:void(0)): Gen. 2.7. [45](javascript:void(0))--[49](javascript:void(0)): *The first man ... the man of dust* is Adam; the *last Adam ... the second man ... the man of heaven* is Christ; cf. 15.21--23n. [49](javascript:void(0)): Christians will be transformed in the resurrection: they will exchange the *image of the man of dust*, which they currently bear as descendants of Adam, for the *image of the man of heaven*, which they will receive through participation in Christ. [50](javascript:void(0)): Paul clarifies that a resurrection of *flesh and blood* is impossible. [51](javascript:void(0))--[57](javascript:void(0)): Paul discloses a *mystery*, a lyrical account of the destiny of those who survive until the resurrection, a Pauline counterpart to the mythological hymn which concludes philosophical proofs of the immortality of the soul. [52](javascript:void(0)): Cf. 1 Thess 4.16. [54](javascript:void(0)): Isa 25.7. [55](javascript:void(0)): Hos 13.14. [56](javascript:void(0)): A later gloss by an editor reflecting thorough acquaintance with Paul\'s mature theology; cf. Rom 5.12; 7.7--8,13. [58](javascript:void(0)): Concluding exhortation.

[16.1](javascript:void(0))--[24](javascript:void(0)): Advice on administrative and personal matters. [1](javascript:void(0))--[4](javascript:void(0)): Paul gives instructions for the implementation of a charitable *collection* for the poor *saints* (believers) in Jerusalem. See further Gal 2.10; 2 Cor 8--9; Rom 15.25--29. [1](javascript:void(0)): The formula *now concerning* (see 7.1n.) indicates that a question about the collection had been raised in the Corinthians' letter to Paul. [4](javascript:void(0)): *If it seems advisable*, better "if it is considerable"---that is, the size of the collection: Paul will only take the collection to Jerusalem in person if the sum is worth the effort. [5](javascript:void(0))--[8](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s account of his travel plans in this passage contrasts sharply with that in 4.18--19; cf. Acts 19.1, 21--22. [10](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0)): Paul is doubtful whether Timothy (see 4.17n.) will be treated with respect by the Corinthians; thus Paul provides the strongest assurance: *he is doing the work of the Lord*. [12](javascript:void(0)): The formula *now concerning* (see 7.1n.) indicates that the Corinthians had asked about Apollos (see 1.12n.) in their letter to Paul. The eagerness of some in Corinth for Apollos\'s speedy return is illuminated by Acts 18.27--28. [13](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0)): This concluding exhortation signals the end of the letter, after which the paragraph on Stephanas (vv. 15--18) makes a surprising new beginning. [15](javascript:void(0))--[18](javascript:void(0)): Appeal for *recognition* of *Stephanas*. On the *household of Stephanas*, see 1.16n. [15](javascript:void(0)): The direct address, *brothers* (*and sisters*), communicates a sense of urgency. Why should Paul need to appeal for recognition of *the first converts in Achaia* (the principal Roman province of southern Greece)? Evidently Paul assumed that the congregation, or some of its members, had no strong inclination to grant it. The phrase *devoted themselves to the service of the saints* (i.e., the believers) employs some of the same vocabulary used by Paul in describing the charitable collection in 16.1; 2 Cor 8.4; 9.1. [17](javascript:void(0)): *Fortunatus* ("Lucky") and *Achaicus* ("the Achaian") are probably Stephanas\'s slaves of freedmen; their names indicate servile origins. **[19](javascript:void(0)):** On *Aquila* and *Prisca* in *Asia* (Minor), see Acts 18.2,18--21,26. **[20](javascript:void(0)):** The *holy kiss* was a form of early Christian greeting; cf. 1 Thess 5.26; Rom 16.16; 1 Pet 5.14. **[21](javascript:void(0)):** Up to this point Paul had been dictating the letter; now he adds a few words in his *own hand.* **[22](javascript:void(0)):** *Our Lord, come!* An early Christian prayer, in Aramaic, expressing hope in an imminent coming of the Messiah; cf. Rev 22.20.

[^c^](javascript:void(0)) Gk *beloved brothers*

[^d^](javascript:void(0)) Or *it was not at all God's will for him*

[^a^](javascript:void(0)) Gk *brothers*

[^b^](javascript:void(0)) Gk *Marana tha*. These Aramaic words can also be read *Maran atha*, meaning *Our Lord has come*

[^c^](javascript:void(0)) Other ancient authorities add *Amen*

#### 2 Corinthians c. 55 CE

The Second Letter Of Paul To The Corinthians

**Name and Authorship**

Like its canonical predecessor, this letter is named for its addressees, the community of believers in Corinth. A change from 1 Corinthians appears, however, in the opening formula where the addressees are expanded to include "all the saints throughout Achaia." It is "second" in the sense that it follows 1 Corinthians in canonical order, but it is almost certainly not a single continuous letter, but rather two or more letters or fragments of letters combined. The opening names two senders, Paul and Timothy, in a formula analogous to the mention of Paul and Sosthenes in 1 Cor 1.2. Timothy, Paul\'s missionary co-worker, has played an important role in communicating between Paul and the Corinthian congregation, perhaps informing Paul of trouble arising in Corinth after he had sent the letter we call 1 Corinthians. Timothy is mentioned here presumably to fortify Paul\'s appeal, but he is not a coauthor of the letter. Titus, another coworker in the Pauline mission, also appears prominently in the letter as a go-between to restore harmony between Paul and the Corinthians ([2.1](javascript:void(0))--[4](javascript:void(0)),[13](javascript:void(0)); cf. [1 Cor 4.17](javascript:void(0)); [Acts 19.21](javascript:void(0))--[22](javascript:void(0))). Traditional dating ranges from 54 to 57 ce. Second Corinthians was sent from Macedonia five to seven years after Paul\'s original visit to Corinth. At least one letter intervened between Paul\'s writing 1 and 2 Corinthians: the "sorrowful letter" he first mentions in [2.3](javascript:void(0))--[4](javascript:void(0)) (see also [2.9](javascript:void(0)); [7.8](javascript:void(0)),[12](javascript:void(0))). This letter may be lost, or may be incorporated in [2 Cor 10](javascript:void(0))--[13](javascript:void(0)).

**Historical Context**

On the Roman city of Corinth in the first century, see Introduction to 1 Corinthians. The historical circumstances of 2 Corinthians are complicated since it appears to comprise sections of two or more letters that Paul sent to Corinth. Some scholars find four blocks of material, separately composed, from which they construct a narrative of conflict and reconciliation occurring after the receipt of 1 Corinthians while Paul was missionizing between Asia (Ephesus) and Macedonia. The principal events reflected in this theory are a "painful visit" ([2.1](javascript:void(0))) to Corinth by Paul (his second visit), which he followed up with the "sorrowful letter," and subsequently a recovery from crisis illustrated in a later letter of reconciliation, [chs 1](javascript:void(0))--[7](javascript:void(0)). Emphasis on the integrity of the letter, on the other hand, finds two crises shaping the rhetoric of the letter; a first caused by a particular offender and resolved according to the reconciliation in [chs 1](javascript:void(0))--[7](javascript:void(0)), and a second ongoing crisis, still troubling Paul in [chs 10](javascript:void(0))--[13](javascript:void(0)), involving the intrusion of "false apostles," perhaps from Jerusalem ([11.13](javascript:void(0)),[22](javascript:void(0))--[23](javascript:void(0))), who denigrate Paul\'s ministry. Within these blocks are two shorter blocks, 6.14--7.1 and [chs 8](javascript:void(0))--[9](javascript:void(0)), dedicated respectively to issues of purity in the community and monetary matters, especially contributions to Paul\'s collection from his churches for the poor in Jerusalem ([1 Cor 16.1](javascript:void(0))--[4](javascript:void(0)); [Rom 15.26](javascript:void(0))--[27](javascript:void(0)); [Gal 2.10](javascript:void(0))). The purity passage ([6.14](javascript:void(0))--[7.1](javascript:void(0))) is so uncharacteristic of Paul in vocabulary and content that many deem it an interpolation by a later editor. Chapters 8 and 9 both concern the collection, though some argue that they, too, are separate letters. In any event they are consistent with the narrative of conciliation both between Paul and this community and between the Gentile churches and Jerusalem.

**Interpretation**

However one imagines the letter\'s composition, its content reflects with power and pathos the difficulties Paul faced in his missionary work, both in suffering persecutions, beatings, and imprisonments, and, in what seems even more painful to him, the volatile relational crises he negotiated in this nascent, fragile community of believers. Lists of apostolic hardships ([4.7](javascript:void(0))--[12](javascript:void(0)); [6.4](javascript:void(0))--[10](javascript:void(0))), charges of vacillation ([1.15](javascript:void(0))--[18](javascript:void(0))), the pain of a personal affront ([2.5](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0))), and the sting of criticism from intruding missionaries ([10.1](javascript:void(0))--[13.10](javascript:void(0))) reveal the afflicted apostle more vividly than in any other letter. "Afflicted in every way" ([4.8](javascript:void(0)); [7.5](javascript:void(0))), "disputes without and fears within" ([7.8](javascript:void(0))), he writes. In the context of forgiving his offender, Paul reveals a strategy of resisting assaults of every kind for the sake of the community, for "in the presence of Christ," he is not to be "outwitted by Satan: for we are not ignorant of his designs" ([2.10](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0)); cf. [10.3](javascript:void(0)); [11.14](javascript:void(0))). The reconciling action facilitated by Christ\'s presence is further nuanced in [5.16](javascript:void(0))--[21](javascript:void(0)) where the death of Christ is the fulcrum between worlds, the ground of a new way of knowing: "So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new!" ([5.17](javascript:void(0))). Paul\'s life both in the presence of Christ and in Christ makes his afflictions a participation in the reconciling suffering, death, and rising of Christ. The turning of the ages in the death of the "one who died for all, so that those who live might live no longer for themselves" ([5.14](javascript:void(0))) is the theological fundament on which this discourse of reconciliation rests. While reconciliation was present in 1 Corinthians, in 2 Corinthians, where Satan\'s designs persist, Paul\'s apocalyptic appeal.

The letter presents a theological narrative of apostolic affliction, including criticism of Paul within the church, relieved by divine comfort grounded in the suffering, death and resurrection of Jesus. Human suffering, inevitable in the world still enthralled to Satan\'s designs, becomes participation in perception and action in Christ\'s suffering and death and life as "new creation" ([5.17](javascript:void(0))). Living the paradox of power in affliction enables Paul to boast (as a "fool," [11.1](javascript:void(0))--[12.13](javascript:void(0))) in his weaknesses and to characterize his ministry "as having nothing, and yet possessing everything" ([6.10](javascript:void(0))). Interwoven with this basic narrative of God\'s reconciling and creative "yes" in Christ ([1.19](javascript:void(0))) is the story of Paul\'s painful visit to Corinth, his own reconciliation with an offender ([chs 1](javascript:void(0))--[7](javascript:void(0))), along with challenges to his ministry in the presence of false apostles ([chs 10](javascript:void(0))--[12](javascript:void(0))). The lengthy appeal for contributions to the Jerusalem church ([chs 8](javascript:void(0))--[9](javascript:void(0))) registers hope that despite these difficulties, the Corinthians' generous contribution will manifest the "surpassing grace of God" whose "gift" is "indescribable" ([9.14](javascript:void(0))--[15](javascript:void(0))). The letter to the Romans, written from Corinth, confirms that the collection from Macedonia and Corinth was completed. At the time that he wrote Romans, Paul was on his way to deliver that gift to the "saints at Jerusalem" ([Rom 15.25](javascript:void(0))--[29](javascript:void(0))).

*Alexandra R. Brown*

[**1**](javascript:void(0)) Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother,

To the church of God that is in Corinth, including all the saints throughout Achaia:

[^2^](javascript:void(0))Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

[^3^](javascript:void(0))Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, [^4^](javascript:void(0))who consoles us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to console those who are in any affliction with the consolation with which we ourselves are consoled by God. [^5^](javascript:void(0))For just as the sufferings of Christ are abundant for us, so also our consolation is abundant through Christ. [^6^](javascript:void(0))If we are being afflicted, it is for your consolation and salvation; if we are being consoled, it is for your consolation, which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we are also suffering. [^7^](javascript:void(0))Our hope for you is unshaken; for we know that as you share in our sufferings, so also you share in our consolation.

[^8^](javascript:void(0))We do not want you to be unaware, brothers and sisters,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) of the affliction we experienced in Asia; for we were so utterly, unbearably crushed that we despaired of life itself. [^9^](javascript:void(0))Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death so that we would rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead. [^10^](javascript:void(0))He who rescued us from so deadly a peril will continue to rescue us; on him we have set our hope that he will rescue us again, [^11^](javascript:void(0))as you also join in helping us by your prayers, so that many will give thanks on our[^a^](javascript:void(0)) behalf for the blessing granted us through the prayers of many.

[^12^](javascript:void(0))Indeed, this is our boast, the testimony of our conscience: we have behaved in the world with frankness[^b^](javascript:void(0)) and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God---and all the more toward you. [^13^](javascript:void(0))For we write you nothing other than what you can read and also understand; I hope you will understand until the end---[^14^](javascript:void(0))as you have already understood us in part---that on the day of the Lord Jesus we are your boast even as you are our boast.

[^15^](javascript:void(0))Since I was sure of this, I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a double favor;[^c^](javascript:void(0)) [^16^](javascript:void(0))I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and have you send me on to Judea. [^17^](javascript:void(0))Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to ordinary human standards,[^d^](javascript:void(0)) ready to say "Yes, yes" and "No, no" at the same time? [^18^](javascript:void(0))As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been "Yes and No." [^19^](javascript:void(0))For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not "Yes and No"; but in him it is always "Yes." [^20^](javascript:void(0))For in him every one of God\'s promises is a "Yes." For this reason it is through him that we say the "Amen," to the glory of God. [^21^](javascript:void(0))But it is God who establishes us with you in Christ and has anointed us, [^22^](javascript:void(0))by putting his seal on us and giving us his Spirit in our hearts as a first installment.

[^23^](javascript:void(0))But I call on God as witness against me: it was to spare you that I did not come again to Corinth. [^24^](javascript:void(0))I do not mean to imply that we lord it over your faith; rather, we are workers with you for your joy, because you stand firm in the faith.

[**2**](javascript:void(0)) So I made up my mind not to make you another painful visit. [^2^](javascript:void(0))For if I cause you pain, who is there to make me glad but the one whom I have pained? [^3^](javascript:void(0))And I wrote as I did, so that when I came, I might not suffer pain from those who should have made me rejoice; for I am confident about all of you, that my joy would be the joy of all of you. [^4^](javascript:void(0))For I wrote you out of much distress and anguish of heart and with many tears, not to cause you pain, but to let you know the abundant love that I have for you.

[^5^](javascript:void(0))But if anyone has caused pain, he has caused it not to me, but to some extent---not to exaggerate it---to all of you. [^6^](javascript:void(0))This punishment by the majority is enough for such a person; [^7^](javascript:void(0))so now instead you should forgive and console him, so that he may not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. [^8^](javascript:void(0))So I urge you to reaffirm your love for him. [^9^](javascript:void(0))I wrote for this reason: to test you and to know whether you are obedient in everything. [^10^](javascript:void(0))Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive. What I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ. [^11^](javascript:void(0))And we do this so that we may not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.

[^12^](javascript:void(0))When I came to Troas to proclaim the good news of Christ, a door was opened for me in the Lord; [^13^](javascript:void(0))but my mind could not rest because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I said farewell to them and went on to Macedonia.

[^14^](javascript:void(0))But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads in every place the fragrance that comes from knowing him. [^15^](javascript:void(0))For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing; [^16^](javascript:void(0))to the one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things? [^17^](javascript:void(0))For we are not peddlers of God\'s word like so many;[^a^](javascript:void(0)) but in Christ we speak as persons of sincerity, as persons sent from God and standing in his presence.

[**3**](javascript:void(0)) Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Surely we do not need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you or from you, do we? [^2^](javascript:void(0))You yourselves are our letter, written on our[^b^](javascript:void(0)) hearts, to be known and read by all; [^3^](javascript:void(0))and you show that you are a letter of Christ, prepared by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.

[^4^](javascript:void(0))Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God. [^5^](javascript:void(0))Not that we are competent of ourselves to claim anything as coming from us; our competence is from God, [^6^](javascript:void(0))who has made us competent to be ministers of a new covenant, not of letter but of spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

[^7^](javascript:void(0))Now if the ministry of death, chiseled in letters on stone tablets,[^c^](javascript:void(0)) came in glory so that the people of Israel could not gaze at Moses' face because of the glory of his face, a glory now set aside, [^8^](javascript:void(0))how much more will the ministry of the Spirit come in glory? [^9^](javascript:void(0))For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, much more does the ministry of justification abound in glory! [^10^](javascript:void(0))Indeed, what once had glory has lost its glory because of the greater glory; [^11^](javascript:void(0))for if what was set aside came through glory, much more has the permanent come in glory!

[^12^](javascript:void(0))Since, then, we have such a hope, we act with great boldness, [^13^](javascript:void(0))not like Moses, who put a veil over his face to keep the people of Israel from gazing at the end of the glory that[^a^](javascript:void(0)) was being set aside. [^14^](javascript:void(0))But their minds were hardened. Indeed, to this very day, when they hear the reading of the old covenant, that same veil is still there, since only in Christ is it set aside. [^15^](javascript:void(0))Indeed, to this very day whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their minds; [^16^](javascript:void(0))but when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed. [^17^](javascript:void(0))Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. [^18^](javascript:void(0))And all of us, with unveiled faces, seeing the glory of the Lord as though reflected in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another; for this comes from the Lord, the Spirit.

[**4**](javascript:void(0)) Therefore, since it is by God\'s mercy that we are engaged in this ministry, we do not lose heart. [^2^](javascript:void(0))We have renounced the shameful things that one hides; we refuse to practice cunning or to falsify God\'s word; but by the open statement of the truth we commend ourselves to the conscience of everyone in the sight of God. [^3^](javascript:void(0))And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. [^4^](javascript:void(0))In their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God. [^5^](javascript:void(0))For we do not proclaim ourselves; we proclaim Jesus Christ as Lord and ourselves as your slaves for Jesus' sake. [^6^](javascript:void(0))For it is the God who said, "Let light shine out of darkness," who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

[^7^](javascript:void(0))But we have this treasure in clay jars, so that it may be made clear that this extraordinary power belongs to God and does not come from us. [^8^](javascript:void(0))We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; [^9^](javascript:void(0))persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed; [^10^](javascript:void(0))always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made visible in our bodies. [^11^](javascript:void(0))For while we live, we are always being given up to death for Jesus' sake, so that the life of Jesus may be made visible in our mortal flesh. [^12^](javascript:void(0))So death is at work in us, but life in you.

[^13^](javascript:void(0))But just as we have the same spirit of faith that is in accordance with scripture---"I believed, and so I spoke"---we also believe, and so we speak, [^14^](javascript:void(0))because we know that the one who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus, and will bring us with you into his presence. [^15^](javascript:void(0))Yes, everything is for your sake, so that grace, as it extends to more and more people, may increase thanksgiving, to the glory of God.

[^16^](javascript:void(0))So we do not lose heart. Even though our outer nature is wasting away, our inner nature is being renewed day by day. [^17^](javascript:void(0))For this slight momentary affliction is preparing us for an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, [^18^](javascript:void(0))because we look not at what can be seen but at what cannot be seen; for what can be seen is temporary, but what cannot be seen is eternal.

[**5**](javascript:void(0)) For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. [^2^](javascript:void(0))For in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling---[^3^](javascript:void(0))if indeed, when we have taken it off[^a^](javascript:void(0)) we will not be found naked. [^4^](javascript:void(0))For while we are still in this tent, we groan under our burden, because we wish not to be unclothed but to be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. [^5^](javascript:void(0))He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee.

[^6^](javascript:void(0))So we are always confident; even though we know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord---[^7^](javascript:void(0))for we walk by faith, not by sight. [^8^](javascript:void(0))Yes, we do have confidence, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord. [^9^](javascript:void(0))So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. [^10^](javascript:void(0))For all of us must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive recompense for what has been done in the body, whether good or evil.

[^11^](javascript:void(0))Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we try to persuade others; but we ourselves are well known to God, and I hope that we are also well known to your consciences. [^12^](javascript:void(0))We are not commending ourselves to you again, but giving you an opportunity to boast about us, so that you may be able to answer those who boast in outward appearance and not in the heart. [^13^](javascript:void(0))For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you. [^14^](javascript:void(0))For the love of Christ urges us on, because we are convinced that one has died for all; therefore all have died. [^15^](javascript:void(0))And he died for all, so that those who live might live no longer for themselves, but for him who died and was raised for them.

[^16^](javascript:void(0))From now on, therefore, we regard no one from a human point of view;[^a^](javascript:void(0)) even though we once knew Christ from a human point of view,^a^ we know him no longer in that way. [^17^](javascript:void(0))So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new! [^18^](javascript:void(0))All this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ, and has given us the ministry of reconciliation; [^19^](javascript:void(0))that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself,[^b^](javascript:void(0)) not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting the message of reconciliation to us. [^20^](javascript:void(0))So we are ambassadors for Christ, since God is making his appeal through us; we entreat you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God. [^21^](javascript:void(0))For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

[**6**](javascript:void(0)) As we work together with him,[^c^](javascript:void(0)) we urge you also not to accept the grace of God in vain. [^2^](javascript:void(0))For he says,

"At an acceptable time I have listened to you,

  and on a day of salvation I have helped you."

See, now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation! [^3^](javascript:void(0))We are putting no obstacle in anyone\'s way, so that no fault may be found with our ministry, [^4^](javascript:void(0))but as servants of God we have commended ourselves in every way: through great endurance, in afflictions, hardships, calamities, [^5^](javascript:void(0))beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, sleepless nights, hunger; [^6^](javascript:void(0))by purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, holiness of spirit, genuine love, [^7^](javascript:void(0))truthful speech, and the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left; [^8^](javascript:void(0))in honor and dishonor, in ill repute and good repute. We are treated as impostors, and yet are true; [^9^](javascript:void(0))as unknown, and yet are well known; as dying, and see---we are alive; as punished, and yet not killed; [^10^](javascript:void(0))as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing everything.

[^11^](javascript:void(0))We have spoken frankly to you Corinthians; our heart is wide open to you. [^12^](javascript:void(0))There is no restriction in our affections, but only in yours. [^13^](javascript:void(0))In return---I speak as to children---open wide your hearts also.

[^14^](javascript:void(0))Do not be mismatched with unbelievers. For what partnership is there between righteousness and lawlessness? Or what fellowship is there between light and darkness? [^15^](javascript:void(0))What agreement does Christ have with Beliar? Or what does a believer share with an unbeliever? [^16^](javascript:void(0))What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we[^a^](javascript:void(0)) are the temple of the living God; as God said,

"I will live in them and walk among them,

  and I will be their God,

  and they shall be my people.

[^17^](javascript:void(0))Therefore come out from them,

   and be separate from them, says the Lord,

and touch nothing unclean;

  then I will welcome you,

[^18^](javascript:void(0))and I will be your father,

  and you shall be my sons and daughters,

says the Lord Almighty."

[**7**](javascript:void(0)) Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and of spirit, making holiness perfect in the fear of God.

[^2^](javascript:void(0))Make room in your hearts[^b^](javascript:void(0)) for us; we have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one. [^3^](javascript:void(0))I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together. [^4^](javascript:void(0))I often boast about you; I have great pride in you; I am filled with consolation; I am overjoyed in all our affliction.

[^5^](javascript:void(0))For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted in every way---disputes without and fears within. [^6^](javascript:void(0))But God, who consoles the downcast, consoled us by the arrival of Titus, [^7^](javascript:void(0))and not only by his coming, but also by the consolation with which he was consoled about you, as he told us of your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more. [^8^](javascript:void(0))For even if I made you sorry with my letter, I do not regret it (though I did regret it, for I see that I grieved you with that letter, though only briefly). [^9^](javascript:void(0))Now I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because your grief led to repentance; for you felt a godly grief, so that you were not harmed in any way by us. [^10^](javascript:void(0))For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret, but worldly grief produces death. [^11^](javascript:void(0))For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what alarm, what longing, what zeal, what punishment! At every point you have proved yourselves guiltless in the matter. [^12^](javascript:void(0))So although I wrote to you, it was not on account of the one who did the wrong, nor on account of the one who was wronged, but in order that your zeal for us might be made known to you before God. [^13^](javascript:void(0))In this we find comfort.

In addition to our own consolation, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his mind has been set at rest by all of you. [^14^](javascript:void(0))For if I have been somewhat boastful about you to him, I was not disgraced; but just as everything we said to you was true, so our boasting to Titus has proved true as well. [^15^](javascript:void(0))And his heart goes out all the more to you, as he remembers the obedience of all of you, and how you welcomed him with fear and trembling. [^16^](javascript:void(0))I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you.

[**8**](javascript:void(0)) We want you to know, brothers and sisters,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) about the grace of God that has been granted to the churches of Macedonia; [^2^](javascript:void(0))for during a severe ordeal of affliction, their abundant joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part. [^3^](javascript:void(0))For, as I can testify, they voluntarily gave according to their means, and even beyond their means, [^4^](javascript:void(0))begging us earnestly for the privilege[^b^](javascript:void(0)) of sharing in this ministry to the saints---[^5^](javascript:void(0))and this, not merely as we expected; they gave themselves first to the Lord and, by the will of God, to us, [^6^](javascript:void(0))so that we might urge Titus that, as he had already made a beginning, so he should also complete this generous undertaking[^c^](javascript:void(0)) among you. [^7^](javascript:void(0))Now as you excel in everything---in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in utmost eagerness, and in our love for you[^d^](javascript:void(0))---so we want you to excel also in this generous undertaking.^c^

[^8^](javascript:void(0))I do not say this as a command, but I am testing the genuineness of your love against the earnestness of others. [^9^](javascript:void(0))For you know the generous act[^e^](javascript:void(0)) of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich. [^10^](javascript:void(0))And in this matter I am giving my advice: it is appropriate for you who began last year not only to do something but even to desire to do something---[^11^](javascript:void(0))now finish doing it, so that your eagerness may be matched by completing it according to your means. [^12^](javascript:void(0))For if the eagerness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what one has---not according to what one does not have. [^13^](javascript:void(0))I do not mean that there should be relief for others and pressure on you, but it is a question of a fair balance between [^14^](javascript:void(0))your present abundance and their need, so that their abundance may be for your need, in order that there may be a fair balance. [^15^](javascript:void(0))As it is written,

"The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little."

[^16^](javascript:void(0))But thanks be to God who put in the heart of Titus the same eagerness for you that I myself have. [^17^](javascript:void(0))For he not only accepted our appeal, but since he is more eager than ever, he is going to you of his own accord. [^18^](javascript:void(0))With him we are sending the brother who is famous among all the churches for his proclaiming the good news;[^a^](javascript:void(0)) [^19^](javascript:void(0))and not only that, but he has also been appointed by the churches to travel with us while we are administering this generous undertaking[^b^](javascript:void(0)) for the glory of the Lord himself[^c^](javascript:void(0)) and to show our goodwill. [^20^](javascript:void(0))We intend that no one should blame us about this generous gift that we are administering, [^21^](javascript:void(0))for we intend to do what is right not only in the Lord\'s sight but also in the sight of others. [^22^](javascript:void(0))And with them we are sending our brother whom we have often tested and found eager in many matters, but who is now more eager than ever because of his great confidence in you. [^23^](javascript:void(0))As for Titus, he is my partner and co-worker in your service; as for our brothers, they are messengers[^d^](javascript:void(0)) of the churches, the glory of Christ. [^24^](javascript:void(0))Therefore openly before the churches, show them the proof of your love and of our reason for boasting about you.

[**9**](javascript:void(0)) Now it is not necessary for me to write you about the ministry to the saints, [^2^](javascript:void(0))for I know your eagerness, which is the subject of my boasting about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year; and your zeal has stirred up most of them. [^3^](javascript:void(0))But I am sending the brothers in order that our boasting about you may not prove to have been empty in this case, so that you may be ready, as I said you would be; [^4^](javascript:void(0))otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated---to say nothing of you---in this undertaking.[^e^](javascript:void(0)) [^5^](javascript:void(0))So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you, and arrange in advance for this bountiful gift that you have promised, so that it may be ready as a voluntary gift and not as an extortion.

[^6^](javascript:void(0))The point is this: the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully. [^7^](javascript:void(0))Each of you must give as you have made up your mind, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. [^8^](javascript:void(0))And God is able to provide you with every blessing in abundance, so that by always having enough of everything, you may share abundantly in every good work. [^9^](javascript:void(0))As it is written, "He scatters abroad, he gives to the poor;

  his righteousness[^a^](javascript:void(0)) endures forever."

[^10^](javascript:void(0))He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.^a^ [^11^](javascript:void(0))You will be enriched in every way for your great generosity, which will produce thanksgiving to God through us; [^12^](javascript:void(0))for the rendering of this ministry not only supplies the needs of the saints but also overflows with many thanksgivings to God. [^13^](javascript:void(0))Through the testing of this ministry you glorify God by your obedience to the confession of the gospel of Christ and by the generosity of your sharing with them and with all others, [^14^](javascript:void(0))while they long for you and pray for you because of the surpassing grace of God that he has given you. [^15^](javascript:void(0))Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift!

[**10**](javascript:void(0)) I myself, Paul, appeal to you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ---I who am humble when face to face with you, but bold toward you when I am away!---[^2^](javascript:void(0))I ask that when I am present I need not show boldness by daring to oppose those who think we are acting according to human standards.[^b^](javascript:void(0)) [^3^](javascript:void(0))Indeed, we live as human beings,[^c^](javascript:void(0)) but we do not wage war according to human standards;^b^ [^4^](javascript:void(0))for the weapons of our warfare are not merely human,[^d^](javascript:void(0)) but they have divine power to destroy strongholds. We destroy arguments [^5^](javascript:void(0))and every proud obstacle raised up against the knowledge of God, and we take every thought captive to obey Christ. [^6^](javascript:void(0))We are ready to punish every disobedience when your obedience is complete.

[^7^](javascript:void(0))Look at what is before your eyes. If you are confident that you belong to Christ, remind yourself of this, that just as you belong to Christ, so also do we. [^8^](javascript:void(0))Now, even if I boast a little too much of our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for tearing you down, I will not be ashamed of it. [^9^](javascript:void(0))I do not want to seem as though I am trying to frighten you with my letters. [^10^](javascript:void(0))For they say, "His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible." [^11^](javascript:void(0))Let such people understand that what we say by letter when absent, we will also do when present.

[^12^](javascript:void(0))We do not dare to classify or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves. But when they measure themselves by one another, and compare themselves with one another, they do not show good sense. [^13^](javascript:void(0))We, however, will not boast beyond limits, but will keep within the field that God has assigned to us, to reach out even as far as you. [^14^](javascript:void(0))For we were not overstepping our limits when we reached you; we were the first to come all the way to you with the good news[^a^](javascript:void(0)) of Christ. [^15^](javascript:void(0))We do not boast beyond limits, that is, in the labors of others; but our hope is that, as your faith increases, our sphere of action among you may be greatly enlarged, [^16^](javascript:void(0))so that we may proclaim the good news^a^ in lands beyond you, without boasting of work already done in someone else\'s sphere of action. [^17^](javascript:void(0))"Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord." [^18^](javascript:void(0))For it is not those who commend themselves that are approved, but those whom the Lord commends.

[**11**](javascript:void(0)) I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. Do bear with me! [^2^](javascript:void(0))I feel a divine jealousy for you, for I promised you in marriage to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. [^3^](javascript:void(0))But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure[^b^](javascript:void(0)) devotion to Christ. [^4^](javascript:void(0))For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus than the one we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit from the one you received, or a different gospel from the one you accepted, you submit to it readily enough. [^5^](javascript:void(0))I think that I am not in the least inferior to these super-apostles. [^6^](javascript:void(0))I may be untrained in speech, but not in knowledge; certainly in every way and in all things we have made this evident to you.

[^7^](javascript:void(0))Did I commit a sin by humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I proclaimed God\'s good news[^c^](javascript:void(0)) to you free of charge? [^8^](javascript:void(0))I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you. [^9^](javascript:void(0))And when I was with you and was in need, I did not burden anyone, for my needs were supplied by the friends[^d^](javascript:void(0)) who came from Macedonia. So I refrained and will continue to refrain from burdening you in any way. [^10^](javascript:void(0))As the truth of Christ is in me, this boast of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia. [^11^](javascript:void(0))And why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do!

[^12^](javascript:void(0))And what I do I will also continue to do, in order to deny an opportunity to those who want an opportunity to be recognized as our equals in what they boast about. [^13^](javascript:void(0))For such boasters are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. [^14^](javascript:void(0))And no wonder! Even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light. [^15^](javascript:void(0))So it is not strange if his ministers also disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness. Their end will match their deeds.

[^16^](javascript:void(0))I repeat, let no one think that I am a fool; but if you do, then accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. [^17^](javascript:void(0))What I am saying in regard to this boastful confidence, I am saying not with the Lord\'s authority, but as a fool; [^18^](javascript:void(0))since many boast according to human standards,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) I will also boast. [^19^](javascript:void(0))For you gladly put up with fools, being wise yourselves! [^20^](javascript:void(0))For you put up with it when someone makes slaves of you, or preys upon you, or takes advantage of you, or puts on airs, or gives you a slap in the face. [^21^](javascript:void(0))To my shame, I must say, we were too weak for that!

But whatever anyone dares to boast of---I am speaking as a fool---I also dare to boast of that. [^22^](javascript:void(0))Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they descendants of Abraham? So am I. [^23^](javascript:void(0))Are they ministers of Christ? I am talking like a madman---I am a better one: with far greater labors, far more imprisonments, with countless floggings, and often near death. [^24^](javascript:void(0))Five times I have received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one. [^25^](javascript:void(0))Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I received a stoning. Three times I was shipwrecked; for a night and a day I was adrift at sea; [^26^](javascript:void(0))on frequent journeys, in danger from rivers, danger from bandits, danger from my own people, danger from Gentiles, danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea, danger from false brothers and sisters;[^b^](javascript:void(0)) [^27^](javascript:void(0))in toil and hardship, through many a sleepless night, hungry and thirsty, often without food, cold and naked. [^28^](javascript:void(0))And, besides other things, I am under daily pressure because of my anxiety for all the churches. [^29^](javascript:void(0))Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not indignant?

[^30^](javascript:void(0))If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness. [^31^](javascript:void(0))The God and Father of the Lord Jesus (blessed be he forever!) knows that I do not lie. [^32^](javascript:void(0))In Damascus, the governor[^c^](javascript:void(0)) under King Aretas guarded the city of Damascus in order to[^d^](javascript:void(0)) seize me, [^33^](javascript:void(0))but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall,[^e^](javascript:void(0)) and escaped from his hands.

[**12**](javascript:void(0)) It is necessary to boast; nothing is to be gained by it, but I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord. [^2^](javascript:void(0))I know a person in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven---whether in the body or out of the body I do not know; God knows. [^3^](javascript:void(0))And I know that such a person---whether in the body or out of the body I do not know; God knows---[^4^](javascript:void(0))was caught up into Paradise and heard things that are not to be told, that no mortal is permitted to repeat. [^5^](javascript:void(0))On behalf of such a one I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses. [^6^](javascript:void(0))But if I wish to boast, I will not be a fool, for I will be speaking the truth. But I refrain from it, so that no one may think better of me than what is seen in me or heard from me, [^7^](javascript:void(0))even considering the exceptional character of the revelations. Therefore, to keep[^f^](javascript:void(0)) me from being too elated, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to torment me, to keep me from being too elated.[^a^](javascript:void(0)) [^8^](javascript:void(0))Three times I appealed to the Lord about this, that it would leave me, [^9^](javascript:void(0))but he said to me, "My grace is sufficient for you, for power[^b^](javascript:void(0)) is made perfect in weakness."

So, I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me. [^10^](javascript:void(0))Therefore I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities for the sake of Christ; for whenever I am weak, then I am strong.

[^11^](javascript:void(0))I have been a fool! You forced me to it. Indeed you should have been the ones commending me, for I am not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing. [^12^](javascript:void(0))The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with utmost patience, signs and wonders and mighty works. [^13^](javascript:void(0))How have you been worse off than the other churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong!

[^14^](javascript:void(0))Here I am, ready to come to you this third time. And I will not be a burden, because I do not want what is yours but you; for children ought not to lay up for their parents, but parents for their children. [^15^](javascript:void(0))I will most gladly spend and be spent for you. If I love you more, am I to be loved less? [^16^](javascript:void(0))Let it be assumed that I did not burden you. Nevertheless (you say) since I was crafty, I took you in by deceit. [^17^](javascript:void(0))Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? [^18^](javascript:void(0))I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Titus did not take advantage of you, did he? Did we not conduct ourselves with the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps?

[^19^](javascript:void(0))Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves before you? We are speaking in Christ before God. Everything we do, beloved, is for the sake of building you up. [^20^](javascript:void(0))For I fear that when I come, I may find you not as I wish, and that you may find me not as you wish; I fear that there may perhaps be quarreling, jealousy, anger, selfishness, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder. [^21^](javascript:void(0))I fear that when I come again, my God may humble me before you, and that I may have to mourn over many who previously sinned and have not repented of the impurity, sexual immorality, and licentiousness that they have practiced.

[**13**](javascript:void(0)) This is the third time I am coming to you. "Any charge must be sustained by the evidence of two or three witnesses." [^2^](javascript:void(0))I warned those who sinned previously and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again, I will not be lenient---[^3^](javascript:void(0))since you desire proof that Christ is speaking in me. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful in you. [^4^](javascript:void(0))For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we are weak in him,[^c^](javascript:void(0)) but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.

[^5^](javascript:void(0))Examine yourselves to see whether you are living in the faith. Test yourselves. Do you not realize that Jesus Christ is in you?---unless, indeed, you fail to meet the test! [^6^](javascript:void(0))I hope you will find out that we have not failed. [^7^](javascript:void(0))But we pray to God that you may not do anything wrong---not that we may appear to have met the test, but that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed. [^8^](javascript:void(0))For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth. [^9^](javascript:void(0))For we rejoice when we are weak and you are strong. This is what we pray for, that you may become perfect. [^10^](javascript:void(0))So I write these things while I am away from you, so that when I come, I may not have to be severe in using the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.

[^11^](javascript:void(0))Finally, brothers and sisters,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) farewell.[^b^](javascript:void(0)) Put things in order, listen to my appeal,[^c^](javascript:void(0)) agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you. [^12^](javascript:void(0))Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.

[^13^](javascript:void(0))The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the communion of[^d^](javascript:void(0)) the Holy Spirit be with all of you.

[1.1](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0)): Opening salutation and blessing.  

[1.1](javascript:void(0))--[2](javascript:void(0)): Opening salutation. *Paul and Timothy*, also co-senders in Phil 1.1; Col. 1.1; Thess 1.1; 2 Thess 1.1; Philem 1. *Brother* (cf. 1 Thess 3.2), and elsewhere "my beloved child" (1 Cor 4.17), was an emissary for Paul (but never called an "apostle") to Corinth (1 Cor 4.17; 16.10). *Apostle by the will of God*, also 1 Cor 1.1; cf. Rom 1.1; Gal 1.1. Here, where that status is being contested, that claim is especially pointed. The addressees include the church at Corinth and *all the saints* (or "the sanctified," Paul\'s designation for all believers) *throughout Achaia* (the Roman province in southern Greece to which the city of Corinth belongs). *Grace to you and peace*, Paul\'s standard greeting, which reflects Greco-Roman epistolary form with modified vocabulary: e.g., *grace* (Gk "charis") instead of the standard Gk term "chaire" ("greeting").

[1.3](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0)): Blessing. [3](javascript:void(0))--[5](javascript:void(0)): *Blessed be God.* Instead of the typical thanksgiving formula, "I give thanks ...," (1 Cor 1.4), Paul here uses the language of *blessing* associated with Jewish benedictions; cf. Eph 1.3. The benediction establishes that the principal agent of comfort in affliction, as of apostolic commission, is God, the *Father of mercies* (Ex 34.6; Pss 25.6; 69.16; Rom 12.1; Phil 2.1) and *God of all consolation* (Isa 40.1; 49.3). [6](javascript:void(0))--[7](javascript:void(0)): Suffering in service to God is answered by the consolation of God. As the Corinthians *patiently endure the same sufferings*, they will experience that comfort. [8](javascript:void(0)): *Affliction in Asia*, what Paul refers to is unclear (cf. 1 Cor 15.32 and Acts 19.23--24); *Asia*, the Roman province in western Asia Minor. *Despaired*, cf. 4.8; Ps 88.16 (LXX). [9](javascript:void(0))--[10](javascript:void(0)). But *God, who raises the dead* (4.14), rescued him from *the sentence of death* then and will *rescue again*. *Blessing*, Gk "charisma."

[1.12](javascript:void(0))--[7.16](javascript:void(0)): Body, Part I: Visitation, trauma, reconciliation.  

[1.12](javascript:void(0))--[2.13](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s change of plans and painful visit. [12](javascript:void(0)): A defensive tone is suggested by *testimony of our conscience*; cf. 7.2. A well-attested variant (see textual note *b*) reads "hagiotēti," "holiness," instead of "haplotēti," *frankness*. [13](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0)): End-time terminology (see 2 Thess 2.2n.) punctuates Paul\'s assertion of sincerity. [15](javascript:void(0))--[20](javascript:void(0)): Paul had intended a double visit ("double favor," v. 15), one on either side of his trip to Macedonia (1 Cor 16.5--6), but altered his plans a second time. [16](javascript:void(0)): *Macedonia*, Roman province in northern Greece where Thessalonica, Philippi, and Beroea were located. [17](javascript:void(0)): Against the charge of *vacillating* Paul identifies his straightforward *word* (cf. Mt 5.37; Jas 5.12) with the *faithfulness of God* (v.18). *Amen, to the glory of God* suggests a liturgical context; see 1 Cor 14.16. [19](javascript:void(0)): *Timothy and Silvanus* were coworkers on his first visit to Corinth; see Acts 18.5. [21](javascript:void(0))--[22](javascript:void(0)): A tone of defensiveness but also reassurance marks the claim to *ongoing* divine confirmation *in Christ* (lit., "Christ-ward") of Paul and the Corinthians together, itself founded upon God\'s past action of anointing, sealing, and giving the *first installment* (the same Gk word is translated "guarantee" in 5.5) of the *Spirit*; cf. Eph 1.13. Early commentators (e.g., Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian) understood this as baptismal language. [1.23](javascript:void(0))--[2.4](javascript:void(0)): A return to the courtroom imagery of 1.12. The prior "tearful" letter (2.3--4) is sometimes identified with chs 10--13, where Paul repeatedly and passionately restates his love for the Corinthians; see Introduction.

[2.5](javascript:void(0))--[13](javascript:void(0)): The specific cause of pain is an unnamed individual. Paul urges forgiveness of this one (cf. 7.12) toward whom some punishment (perhaps exclusion) has been applied by "the majority" (v. 6). [11](javascript:void(0)): *Satan* appears elsewhere as "the god of this world" (4.4), Beliar (6.15), and the serpent who deceived Eve (11.3). [12](javascript:void(0)): *Troas*, a city in northwest Asia Minor, near ancient Troy. *Titus*, likely the carrier of the "tearful letter" (see 7.6--13; 8.6,18,23; 12.18).

[2.14](javascript:void(0))--[3.18](javascript:void(0)): Divine commissioning and ministry in the new covenant. [14](javascript:void(0))--[17](javascript:void(0)): A paragraph of thanks (cf. 1.3--11) reverses the mood of restlessness. [14](javascript:void(0))--[15](javascript:void(0)): *Triumphal procession* alludes to the Roman imperial practice of leading captives in a victory parade. Here, God is the victor; Paul with others *in Christ* is being led in spectacle. *Fragrance* and *aroma* suggest sacrificial ritual (Gen 8.21; Lev 1.9); see also the aroma of divine presence in *1 En*. 24.4--25.6 and of Wisdom in Sirach 24.15. In analogy to the effects of the message of the cross in 1 Cor 1.18--25, also associated with divine Wisdom, this aroma is for the ones *being saved* the fragrance of life, but for the ones *perishing*, the fragrance of death. [17](javascript:void(0)): *Peddlers* translates a verb of monetary transaction and suggests preaching for financial gain or preaching a diluted message. [3.1](javascript:void(0)): The Greek epistolary form *letter of recommendation* was used by early Christians to introduce believers to one another (cf. Acts 18.27; Rom 16). [2](javascript:void(0))--[3](javascript:void(0)): Paul defends his lack of such a letter since the Corinthian congregants constitute his *letter of Christ*. Contrasting tablets of stone (the medium for the Ten Commandments, e.g., Ex 20.1--17; 24.12; 31.18; 34.1) with human hearts, Paul invokes the "new covenant*"* (see v. 6) language of Jer 31.31--33 and Ezek 11.19; 36.26--27. [4](javascript:void(0))--[6](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s own *confidence ... through Christ toward God* reiterates the source of Paul\'s ministry. Concentrated "diakonos" ("servant, minister") language in chs 1--9 supports Paul\'s claim to be an authoritative go-between. *Competence* for the new covenant ministry is from God and bears the life of the Spirit in contrast to the dead letter of the written code. [7](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0)): *Stone tablets* connect with Moses' reflection of divine glory at Sinai (Ex 34.29--35). An extended three-part rhetorical figure, known in rabbinic literature as "qal va-ḥomer" (lit., "light and heavy," i.e., "from the lesser to the greater"), follows through v. 11. Cf. Rom 5.16,18. [12](javascript:void(0))--[18](javascript:void(0)): Paul contrasts his own boldness to Moses' hiding. [13](javascript:void(0)): *End* may suggest simply "cessation," or alternately, "goal." [14](javascript:void(0)): *Their minds were hardened* recalls Deut. 29.4; Isa 29.10 (cited verbatim in Rom 11.8). Divine agency may be reflected in the passive voice of the verb "to harden." Temporal distinctions (cf. Deut 29.4 "but to this day") between the time of Moses and the present collapse: *to this very day* the veil remains when they hear the *old covenant* read. A second passive verb completes the thought: only in Christ is the veil *set aside*. [15](javascript:void(0)): Paul reiterates the temporal duration "to this day." Heart (Gk "kardia"; NRSV *minds*) is now the veiled organ. [16](javascript:void(0)): Partial human agency appears within the passive construction: *when one turns to the Lord* the veil *is removed*; *one* is indefinite. [17](javascript:void(0)): *The Lord* (Ex 34.34) is identified by Paul with the *Spirit* and the Spirit with *freedom* (cf. v. 18; Gal 5.1--5). [18](javascript:void(0)): *All of us* continues Paul\'s emphasis on *all* throughout the Corinthian correspondence. *With unveiled faces*, cf. Moses' repeated unveiling in Ex 34.34. *Glory ... reflected in a mirror* may suggest the reflection of the *Lord God* in *Christ* (4.6). Some translate the verb differently, e.g., "to behold," "to contemplate." Metamorphosis to the divine *image* figures in Hellenistic religion and in Rom 8.29; 1 Cor 15.49; Col 3.10.

[4.1](javascript:void(0))--[5.10](javascript:void(0)): Ministry, momentary affliction, and the surpassing weight of glory. [1](javascript:void(0)): *Lose heart*, cf. 4.16; Gal 6.9; Eph 3.13; 2 Thess 3.13. [2](javascript:void(0)): Paul is accused of *cunning* (12.16; cf. 11.3; 1 Cor 3.19) and of *falsifying* the divine word (cf. 2.17). *Conscience*,1.12. [3](javascript:void(0)): A return to the *veil* image encapsulates and reinforces the argument in 3.12--17. [4](javascript:void(0)): *The god of this world* is the sole reference in the New Testament to Satan as a "god"; cf. 1 Cor 2.6n.; Eph 2.2. *This world* appears in 1 Cor 3.19; 5.10; 7.31 (twice). *Minds* recalls the *minds hardened* by an unidentified, but likely divine agent in 3.14; cf. Rom 11.8. *Unbelievers*, see 6.14 and cf. 1 Cor 6.6; 7.12--15; 10.27; 14.22. Christ as *image of God* occurs only here and Col 1.15; cf. 3.18. In Wis 7.25--26, Wisdom is "image of his (God\'s) goodness." Elsewhere the term refers to human beings, e.g., Gen 1.26; cf. Rom 8.29; 1 Cor 11.7; 15.49. *Glory*, a central attribute of the divine presence for Paul, especially thematic in 3.7--11,17--18; 4.15--17. [5](javascript:void(0)): *Jesus Christ as Lord*, see 1 Cor 12.2; Rom 10.9; Phil 2.11; Col 2.6. *Your slaves*, see Rom 1.2; Gal 1.10; Phil 1.1. [6](javascript:void(0)): *Let light shine out of the darkness*, cf. Gen 1.3; Ps 112.4; Isaiah 9.2; Job 37.15. [7](javascript:void(0)): *Treasure*, the ministry described above. *Clay jars*, earthenware, vulnerable to breakage. [8](javascript:void(0))--[9](javascript:void(0)): Catalogues of affliction were common in Stoic philosophy to demonstrate the moral strength of the philosopher. Here, the power of God upholds the apostle through adversity. Cf. 6.4--10; 11.23--28; 12.10; Rom 8.35--39; 1 Cor 4.11--13; Phil 4.12. **[10](javascript:void(0)):** *Death*, Gk "nekrōsis," "dead or decaying flesh"; cf. Rom 4.19. *Carrying in the body*, cf. Gal 6.17. The *body*, i.e., *mortal flesh* (v. 11), is where both the death and the life of Jesus are simultaneous ly manifested; cf. 1 Cor 13.3. The apostle *gives up* the body (Gal 2.20; Eph 5.2), or allows his body to be *given up* (if read as a passive) **[13](javascript:void(0))--[15](javascript:void(0)):** Ps 116.10 (Ps 115.1 LXX) echoes Paul\'s own experience and ends with assurance of entering God\'s presence with thanksgiving. **[15](javascript:void(0)):** *For your sake*, 2.10; see also 1.6; 5.13; 8.23. *Grace* (Gk "charis") occurs seventeen times in 2 Cor and emphasizes extension and plenitude at 8.6; 9.8. **[16](javascript:void(0)):** *Lose heart*, 4.1; Eph 3.13. *Outer ... inner*, "nature" is supplied for translation; cf. Rom 7.22; Eph 3.16. *Wasting away ... being renewed:* Simultaneous actions corresponding to the dual activity in v. 10 of carrying necrosis ("death") in the body and manifesting life in our bodies. *Being renewed*, the verb "to renew" occurs only here and in Col 3.10; the noun "renewal/renewing" occurs in Rom 12.2 (of the mind) and Titus 3.5. Cf. 5.17; Gal 6.15. **[17](javascript:void(0))--[18](javascript:void(0)):** Two more pairs of antitheses end the section. Antitheses, temporal and sensory, here and elsewhere in Paul, often indicate overlapping realities, e.g., glory shining through affliction. **[5.1](javascript:void(0))--[10](javascript:void(0)):** Eschatological transformation. **[1](javascript:void(0)):** *The earthly tent we live in*, lit., "our earthly house of the tent"; cf. Wis 9.15; 2 Pet 1.13. Three forms of the Gk word "oikos" ("house, home") build the transition from earthly to heavenly dwelling; cf. 4.7 where the body is a "clay jar." *Destroyed*, death of the mortal body. *A house not made with hands*, i.e., "God-made" (cf. Mk 14.58; Col 2.11; Heb 9.11,24), the believer\'s resurrection body (cf. "spiritual body" in 1 Cor 15.44). See also Jn 2.19--21 where Jesus\'s resurrected body will replace the Temple. For the gathered community as God\'s temple, see 6.16; 1 Cor 3.16--17; cf. 2 Esd 10.40--57. **[2](javascript:void(0)):** *Groan*, 5.4; Rom 8.23,26. *To be clothed ... to be further clothed* (v. 4) to put a garment on over an existing garment, so perhaps the heavenly dwelling over the earthly one, i.e., the resurrection body over the earthly one; cf. 1 Cor 15.54. **[3](javascript:void(0)):** *Not found naked*, i.e., clothed in the resurrection body. **[4](javascript:void(0)):** *In this tent ... under our burden*, see Wis 9.15. The *mortal* (body), when *further clothed* (at death), will be *swallowed up by life.* (Cf. 1 Cor 15.53--54). **[5](javascript:void(0)):** *Guarantee*, see 1.22n. **[6](javascript:void(0)):** *Confident*: In some Hellenistic philosophers, death is met with confidence because the soul endures or because all things are regulated by a manifold order; e.g., Plato, *Phaedo* 63 E; Epictetus, *Dissertaiones* 2.1.14. *In the body ... away from the Lord*, see Phil 1.21,23. **[7](javascript:void(0)):** *By faith not sight*, see 4.18; 1 Cor 13.12; Rom 8.24--25; 1 Pet 1.8. **[10](javascript:void(0)):** *The judgment seat*, see 1 Cor 4.5; Rom 2.16; Rom 14.9--10. *Recompense ...*, the body is the locus of consequential moral action.

**[5.11](javascript:void(0))--[6.13](javascript:void(0)): The ministry of reconciliation amid manifold afflictions.** **[11](javascript:void(0)):** *Fear of the Lord*, cf. 7.1; see also, e.g., Prov 1.7; 2.5; 9.10; etc., and Sir 1.11,12--14. *Consciences*, 1.12; 4.2. **[12](javascript:void(0)):** *Commending ourselves*, see 3.2n. *In outward appearances*, lit., "in the face," *not in the heart*, perhaps referring to Paul\'s opponents; see 10.12; 11.5--6,12--15; 12.11 for Paul\'s opponents. **[13](javascript:void(0)):** *Are beside ourselves*, perhaps a reference to spiritual ecstasy; see 12.1--8; cf. 1 Cor 14.2,28. *In our right mind*, cf. 1 Cor 14.19. **[14](javascript:void(0))--[15](javascript:void(0)):** *Love of Christ*, Christ\'s love for *us*, expressed in his *one* death on behalf of *all. All have died*, cf. Rom 6.3--4; see also Rom 7.4; 14.7--9; Gal 2.19--20. **[16](javascript:void(0)):** *From a human point of view*, lit., "according to the flesh," can be read as an adjective modifying "no one," or adverbially, modifying "regard." **[17](javascript:void(0)):** *New creation*, see Isa 43.18--19; 48.6; 65.17; 66.22; Gal 6.15; Eph 2.15; 2 Pet 3.13; Rev 21.1--5; cf. Rom 8.19--21. **[18](javascript:void(0))--[19](javascript:void(0)):** *Reconciled us*, cf. Rom 5.10--11. Reconciliation is a term found only in Pauline letters in the NT; cf. 2 Macc 1.5; 7.33; 8.29. **[20](javascript:void(0)):** *Ambassadors* has political resonance, it can refer to Roman legates, sent by the emperor to govern imperial provinces, or to envoys sent on a diplomatic mission. **[21](javascript:void(0)):** *Made him to be sin* (Gk "hamartia"; cf. Gal 3.13--14; Rom 8.3--4) is variously interpreted: Christ is a sin-offering for humanity, an atonement offering (Isa 53.9--11; Rom 3.25; 1 Cor 5.7), or Christ himself took the place of the sinner, though he remained sinless. *Righteousness of God*, either the righteousness that belongs to God and brings about the salvation of humanity, or the righteousness God imparts to human beings to justify them; see Rom 1.17; 3.5,21--22,25--26; 10.3; Phil 3.9. **[6.1](javascript:void(0))--[10](javascript:void(0)):** Summary of defense and appeal to affection. **[2](javascript:void(0)):** *At an acceptable time ...*, Isa 49.8. *Now*, see 5.16. **[3](javascript:void(0)):** *Obstacle*, 1 Cor 9.12. **[4a](javascript:void(0)):** *Commend ourselves* intensifies the theme of boasting, prominent in 1 Cor, using language of self-commendation and defense: cf. 3.1; 4.2; 5.12; 10.12; 10.18; 12.11. **[4b](javascript:void(0))--[5](javascript:void(0)):** A catalogue of afflictions followed by a catalogue of divinely empowered virtues (vv. 6--7). **[7](javascript:void(0)):** *Weapons of righteousness*, Paul often uses military metaphors, e.g., 2.14n.; 10.4--5; Phil 2.25; Philem 1.2; Gal 5.13,17; Rom 13.12; 1 Thess 5.8. **[8](javascript:void(0))--[10](javascript:void(0)):** A series of paired antitheses illustrates the paradoxical nature of apostolic work; see Gal 5.22--23; Phil 4.8; Col 3.12; 1 Pet 3.8; 2 Pet 1.5--7. In Stoic philosophy such lists describe the philosopher\'s self-sufficiency, but here support Paul\'s God-sourced self-defense. [**11**](javascript:void(0)). *Frankly*, lit., "our mouth is open." **[12](javascript:void(0)):** *Affections*, lit., "the inner organs," the seat of the emotions.

**[6.14](javascript:void(0))--[7.1](javascript:void(0)): Warnings about purity.** These verses insert an uncharacteristic theme into the discourse on affection that resumes at 7.2. **[14](javascript:void(0)):** *Mismatched*, lit., "misyoked," a term related to the injunction against interbreeding animals in Lev 19.19; it may relate to marriages (cf. 1 Cor 7.12--16), but also to business relations. *Righteousness and lawlessness* (Rom 6.19); *darkness and light* (Rom 2.19; 13.12; 1 Cor 4.5; 1 Thess 5.4--5). **[15](javascript:void(0)):** *Beliar*, variant of Belial (Heb "worthlessness"), is attested only here in biblical literature; more commonly "Satan" (see 2.11n.; 11.14; 12.7). **[16](javascript:void(0)):** *Temple of the living God*, see 1 Cor 3.16. *As God said*, a chain of scriptural citations follows: [**16d**](javascript:void(0)) conflates Ezek 37.27 and Lev 26.12; **[17a](javascript:void(0))--[c](javascript:void(0)):** Isa 52.11; **[17d](javascript:void(0)):** Ezek 20.34 (LXX); **[18a](javascript:void(0)):** 2 Sam 7.14; **[18b](javascript:void(0)):** Isa 43.6. **[7.1](javascript:void(0)):** *We have these promises*. Indicating either a present state or a future hope. *Making holiness*, cf. text variant at 1.12 and 1 Cor 3.17.

**[7.2](javascript:void(0))--[16](javascript:void(0)): Return to personal defense and affection.** **[2](javascript:void(0)):** *Wronged ... corrupted ... taken advantage of.* Denial of these charges indicates strained relations with opponents. The last charge returns in 12.17. **[5](javascript:void(0))--[16](javascript:void(0)):** Travel narrative resumes from 2.13. Paul\'s reunion with Titus in Macedonia brings the welcome news of the Corinthians' good will (see 2.2--4). **[6](javascript:void(0)):** *God who consoles the downcast*, Isa 49.13. **[8](javascript:void(0)):** *My letter*, 2.2--4. **[11](javascript:void(0)):** Heightened rhetoric raises the question of whether Paul had been mistaken in his prior assessment of their guilt. *Eagerness to clear* (Gk "apologia") and *punishment* carry legal overtones. **[12](javascript:void(0)):** *The one who did the wrong*, presumably the individual of 2.5--11. *The one who was wronged*, Paul. **[13](javascript:void(0)):** *Comfort ... consolation*, see 1.3--7. **[15](javascript:void(0)):** *Obedience*, see 2.9. *Fear and trembling*, cf. Phil 2.12; Eph 6.5. **[16](javascript:void(0)):** Expression of *complete confidence* (5.6,8) sums up the preceding section and looks ahead to the concrete financial requests in chs 8--9.

[8.1](javascript:void(0))--[9.15](javascript:void(0)): Body, Part II, [8.1](javascript:void(0))--[9.15](javascript:void(0)): The collection.  

[8.1](javascript:void(0))--[24](javascript:void(0)): Exhortation to contribute for relief of the saints in Jerusalem. Chapters 8 and 9, thought by some to be separate letters, discuss the collection Paul is gathering for the believers in Jerusalem; see Rom 15.25--32; 1 Cor 16.1--4; Gal 2.10; also Acts 24.17. [1](javascript:void(0)): *Grace* (Gk "charis"), here meaning "divine beneficence." The term is used ten times in chs 8--9 with rich nuance as shown in the wide range of translations of the term: "privilege" (8.4); "generous undertaking" (8.6,7,19); "generous act" (8.9); "thanks" (8.16; 9.15); "blessing" (9.8). *Macedonia, s*ee 1.16n. [2](javascript:void(0)): *Severe ordeal*, cf. Phil 1.29--30; 1 Thess 1.6; 2.14; 3.3--4. [4](javascript:void(0)): *Sharing* (Gk "koinōnia") refers to the collection in 8.4; 9.13; Rom 15.26. The same noun denotes participating in Christ (1 Cor 1.9; 10.16; 2 Cor 2.7; Phil 3.10) and with the Spirit (2 Cor 13.13; Phil 2.1); see also, "sharing in the gospel" (Phil 1.5) and "sharing of faith" (Philem 6). *Ministry* (Gk "diakonia"), see 3.4--6n. *Saints*, the believers in Jerusalem for whom the collection is taken; see 1.1--2n. [6](javascript:void(0)): *Titus*, having already begun (7.13), may now complete *this generous undertaking*, i.e., the collection (8.1). On *Titus* see 2.13; 8.16--24.
