[^i^](javascript:void(0)) Or *minister* [^j^](javascript:void(0)) Gk *first fruits*

[^k^](javascript:void(0)) Or *Junias*; other ancient authorities read *Julia*

[^a^](javascript:void(0)) Or *compatriots* [^b^](javascript:void(0)) Or *compatriot* [^c^](javascript:void(0)) Gk *brothers*

[^d^](javascript:void(0)) Gk *their own belly* [^e^](javascript:void(0)) Other ancient authorities lack this sentence

[^f^](javascript:void(0)) Or *I Tertius, writing this letter in the Lord, greet you*

[^g^](javascript:void(0)) Other ancient authorities add verse 24, *The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you. Amen.*

[^h^](javascript:void(0)) Gk *the one*

[^i^](javascript:void(0)) Other ancient authorities lack *to whom*. The verse then reads, *to the only wise God be the glory through Jesus Christ forever. Amen.*

[^j^](javascript:void(0)) Other ancient authorities lack 16.25-27 or include it after 14.23 or 15.33; others put verse 24 after verse 27

#### Philippians c. 58--62 CE

The Letter of Paul to The Philippians

**NAME AND AUTHORSHIP**

The letter to the Philippians is one of the richest of Paul\'s letters and has never been seriously questioned as genuine. Philippi was a major city of Macedonia in northern Greece and a Roman colony on the Via Egnatia, the Roman road linking Byzantium in the East to the western coast of Macedonia, from which ships could easily reach Italy. The Christian community in Philippi was the westernmost Pauline church at the time of its founding ([Acts 16.11](javascript:void(0))--[13](javascript:void(0))). The mutual affection between Paul and the Philippians is evident in the letter and contrasts with the problems he had with other churches.

**DATE AND PLACE OF COMPOSITION**

Except that Paul was in prison and awaiting trial at the time of writing ([1.7](javascript:void(0))--[18](javascript:void(0))), it is impossible to speak confidently of the time and place of the writing of this letter. Because of references to the imperial guard or praetorium ([1.13](javascript:void(0))) and to the emperor\'s household ([4.22](javascript:void(0))), and also because the situation reflected in the letter bears some resemblance to that described at the end of Acts, the traditional date of the letter has been during the period of Paul\'s imprisonment at Rome (about 61--63 ce). The indications are by no means conclusive, however, and more recently some scholars have thought that the place of composition is perhaps Caesarea before Paul\'s arrival in Rome ([Acts 24](javascript:void(0))--[26](javascript:void(0))) or Ephesus at an earlier stage in Paul\'s career, especially because of frequent communication and emissaries between Paul and Philippi implied in the letter ([2.19](javascript:void(0)),[25](javascript:void(0))--[26](javascript:void(0)); [4.10](javascript:void(0)),[18](javascript:void(0))). This information seems to be inconsistent with the great distance from Philippi to Rome, about 800 miles, taking perhaps a month of travel, or an even greater distance of almost 1,200 miles from Caesarea, requiring perhaps two months of travel, whereas Ephesus was only about 300 miles away, a relatively easy week by sea. The term referring to the emperor\'s household was also used for provincial government centers and the imperial civil service outside Rome. Elsewhere Paul notes an unhappy situation in Ephesus ([1 Cor 15.32](javascript:void(0))) and in the Roman province of Asia, of which Ephesus was a major center ([2 Cor 1.8](javascript:void(0))), and in [Acts 20.16](javascript:void(0)) he bypasses Ephesus on his way south down the coast. For these reasons it is likely that Paul wrote the letters while imprisoned in Ephesus in the mid-50s. The immediate occasion of Paul\'s writing was the return to Philippi of Epaphroditus ([2.25](javascript:void(0))--[30](javascript:void(0))), sent by the Philippian church with gifts for Paul ([4.18](javascript:void(0))), then seriously ill while staying with him. Paul took this opportunity to thank them for their gifts and to set their difficulties in a wider framework by describing his and their situation in light of the reality of his and their faith in Christ.

**STRUCTURE AND INTERPRETATION**

The letter follows the usual pattern of Paul\'s letters, but some seemingly abrupt changes of topic (especially between [3.1](javascript:void(0)) and [2](javascript:void(0)), and [4.3](javascript:void(0)) and [4](javascript:void(0))), in addition to the fact that an early Christian writer (Polycarp, *Philippians* 2.3), speaks of "letters" of Paul to the Philippians, has led some scholars to conclude that our present Philippians is composed of as many as three letters that Paul wrote to Philippi. Many scholars, however, find that Philippians is a coherent whole as it stands. After the greeting ([1.1](javascript:void(0))--[2](javascript:void(0))) and thanksgiving ([1.3](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0))), Paul lays out the situation ([1.12](javascript:void(0))--[26](javascript:void(0))) and exhorts the community to unity ([1.27](javascript:void(0))--[4.3](javascript:void(0))) with many arguments, including proposing Christ ([2.5](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0))), Timothy and Epaphroditus ([2.19](javascript:void(0))--[30](javascript:void(0))), and himself ([3.4](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0))) as models of self-giving for the good of the whole. He thanks them for their recent gifts ([4.10](javascript:void(0))--[20](javascript:void(0))) and concludes the letter ([4.21](javascript:void(0))--[23](javascript:void(0))).

Paul writes from prison and is uncertain of the outcome for himself. The themes of opposition and the possibility of death are therefore prominent. Yet in the midst of suffering and uncertainty, the theme of joy emerges quite clearly and remarkably ([1.4](javascript:void(0)),[18](javascript:void(0)),[25](javascript:void(0)); [2.2](javascript:void(0)),[17](javascript:void(0))--[18](javascript:void(0)),[28](javascript:void(0)); [4.4](javascript:void(0)),[10](javascript:void(0))). The Philippians too are experiencing opposition ([1.29](javascript:void(0))), but Paul\'s major concern is to bring them together and thus overcome the threat of internal disharmony. In keeping with that purpose, he uses a hymnic passage that celebrates the self-emptying of Christ even to death, for which God bestowed on him the name of "Lord," the "name above all names" ([2.6](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0))). The poetic reflection, was probably composed by a prior author known to both Paul and the Philippians. Here it is the prime example of why they should be willing also to empty themselves of their own opinions. The example of Paul himself follows and supports the argument ([3.4](javascript:void(0))--[16](javascript:void(0))). Paul offers both Christ and himself as examples of courage and self-surrender in the face of suffering and death. Thus he attempts to turn the Philippians from partisanship to unity.

*Carolyn Osiek*

[**1**](javascript:void(0)) Paul and Timothy, servants[^a^](javascript:void(0)) of Christ Jesus, To all the saints in Christ Jesus who are in Philippi, with the bishops[^b^](javascript:void(0)) and deacons:[^c^](javascript:void(0))

[^2^](javascript:void(0))Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

[^3^](javascript:void(0))I thank my God every time I remember you, [^4^](javascript:void(0))constantly praying with joy in every one of my prayers for all of you, [^5^](javascript:void(0))because of your sharing in the gospel from the first day until now. [^6^](javascript:void(0))I am confident of this, that the one who began a good work among you will bring it to completion by the day of Jesus Christ. [^7^](javascript:void(0))It is right for me to think this way about all of you, because you hold me in your heart,[^d^](javascript:void(0)) for all of you share in God\'s grace[^e^](javascript:void(0)) with me, both in my imprisonment and in the defense and confirmation of the gospel. [^8^](javascript:void(0))For God is my witness, how I long for all of you with the compassion of Christ Jesus. [^9^](javascript:void(0))And this is my prayer, that your love may overflow more and more with knowledge and full insight [^10^](javascript:void(0))to help you to determine what is best, so that in the day of Christ you may be pure and blameless, [^11^](javascript:void(0))having produced the harvest of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ for the glory and praise of God.

[^12^](javascript:void(0))I want you to know, beloved,[^f^](javascript:void(0)) that what has happened to me has actually helped to spread the gospel, [^13^](javascript:void(0))so that it has become known throughout the whole imperial guard[^g^](javascript:void(0)) and to everyone else that my imprisonment is for Christ; [^14^](javascript:void(0))and most of the brothers and sisters,^f^ having been made confident in the Lord by my imprisonment, dare to speak the word[^h^](javascript:void(0)) with greater boldness and without fear.

[^15^](javascript:void(0))Some proclaim Christ from envy and rivalry, but others from goodwill. [^16^](javascript:void(0))These proclaim Christ out of love, knowing that I have been put here for the defense of the gospel; [^17^](javascript:void(0))the others proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely but intending to increase my suffering in my imprisonment. [^18^](javascript:void(0))What does it matter? Just this, that Christ is proclaimed in every way, whether out of false motives or true; and in that I rejoice.

Yes, and I will continue to rejoice, [^19^](javascript:void(0))for I know that through your prayers and the help of the Spirit of Jesus Christ this will turn out for my deliverance. [^20^](javascript:void(0))It is my eager expectation and hope that I will not be put to shame in any way, but that by my speaking with all boldness, Christ will be exalted now as always in my body, whether by life or by death. [^21^](javascript:void(0))For to me, living is Christ and dying is gain. [^22^](javascript:void(0))If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me; and I do not know which I prefer. [^23^](javascript:void(0))I am hard pressed between the two: my desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better; [^24^](javascript:void(0))but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for you. [^25^](javascript:void(0))Since I am convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with all of you for your progress and joy in faith, [^26^](javascript:void(0))so that I may share abundantly in your boasting in Christ Jesus when I come to you again.

[^27^](javascript:void(0))Only, live your life in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ, so that, whether I come and see you or am absent and hear about you, I will know that you are standing firm in one spirit, striving side by side with one mind for the faith of the gospel, [^28^](javascript:void(0))and are in no way intimidated by your opponents. For them this is evidence of their destruction, but of your salvation. And this is God\'s doing. [^29^](javascript:void(0))For he has graciously granted you the privilege not only of believing in Christ, but of suffering for him as well---[^30^](javascript:void(0))since you are having the same struggle that you saw I had and now hear that I still have.

[**2**](javascript:void(0)) If then there is any encouragement in Christ, any consolation from love, any sharing in the Spirit, any compassion and sympathy, [^2^](javascript:void(0))make my joy complete: be of the same mind, having the same love, being in full accord and of one mind. [^3^](javascript:void(0))Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility regard others as better than yourselves. [^4^](javascript:void(0))Let each of you look not to your own interests, but to the interests of others. [^5^](javascript:void(0))Let the same mind be in you that was[^a^](javascript:void(0)) in Christ Jesus,

[^6^](javascript:void(0))who, though he was in the form of God,

  did not regard equality with God

  as something to be exploited,

[^7^](javascript:void(0))but emptied himself,

  taking the form of a slave,

  being born in human likeness.

And being found in human form,

[^8^](javascript:void(0))he humbled himself

and became obedient to the point of death---

even death on a cross.

[^9^](javascript:void(0))Therefore God also highly exalted him

  and gave him the name

  that is above every name,

[^10^](javascript:void(0))so that at the name of Jesus

  every knee should bend,

  in heaven and on earth and under the earth,

[^11^](javascript:void(0))and every tongue should confess

  that Jesus Christ is Lord,

  to the glory of God the Father.

[^12^](javascript:void(0))Therefore, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed me, not only in my presence, but much more now in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling; [^13^](javascript:void(0))for it is God who is at work in you, enabling you both to will and to work for his good pleasure.

[^14^](javascript:void(0))Do all things without murmuring and arguing, [^15^](javascript:void(0))so that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, in which you shine like stars in the world. [^16^](javascript:void(0))It is by your holding fast to the word of life that I can boast on the day of Christ that I did not run in vain or labor in vain. [^17^](javascript:void(0))But even if I am being poured out as a libation over the sacrifice and the offering of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with all of you---[^18^](javascript:void(0))and in the same way you also must be glad and rejoice with me.

[^19^](javascript:void(0))I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, so that I may be cheered by news of you. [^20^](javascript:void(0))I have no one like him who will be genuinely concerned for your welfare. [^21^](javascript:void(0))All of them are seeking their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. [^22^](javascript:void(0))But Timothy\'s[^a^](javascript:void(0)) worth you know, how like a son with a father he has served with me in the work of the gospel. [^23^](javascript:void(0))I hope therefore to send him as soon as I see how things go with me; [^24^](javascript:void(0))and I trust in the Lord that I will also come soon.

[^25^](javascript:void(0))Still, I think it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus---my brother and co-worker and fellow soldier, your messenger[^b^](javascript:void(0)) and minister to my need; [^26^](javascript:void(0))for he has been longing for[^c^](javascript:void(0)) all of you, and has been distressed because you heard that he was ill. [^27^](javascript:void(0))He was indeed so ill that he nearly died. But God had mercy on him, and not only on him but on me also, so that I would not have one sorrow after another. [^28^](javascript:void(0))I am the more eager to send him, therefore, in order that you may rejoice at seeing him again, and that I may be less anxious. [^29^](javascript:void(0))Welcome him then in the Lord with all joy, and honor such people, [^30^](javascript:void(0))because he came close to death for the work of Christ,[^d^](javascript:void(0)) risking his life to make up for those services that you could not give me.

[**3**](javascript:void(0)) Finally, my brothers and sisters,[^e^](javascript:void(0)) rejoice[^f^](javascript:void(0)) in the Lord.

To write the same things to you is not troublesome to me, and for you it is a safeguard.

[^2^](javascript:void(0))Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers, beware of those who mutilate the flesh\![^g^](javascript:void(0)) [^3^](javascript:void(0))For it is we who are the circumcision, who worship in the Spirit of God[^h^](javascript:void(0)) and boast in Christ Jesus and have no confidence in the flesh---[^4^](javascript:void(0))even though I, too, have reason for confidence in the flesh.

If anyone else has reason to be confident in the flesh, I have more: [^5^](javascript:void(0))circumcised on the eighth day, a member of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew born of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee; [^6^](javascript:void(0))as to zeal, a persecutor of the church; as to righteousness under the law, blameless.

[^7^](javascript:void(0))Yet whatever gains I had, these I have come to regard as loss because of Christ. [^8^](javascript:void(0))More than that, I regard everything as loss because of the surpassing value of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things, and I regard them as rubbish, in order that I may gain Christ [^9^](javascript:void(0))and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but one that comes through faith in Christ,[^i^](javascript:void(0)) the righteousness from God based on faith. [^10^](javascript:void(0))I want to know Christ[^j^](javascript:void(0)) and the power of his resurrection and the sharing of his sufferings by becoming like him in his death, [^11^](javascript:void(0))if somehow I may attain the resurrection from the dead.

[^12^](javascript:void(0))Not that I have already obtained this or have already reached the goal;[^a^](javascript:void(0)) but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own. [^13^](javascript:void(0))Beloved,[^b^](javascript:void(0)) I do not consider that I have made it my own;[^c^](javascript:void(0)) but this one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, [^14^](javascript:void(0))I press on toward the goal for the prize of the heavenly[^d^](javascript:void(0)) call of God in Christ Jesus. [^15^](javascript:void(0))Let those of us then who are mature be of the same mind; and if you think differently about anything, this too God will reveal to you. [^16^](javascript:void(0))Only let us hold fast to what we have attained.

[^17^](javascript:void(0))Brothers and sisters,^b^ join in imitating me, and observe those who live according to the example you have in us. [^18^](javascript:void(0))For many live as enemies of the cross of Christ; I have often told you of them, and now I tell you even with tears. [^19^](javascript:void(0))Their end is destruction; their god is the belly; and their glory is in their shame; their minds are set on earthly things. [^20^](javascript:void(0))But our citizenship[^e^](javascript:void(0)) is in heaven, and it is from there that we are expecting a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ. [^21^](javascript:void(0))He will transform the body of our humiliation[^f^](javascript:void(0)) that it may be conformed to the body of his glory,[^g^](javascript:void(0)) by the power that also enables him to make all things subject to himself.

**[4](javascript:void(0))** Therefore, my brothers and sisters,[^h^](javascript:void(0)) whom I love and long for, my joy and crown, stand firm in the Lord in this way, my beloved.

[^2^](javascript:void(0))I urge Euodia and I urge Syntyche to be of the same mind in the Lord. [^3^](javascript:void(0))Yes, and I ask you also, my loyal companion,[^i^](javascript:void(0)) help these women, for they have struggled beside me in the work of the gospel, together with Clement and the rest of my co-workers, whose names are in the book of life.

[^4^](javascript:void(0))Rejoice[^j^](javascript:void(0)) in the Lord always; again I will say, Rejoice.^j^ [^5^](javascript:void(0))Let your gentleness be known to everyone. The Lord is near. [^6^](javascript:void(0))Do not worry about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. [^7^](javascript:void(0))And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

[^8^](javascript:void(0))Finally, beloved,[^k^](javascript:void(0)) whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is pleasing, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence and if there is anything worthy of praise, think about[^l^](javascript:void(0)) these things. [^9^](javascript:void(0))Keep on doing the things that you have learned and received and heard and seen in me, and the God of peace will be with you.

[^10^](javascript:void(0))I rejoice[^m^](javascript:void(0)) in the Lord greatly that now at last you have revived your concern for me; indeed, you were concerned for me, but had no opportunity to show it.[^n^](javascript:void(0)) [^11^](javascript:void(0))Not that I am referring to being in need; for I have learned to be content with whatever I have. [^12^](javascript:void(0))I know what it is to have little, and I know what it is to have plenty. In any and all circumstances I have learned the secret of being well-fed and of going hungry, of having plenty and of being in need. [^13^](javascript:void(0))I can do all things through him who strengthens me. [^14^](javascript:void(0))In any case, it was kind of you to share my distress.

[^15^](javascript:void(0))You Philippians indeed know that in the early days of the gospel, when I left Macedonia, no church shared with me in the matter of giving and receiving, except you alone. [^16^](javascript:void(0))For even when I was in Thessalonica, you sent me help for my needs more than once. [^17^](javascript:void(0))Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the profit that accumulates to your account. [^18^](javascript:void(0))I have been paid in full and have more than enough; I am fully satisfied, now that I have received from Epaphroditus the gifts you sent, a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God. [^19^](javascript:void(0))And my God will fully satisfy every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus. [^20^](javascript:void(0))To our God and Father be glory forever and ever. Amen.

[^21^](javascript:void(0))Greet every saint in Christ Jesus. The friends[^a^](javascript:void(0)) who are with me greet you. [^22^](javascript:void(0))All the saints greet you, especially those of the emperor\'s household.

[^23^](javascript:void(0))The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.[^b^](javascript:void(0))

[1.1](javascript:void(0))--[2](javascript:void(0)): Salutation. [1](javascript:void(0)): *Bishops and deacons*, the alternate translation *overseers and helpers* is preferable. These functions are not yet the church offices that they will later become.

[1.3](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0)): Thanksgiving. A common feature of a Pauline letter. [5](javascript:void(0)): *Sharing*, "koinônia," an important Pauline concept (2.1; 3.10; 4.15). *From the first day*, when Paul first preached at Philippi (Acts 16.12). [6](javascript:void(0)): *The day of Jesus Christ*, when he will return and the present age will end (2.16; see 1 Cor 1.8; cf. 2 Thess 2.1 and 2 Pet 3.10). [10](javascript:void(0)): Rom 2.18.

**[1.12](javascript:void(0))--[26](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s situation in chains.** **[13](javascript:void(0)):** Paul is confined in some Roman administrative center, where he has had the opportunity to preach the gospel. **[15](javascript:void(0))--[18](javascript:void(0)):** Not all Christian preachers agreed with Paul or liked him; this is clear in Galatians and 1 and 2 Corinthians (especially 2 Cor 10--13), and here Paul questions their motives. **[19](javascript:void(0)):** See Job 13.16. **[21](javascript:void(0))--[24](javascript:void(0)):** His life is not his own but is given over to Christ, so that he is indifferent to the outcome of life or death; nevertheless, his death would mean loss to his churches.

**[1.27](javascript:void(0))--[4.1](javascript:void(0)): Appeal to unity, followed by examples.** **[2.1](javascript:void(0))--[18](javascript:void(0))**: First example: self-emptying of Christ. **[6](javascript:void(0)):** *In the form of God, equality with God*, may refer to divine status, or simply preexistence as a heavenly being (Dan 7.13), or Adam\'s original immortality (Wis 2.23--24), which Christ renounced by becoming subject to death. **[7](javascript:void(0)):** *But emptied himself*, the extreme limit of self-denial. **[8](javascript:void(0)):** Mt 26.39; Jn 10.18; Rom 5.19; Heb 5.8; 12.2. **[9](javascript:void(0)):** *Exalted*, in raising him from the dead. *The name ... above every name* is Lord. **[10](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0)):** Cf. Isa 45.23. **[12](javascript:void(0)):** *With fear and trembling*, a frequent biblical expression (Ex 15.16; Deut 2.25; Ps 2.11; Isa 19.6; 4 Macc 4.10) that had become a commonplace (1 Cor 2.3; 2 Cor 7.15; Eph 6.5). **[15](javascript:void(0)):** *Shine like stars*, Dan 12.3. **[16](javascript:void(0)):** *Day of Christ*, see 1.6n. **[17](javascript:void(0)):** Paul\'s possible death is compared to a temple sacrifice.

**[2.19](javascript:void(0))--[3.1a](javascript:void(0)): Second example: Timothy and Epaphroditus.** **[19](javascript:void(0)):** *Timothy*, Acts 16.1--3; 1 Cor 16.10--11. **[24](javascript:void(0)):** *I trust ... that I will also come soon*, an argument against Rome as place of writing (see Rom 15.23--25). **[25](javascript:void(0)):** *Epaphroditus*, apostle and coworker of Paul who brought the gift from Philippi (4.18), now being sent home.

**[3.1b](javascript:void(0))--[3](javascript:void(0)): A digression** about those who preach the necessity of circumcision, requiring Christians to observe the laws of Judaism. They were Paul\'s bitter opponents elsewhere, especially in Galatia, and are introduced here as a negative example (cf. Gal 5.1--12). **[3](javascript:void(0)):** *The flesh*, emphasis on physical rituals.

**[3.4](javascript:void(0))--[4.1](javascript:void(0)): Third example: Paul himself.** **[5](javascript:void(0)):** *Hebrew*, a more preferred self-designation than *Jew*, which was used more often by and for outsiders. *Pharisee*, member of the group concerned with interpretation of the Jewish law. **[6](javascript:void(0)):** *A persecutor*, Acts 9.1--2; 1 Cor 15.9; Gal 1.13. *As to righteousness under the law, blameless*, Paul did not see himself as guilty or incomplete before his encounter with Christ. **[8](javascript:void(0)):** *Rubbish*, or excrement. **[9](javascript:void(0)):** *The righteousness from God based on faith*, a free gift bestowed by God through the grace of Christ (Rom 1.16--4.25). **[10](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0)):** Actually to know Christ as risen and living is to have power to suffer and die like him, and to possess the hope of rising and living with him. **[12](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0)):** *The goal* and *the prize*, allusion to popular sports, the Greek foot races, their finishing post, and the award to the winner (see 2.16; 1 Cor 9.24--27). **[18](javascript:void(0))--[19](javascript:void(0)):** *Many live as enemies of the cross of Christ*, presumably professing Christians who cannot accept Paul\'s cross theology. **[20](javascript:void(0)):** *Our citizenship*, our ultimate political loyalty and real homeland, contrasting with the status of many of the Philippians as Roman citizens. **[21](javascript:void(0)):** Rom 8.23; 1 Cor 15.47--57; 2 Cor 5.1--5; Col **3.1**--**4**.**[1](javascript:void(0)):** 1 Thess 2.19--20. A *crown* was often awarded to the winner of a race (see 3.12--14n.).

**[4.2](javascript:void(0))--[9](javascript:void(0)): Dissension.** **[2](javascript:void(0)):** *Euodia ... Syntyche*, two women leaders in the Philippian church, most likely heads of house-churches (John Chrysostom, *Hom. Phil.* 13) and therefore among the overseers and helpers (1.1) whose disagreement has caused factions in the church that have seriously affected the community. **[3](javascript:void(0)):** *My loyal companion*, an unknown but influential figure who could serve as mediator between the two. Less likely, the Greek word for *companion* may be understood as a proper name, *Syzygus. Book of life*, a book kept by God containing names of those to be saved (Ps 69.28; Dan 12.1; Lk 10.20; Rev 3.5; etc.).

**[4.10](javascript:void(0))--[20](javascript:void(0)): Acknowledgment of their gifts.** **[11](javascript:void(0)):** *Content*, Paul here expresses the Stoic ideal of indifference, but with new motivation because of Christ. **[15](javascript:void(0))--[16](javascript:void(0)):** *Macedonia, Thessalonica*, according to Acts 17.1, Paul had gone to Thessalonica immediately after his stay in Philippi. [**15**](javascript:void(0)),[**17**](javascript:void(0)),**[18](javascript:void(0)):** *Giving and receiving, profit ... account, paid in full*, a series of business terms used metaphorically here and in other contexts of friendship. **[18](javascript:void(0)):** *Fragrant offering*, Gen 8.21; Ex 29.18; Ezek 20.41.

**[4.21](javascript:void(0))--[23](javascript:void(0)): Conclusion.** **[22](javascript:void(0)):** *The emperor\'s household*, members of the imperial civil service who are believers where Paul is confined, but not necessarily located in Rome.

#### Philemon c. 58--62 CE

The Letter of Paul to Philemon

**NAME AND AUTHORSHIP**

This enigmatic letter is a piece of the apostle Paul\'s business correspondence, containing an intentionally designed blend of personal and public appeal, addressed to three individuals, Philemon (for whom the letter is named), Apphia, and Archippus, and to the church that meets in one of their houses ([v. 2](javascript:void(0))). Though its meaning is much debated, its genuineness is not disputed.

**STRUCTURE AND INTERPRETATION**

The structure of Philemon is straightforward. After the epistolary prescript ([vv. 1](javascript:void(0))--[3](javascript:void(0))) and thanksgiving ([vv. 4](javascript:void(0))--[7](javascript:void(0))), which praise Philemon for his past benefactions, in the epistolary body ([vv. 8](javascript:void(0))--[22](javascript:void(0))) Paul makes a fresh request for the present situation involving the slave Onesimus, through various forms of subtle and not-so-subtle appeal, ending with the suggestion that Paul will soon visit Philemon ([v. 22](javascript:void(0))). He closes the letter with epistolary greetings from missionary co-workers that accent the public visibility of Philemon\'s decision ([vv. 23](javascript:void(0))--[24](javascript:void(0))), and a final benediction ([v. 25](javascript:void(0))).

The letter employs a carefully calibrated rhetoric to make a request of Philemon. In order to interpret this letter one must reconstruct the situation it presupposes, but in doing so the reader must largely depend upon the letter itself, which is cryptic, partly because Paul and his recipients already know the circumstances, and partly because Paul chooses to be indirect. We know that Paul writes this letter from prison ([vv. 1](javascript:void(0)),[9](javascript:void(0))--[10](javascript:void(0))) in a location not specified, where he has been joined by someone named Onesimus, whom Paul has converted to the gospel there ([v. 10](javascript:void(0))). This Onesimus, who is the slave of Philemon ([v. 16](javascript:void(0))), is the object of Paul\'s appeal ([v. 10](javascript:void(0))). While the circumstances that led to Onesimus\'s encounter with Paul are not described in the letter ([v. 15](javascript:void(0)) merely says "he was separated from you"), two quite different possibilities suggest themselves: either Onesimus ran away from his master, perhaps after causing him some financial loss ([vv. 15](javascript:void(0)),[18](javascript:void(0))), or Onesimus was sent by his owner to serve Paul in prison ([v. 13](javascript:void(0))), much as Epaphroditus was sent to Paul in prison by the Philippians ([Phil 2.25](javascript:void(0))--[30](javascript:void(0))). The advantage of the latter possibility is that it explains how Onesimus came to be in prison with Paul, whereas the former option must explain why a slave would run away to a prison. Perhaps Onesimus, according to legal precedent, sought out a friend of his master to act as an intermediary in a dispute between himself and his owner. The precise occasion of the letter is the moment of Paul\'s sending Onesimus back to his master ([v. 12](javascript:void(0))). The letter is meant to accompany Onesimus and register an appeal "for my child, Onesimus" ([v. 10](javascript:void(0))).

What is Paul asking Philemon to do? The history of interpretation has focused on several different possibilities: (1) Paul is asking Philemon to receive Onesimus back as his slave (though a "brother in Christ") and forgive whatever transgressions he had committed ([vv. 17](javascript:void(0))--[18](javascript:void(0))); (2) Paul is asking Philemon to send Onesimus back to him to continue serving the apostle\'s physical needs while in prison ([vv. 13](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0))); (3) Paul is strongly hinting that Philemon should not only receive Onesimus back but grant this new Christian brother his freedom through formal manumission ([vv. 16](javascript:void(0)),[21](javascript:void(0))). Each of these options has some grounding in the text, and which one the reader adopts depends upon which verses are thought to be the focal point of the argument and upon how one assesses Paul\'s tone at various points. The decision may also depend on how one reads [1 Cor 7.17](javascript:void(0))--[21](javascript:void(0)), and the famously ambiguous [7.21](javascript:void(0)) (see n. there), as representing Paul\'s general view on whether Christ-believing slaves should be manumitted. One thing, however, is certain about this letter: Paul engages in full-strength arm-twisting of Philemon to do his "good deed" ([v. 14](javascript:void(0))). But the final decision of what to do is left up to Philemon himself---in the context of a host of onlookers among his fellow Christians. One of the most remarkable things about this letter is that it was preserved and ultimately incorporated into the canonical collection of Paul\'s letters, perhaps an indication that Philemon\'s ultimate decision met Paul\'s request.

This letter has played a role in the history of Christian social ethics disproportionate to its size. The extent to which Paul challenged the institution of chattel slavery or not, and the legacy of this text (and others in the Pauline tradition, such as [1 Cor 7.17](javascript:void(0))--[24](javascript:void(0)); [Col 3.22](clbr://internal.sandbox/book/OEBPS/012_part1zzf.xhtml#colo3_22)--[4.1](clbr://internal.sandbox/book/OEBPS/012_part1zzf.xhtml#colo4_1); [Eph 6.5](javascript:void(0))--[9](javascript:void(0))) for Christian social and political thought, has long been debated. This is especially so in the American context, where the Bible was appealed to by both abolitionists and defenders of slavery in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

*Margaret M. Mitchell*

[^1^](javascript:void(0))Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother,[^a^](javascript:void(0))

To Philemon our dear friend and coworker, [^2^](javascript:void(0))to Apphia our sister,[^b^](javascript:void(0)) to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church in your house:

[^3^](javascript:void(0))Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

[^4^](javascript:void(0))When I remember you[^c^](javascript:void(0)) in my prayers, I always thank my God [^5^](javascript:void(0))because I hear of your love for all the saints and your faith toward the Lord Jesus. [^6^](javascript:void(0))I pray that the sharing of your faith may become effective when you perceive all the good that we[^d^](javascript:void(0)) may do for Christ. [^7^](javascript:void(0))I have indeed received much joy and encouragement from your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, my brother.

[^8^](javascript:void(0))For this reason, though I am bold enough in Christ to command you to do your duty, [^9^](javascript:void(0))yet I would rather appeal to you on the basis of love---and I, Paul, do this as an old man, and now also as a prisoner of Christ Jesus.[^e^](javascript:void(0)) [^10^](javascript:void(0))I am appealing to you for my child, Onesimus, whose father I have become during my imprisonment. [^11^](javascript:void(0))Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful[^f^](javascript:void(0)) both to you and to me. [^12^](javascript:void(0))I am sending him, that is, my own heart, back to you. [^13^](javascript:void(0))I wanted to keep him with me, so that he might be of service to me in your place during my imprisonment for the gospel; [^14^](javascript:void(0))but I preferred to do nothing without your consent, in order that your good deed might be voluntary and not something forced. [^15^](javascript:void(0))Perhaps this is the reason he was separated from you for a while, so that you might have him back forever, [^16^](javascript:void(0))no longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother---especially to me but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.

[^17^](javascript:void(0))So if you consider me your partner, welcome him as you would welcome me. [^18^](javascript:void(0))If he has wronged you in any way, or owes you anything, charge that to my account. [^19^](javascript:void(0))I, Paul, am writing this with my own hand: I will repay it. I say nothing about your owing me even your own self. [^20^](javascript:void(0))Yes, brother, let me have this benefit from you in the Lord! Refresh my heart in Christ. [^21^](javascript:void(0))Confident of your obedience, I am writing to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say.

[^22^](javascript:void(0))One thing more---prepare a guest room for me, for I am hoping through your prayers to be restored to you.

[^23^](javascript:void(0))Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends greetings to you,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) [^24^](javascript:void(0))and so do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers.

[^25^](javascript:void(0))The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.[^b^](javascript:void(0))

**[1](javascript:void(0))--[3](javascript:void(0)): Epistolary prescript** (senders, addressees, and salutation), with each sender and recipient carefully designated. **[1](javascript:void(0)):** *Timothy*, see Introduction to 2 Timothy. **[2](javascript:void(0)):** *Our sister*, fellow Christian. *Apphia*, named only here. *Archippus*, see Col 4.17. *And to the church in your house*, Paul puts Philemon\'s decision in a more public context.

**[4](javascript:void(0))--[7](javascript:void(0)): Thanksgiving for Philemon\'s past good deeds.** In vv. 4--22a Paul uses the singular address (*you*). Because he calls him "brother" in v. 20, it must refer either to Philemon or Archippus; tradition and current scholarship almost unanimously choose Philemon, on the grounds that he is the first named. **[4](javascript:void(0)):** *Remember you in my prayers*, cf. 2 Tim 1.3. **[5](javascript:void(0)):** *Saints*, lit., "holy ones," believers in Christ Jesus. **[7](javascript:void(0)):** *Hearts*, Gk "splanchna," lit., "inner organs," refers to the emotional center of a person (see vv. 12,20).

**[8](javascript:void(0))--[22](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s appeal for another good deed from Philemon.** **[10](javascript:void(0)):** *Whose father I have become*, lit., "whom I begot" to new life in the gospel (cf. 1 Cor 4.15). **[11](javascript:void(0)):** *Useful* ("eu-chrestos") is a double pun, referring both to Onesimus\'s name (see textual note *f*) and his identity in Christ ("eu-Christos" = "good in Christ"). **[14](javascript:void(0)):** *Voluntary*, Paul does not command (cf. v. 8), but prefers to persuade. **[15](javascript:void(0)):** *Was separated*, a perhaps deliberately vague reference to Onesimus\'s absence. **[16](javascript:void(0)):** *No longer as a slave*, finally the problem is stated: status dissonance (i.e., when a person occupies two or more social positions simultaneously). What happens when a slave of a Christian master becomes a Christian? Some scholars take Paul to mean the slave stops being a slave by becoming a brother, but others think Paul considers the new status of *brother* as relativizing, but not changing, the slave\'s station in the world. *In the flesh and in the Lord*, in the world and in the church. **[17](javascript:void(0))--[19](javascript:void(0)):** *Partner, charge* ... *to my account, repay*, business terminology signalling Paul\'s financial obligations to Philemon. *Writing this with my own hand*, cf. 1 Cor 16.21; Gal 6.11. *Owing me even your own self*, Philemon\'s spiritual obligation to the one who converted him. **[21](javascript:void(0)):** *More than I say*, a mere commonplace, or perhaps a diplomatically framed hint to release him from slavery through manumission? **[22b](javascript:void(0)):** *Your* prayers, in the plural. Paul here joins the co-recipients (v. 2) with him in registering his plea to Philemon.

**[23](javascript:void(0))--[24](javascript:void(0)): Greetings,** the same five people are named in Col 4.10--14. *Epaphras*, Col 1.7; 4.12.

**[25](javascript:void(0)):Concluding benediction.**

#### Colossians (D) c. 60--62 CE

The Letter of Paul to The Colossians

**NAME AND CONTENTS**

This letter is named for its recipients, the Christian community in the Phrygian city of Colossae ([1.2](javascript:void(0))), a community founded by Epaphras, a Colossian associate of Paul ([1.7](javascript:void(0))--[8](javascript:void(0)); [4.12](javascript:void(0))--[13](javascript:void(0))). Once a thriving town on the Lycus River in the Roman province of Asia, Colossae had a significant Jewish population. The city fell into decline after an earthquake ca. 60 ce; the site has not yet been excavated.

**AUTHORSHIP, DATE OF COMPOSITION, HISTORICAL CONTEXT, AND LITERARY HISTORY**

Despite its similarity to the undisputed letters of Paul in structure, language, and theology, Colossians lacks some central Pauline terms (e.g., righteousness, justification), uses new theological vocabulary (e.g., to be raised with Christ), and is composed in a more elevated, liturgical style. Colossians presents a vision of believers' present lives as almost completely transformed by Christ\'s death and resurrection ([3.1](javascript:void(0))--[4](javascript:void(0))), a contrast to Paul\'s characteristic tension between the partial experience of God\'s blessings in the present in light of the future resurrection (e.g., [Rom 6.4](javascript:void(0)); [1 Cor 15.50](javascript:void(0))--[58](javascript:void(0))). Colossians also uses the Greco-Roman format of household rules to define ethical norms ([3.18](javascript:void(0))--[4.1](javascript:void(0))), which is more characteristic of the post-Pauline Ephesians, Pastoral Letters, and 1 Peter. Paul\'s own ethical instructions did not reinforce or even focus on these household relationships; Paul instead adopted a baptismal creed that overturns social, ethnic, and gender hierarchies ([Gal 3.28](javascript:void(0))), and elevated celibacy over marriage (e.g., [1 Cor 7](javascript:void(0))). Some scholars conclude that Colossians is pseudonymous---written in Paul\'s name by one of his disciples, either during Paul\'s lifetime or shortly after his death (ca. 65 ce), in order to authorize the application of Paul\'s thought to a new situation. Other scholars think the letter was written by Paul while imprisoned ([4.3](javascript:void(0)),[10](javascript:void(0)),[18](javascript:void(0))) at Rome near the end of his life and attribute any theological differences to developments in Paul\'s thinking and the particulars of the situation addressed.

After beginning with a glowing description of the Colossians' lives, the author soon alludes to unnamed teachers who pose a threat to their faith. Without an independent description of these teachings, precise identification is difficult. It appears that these teachers advocated observance of ascetic rituals, where the adherent seeks the help of spiritual powers to reach the divine throne ([2.8](javascript:void(0))--[23](javascript:void(0))). Many scholars understand these rituals to be indebted to Jewish mysticism; others emphasize the influence of local Phrygian religious practices or Hellenistic philosophy. The attractiveness of Jewish ritual elements within the church at Colossae reflects not only the ongoing close connections between Jewish and Christian communities, but also the fluidity of practices across porous religious boundaries. The polemical tone of Colossians, however, represents an emerging first-century Christian ambivalence toward Jewish rituals and the desire to more clearly define community boundaries.

**STRUCTURE**

Colossians follows the usual structure of a Pauline letter (see pp. [1611--12](javascript:void(0))), beginning with a greeting ([1.1](javascript:void(0))--[2](javascript:void(0))), an introductory thanksgiving ([1.3](javascript:void(0))--[8](javascript:void(0))) and prayer ([1.9](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0))), and ending with greetings and instructions ([4.7](javascript:void(0))--[18](javascript:void(0))). The body of the letter includes both a theological argument ([2.6](javascript:void(0))--[23](javascript:void(0))) and ethical instructions ([3.1](javascript:void(0))--[4.6](javascript:void(0))). The basis of the theological argument---focused on Christ---is presented in [1.12](javascript:void(0))--[2.5](javascript:void(0)). In the elevated words of an early Christian hymn, Christ is praised as the supreme power over the cosmos and the church ([1.15](javascript:void(0))--[20](javascript:void(0))). Although cosmic forces enslaved humanity in the past, believers have been freed from their malevolent influence, forgiven through Christ\'s death, and made full citizens of the kingdom of Christ, to whom they now owe complete allegiance ([1.12](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0)), [21](javascript:void(0))--[23](javascript:void(0))). Christ is the perfect revelation of God ([1.19](javascript:void(0)); [2.9](javascript:void(0))--[10](javascript:void(0))) and the single source of wisdom about how to live rightly ([1.9](javascript:void(0))--[10](javascript:void(0)); [2.2](javascript:void(0))--[3](javascript:void(0))).

**INTERPRETATION**

The main theological argument of Colossians focuses on the change in believers' spiritual existence achieved by Christ\'s death on the cross ([2.9](javascript:void(0))--[15](javascript:void(0))). The recurring contrasts of death and life ([2.12](javascript:void(0))--[13](javascript:void(0)),[20](javascript:void(0)); [3.1](javascript:void(0))--[5](javascript:void(0))), old and new ([3.9](javascript:void(0))--[10](javascript:void(0))), and past and present ([1.12](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0)),[21](javascript:void(0))--[23](javascript:void(0))) emphasize the fundamental psychological and moral reorientation required of those who would be faithful to Christ. This letter presupposes a world populated by a multitude of spiritual or cosmic entities enmeshed in conflict with humans and the divine ([1.16](javascript:void(0)); [2.8](javascript:void(0)),[15](javascript:void(0)),[18](javascript:void(0))). Our author believes that rituals of mystical ascension to the heavenly realm (see above) belong to the old, inferior world and entail subjection to cosmic entities; they must be rejected as denials of Christ\'s lordship.

The members of a true Christian community, rejecting their previous immoral lifestyle ([3.5](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0))) and reorienting their entire lives around Christ as Lord ([3.1](javascript:void(0))--[4](javascript:void(0))), are to live in harmony with each other as they worship and give thanks to God and Christ ([3.12](javascript:void(0))--[17](javascript:void(0))). It is therefore surprising that the idealized household ([3.18](javascript:void(0))--[4.1](javascript:void(0))) is only a mildly Christianized version of the ancient patriarchal family rather than a reconsideration of household relationships based on the equality of all in Christ and on mutual love and forgiveness ([3.10](javascript:void(0))--[15](javascript:void(0))). The letter\'s elevated language of death, ascension, and spiritual wisdom provided fertile ground for theological speculation since the second century ce; perhaps most significant, however, is the Christological language in 1.15--20 that shaped the debates of the fourth century and the formation of the church\'s creeds.

*Jennifer K. Berenson*

[**1**](javascript:void(0)) Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother,

[^2^](javascript:void(0))To the saints and faithful brothers and sisters[^a^](javascript:void(0)) in Christ in Colossae:

Grace to you and peace from God our Father.

[^3^](javascript:void(0))In our prayers for you we always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, [^4^](javascript:void(0))for we have heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love that you have for all the saints, [^5^](javascript:void(0))because of the hope laid up for you in heaven. You have heard of this hope before in the word of the truth, the gospel [^6^](javascript:void(0))that has come to you. Just as it is bearing fruit and growing in the whole world, so it has been bearing fruit among yourselves from the day you heard it and truly comprehended the grace of God. [^7^](javascript:void(0))This you learned from Epaphras, our beloved fellow servant.[^b^](javascript:void(0)) He is a faithful minister of Christ on your[^c^](javascript:void(0)) behalf, [^8^](javascript:void(0))and he has made known to us your love in the Spirit.

[^9^](javascript:void(0))For this reason, since the day we heard it, we have not ceased praying for you and asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of God\'s[^d^](javascript:void(0)) will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding, [^10^](javascript:void(0))so that you may lead lives worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing to him, as you bear fruit in every good work and as you grow in the knowledge of God. [^11^](javascript:void(0))May you be made strong with all the strength that comes from his glorious power, and may you be prepared to endure everything with patience, while joyfully [^12^](javascript:void(0))giving thanks to the Father, who has enabled[^e^](javascript:void(0)) you[^f^](javascript:void(0)) to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light. [^13^](javascript:void(0))He has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son, [^14^](javascript:void(0))in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.[^a^](javascript:void(0))

[^15^](javascript:void(0))He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation; [^16^](javascript:void(0))for in[^b^](javascript:void(0)) him all things in heaven and on earth were created, things visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or powers---all things have been created through him and for him. [^17^](javascript:void(0))He himself is before all things, and in him^b^ all things hold together. [^18^](javascript:void(0))He is the head of the body, the church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he might come to have first place in everything. [^19^](javascript:void(0))For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell, [^20^](javascript:void(0))and through him God was pleased to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, by making peace through the blood of his cross.

[^21^](javascript:void(0))And you who were once estranged and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds, [^22^](javascript:void(0))he has now reconciled[^c^](javascript:void(0)) in his fleshly body[^d^](javascript:void(0)) through death, so as to present you holy and blameless and irreproachable before him---[^23^](javascript:void(0))provided that you continue securely established and steadfast in the faith, without shifting from the hope promised by the gospel that you heard, which has been proclaimed to every creature under heaven. I, Paul, became a servant of this gospel.

[^24^](javascript:void(0))I am now rejoicing in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am completing what is lacking in Christ\'s afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church. [^25^](javascript:void(0))I became its servant according to God\'s commission that was given to me for you, to make the word of God fully known, [^26^](javascript:void(0))the mystery that has been hidden throughout the ages and generations but has now been revealed to his saints. [^27^](javascript:void(0))To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory. [^28^](javascript:void(0))It is he whom we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone in all wisdom, so that we may present everyone mature in Christ. [^29^](javascript:void(0))For this I toil and struggle with all the energy that he powerfully inspires within me.

[**2**](javascript:void(0)) For I want you to know how much I am struggling for you, and for those in Laodicea, and for all who have not seen me face to face. [^2^](javascript:void(0))I want their hearts to be encouraged and united in love, so that they may have all the riches of assured understanding and have the knowledge of God\'s mystery, that is, Christ himself,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) [^3^](javascript:void(0))in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. [^4^](javascript:void(0))I am saying this so that no one may deceive you with plausible arguments. [^5^](javascript:void(0))For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, and I rejoice to see your morale and the firmness of your faith in Christ.

[^6^](javascript:void(0))As you therefore have received Christ Jesus the Lord, continue to live your lives[^b^](javascript:void(0)) in him, [^7^](javascript:void(0))rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.

[^8^](javascript:void(0))See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the universe,[^c^](javascript:void(0)) and not according to Christ. [^9^](javascript:void(0))For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, [^10^](javascript:void(0))and you have come to fullness in him, who is the head of every ruler and authority. [^11^](javascript:void(0))In him also you were circumcised with a spiritual circumcision,[^d^](javascript:void(0)) by putting off the body of the flesh in the circumcision of Christ; [^12^](javascript:void(0))when you were buried with him in baptism, you were also raised with him through faith in the power of God, who raised him from the dead. [^13^](javascript:void(0))And when you were dead in trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God[^e^](javascript:void(0)) made you[^f^](javascript:void(0)) alive together with him, when he forgave us all our trespasses, [^14^](javascript:void(0))erasing the record that stood against us with its legal demands. He set this aside, nailing it to the cross. [^15^](javascript:void(0))He disarmed[^g^](javascript:void(0)) the rulers and authorities and made a public example of them, triumphing over them in it.

[^16^](javascript:void(0))Therefore do not let anyone condemn you in matters of food and drink or of observing festivals, new moons, or sabbaths. [^17^](javascript:void(0))These are only a shadow of what is to come, but the substance belongs to Christ. [^18^](javascript:void(0))Do not let anyone disqualify you, insisting on self-abasement and worship of angels, dwelling[^h^](javascript:void(0)) on visions,[^i^](javascript:void(0)) puffed up without cause by a human way of thinking,[^a^](javascript:void(0)) [^19^](javascript:void(0))and not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, nourished and held together by its ligaments and sinews, grows with a growth that is from God.

[^20^](javascript:void(0))If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the universe,[^b^](javascript:void(0)) why do you live as if you still belonged to the world? Why do you submit to regulations, [^21^](javascript:void(0))"Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch"? [^22^](javascript:void(0))All these regulations refer to things that perish with use; they are simply human commands and teachings. [^23^](javascript:void(0))These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-imposed piety, humility, and severe treatment of the body, but they are of no value in checking selfindulgence.[^c^](javascript:void(0))

[**3**](javascript:void(0)) So if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. [^2^](javascript:void(0))Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth, [^3^](javascript:void(0))for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. [^4^](javascript:void(0))When Christ who is your[^d^](javascript:void(0)) life is revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory.

[^5^](javascript:void(0))Put to death, therefore, whatever in you is earthly: fornication, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed (which is idolatry). [^6^](javascript:void(0))On account of these the wrath of God is coming on those who are disobedient.[^e^](javascript:void(0)) [^7^](javascript:void(0))These are the ways you also once followed, when you were living that life.[^f^](javascript:void(0)) [^8^](javascript:void(0))But now you must get rid of all such things---anger, wrath, malice, slander, and abusive[^g^](javascript:void(0)) language from your mouth. [^9^](javascript:void(0))Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have stripped off the old self with its practices [^10^](javascript:void(0))and have clothed yourselves with the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of its creator. [^11^](javascript:void(0))In that renewal[^h^](javascript:void(0)) there is no longer Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave and free; but Christ is all and in all!

[^12^](javascript:void(0))As God\'s chosen ones, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience. [^13^](javascript:void(0))Bear with one another and, if anyone has a complaint against another, forgive each other; just as the Lord[^i^](javascript:void(0)) has forgiven you, so you also must forgive. [^14^](javascript:void(0))Above all, clothe yourselves with love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony. [^15^](javascript:void(0))And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in the one body. And be thankful. [^16^](javascript:void(0))Let the word of Christ[^a^](javascript:void(0)) dwell in you richly; teach and admonish one another in all wisdom; and with gratitude in your hearts sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs to God.[^b^](javascript:void(0)) [^17^](javascript:void(0))And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.

[^18^](javascript:void(0))Wives, be subject to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. [^19^](javascript:void(0))Husbands, love your wives and never treat them harshly.

[^20^](javascript:void(0))Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is your acceptable duty in the Lord. [^21^](javascript:void(0))Fathers, do not provoke your children, or they may lose heart. [^22^](javascript:void(0))Slaves, obey your earthly masters[^c^](javascript:void(0)) in everything, not only while being watched and in order to please them, but wholeheartedly, fearing the Lord.^c^ [^23^](javascript:void(0))Whatever your task, put yourselves into it, as done for the Lord and not for your masters,[^d^](javascript:void(0)) [^24^](javascript:void(0))since you know that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward; you serve[^e^](javascript:void(0)) the Lord Christ. [^25^](javascript:void(0))For the wrongdoer will be paid back for whatever wrong has been done, and there is no partiality.

[**4**](javascript:void(0)) Masters, treat your slaves justly and fairly, for you know that you also have a Master in heaven.

[^2^](javascript:void(0))Devote yourselves to prayer, keeping alert in it with thanksgiving. [^3^](javascript:void(0))At the same time pray for us as well that God will open to us a door for the word, that we may declare the mystery of Christ, for which I am in prison, [^4^](javascript:void(0))so that I may reveal it clearly, as I should.

[^5^](javascript:void(0))Conduct yourselves wisely toward outsiders, making the most of the time.[^f^](javascript:void(0)) [^6^](javascript:void(0))Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer everyone.

[^7^](javascript:void(0))Tychicus will tell you all the news about me; he is a beloved brother, a faithful minister, and a fellow servant[^g^](javascript:void(0)) in the Lord. [^8^](javascript:void(0))I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that you may know how we are[^h^](javascript:void(0)) and that he may encourage your hearts; [^9^](javascript:void(0))he is coming with Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you about everything here.

[^10^](javascript:void(0))Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you, as does Mark the cousin of Barnabas, concerning whom you have received instructions---if he comes to you, welcome him. [^11^](javascript:void(0))And Jesus who is called Justus greets you. These are the only ones of the circumcision among my co-workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me. [^12^](javascript:void(0))Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant[^a^](javascript:void(0)) of Christ Jesus, greets you. He is always wrestling in his prayers on your behalf, so that you may stand mature and fully assured in everything that God wills. [^13^](javascript:void(0))For I testify for him that he has worked hard for you and for those in Laodicea and in Hierapolis. [^14^](javascript:void(0))Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas greet you. [^15^](javascript:void(0))Give my greetings to the brothers and sisters[^b^](javascript:void(0)) in Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church in her house. [^16^](javascript:void(0))And when this letter has been read among you, have it read also in the church of the Laodiceans; and see that you read also the letter from Laodicea. [^17^](javascript:void(0))And say to Archippus, "See that you complete the task that you have received in the Lord."

[^18^](javascript:void(0))I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.[^c^](javascript:void(0))

**[1.1](javascript:void(0))--[2](javascript:void(0)): Salutation.** **[1](javascript:void(0)):** *Apostle ... by the will of God*, see 1.25; Rom 1.1n. *Timothy*, Paul\'s fellow missionary and emissary (Philem 1; 2 Cor 1.1; Phil 1.1; 2.19--24). *Brother* indicates a bond of affection and loyalty. **[2](javascript:void(0)):** *Saints*, literally "holy ones," refers to all followers of the Christian movement. *Brothers and sisters*, the Gk plural *adelphoi* (see note *a*) has the sense of "siblings." *Grace ... peace*, a common Pauline greeting building upon conventional salutations in Gk (*grace*) and Heb (*peace*).

**[1.3](javascript:void(0))--[8](javascript:void(0)): Thanksgiving for obedient lives.** **[3](javascript:void(0))--[5](javascript:void(0)):** *Faith, hope*, and *love*, a summary of Christian virtues (1 Cor 13.13; 1 Thess 5.8). **[4](javascript:void(0)):** *Faith*, here allegiance or loyalty. **[5](javascript:void(0)):** *Gospel*, proclamation of good news, here referring to the message of Christ\'s victory over death (see 2.15). **[6](javascript:void(0)):** *The whole world*, hyperbole for all the Christian communities in the ancient world. **[7](javascript:void(0)):** *Epaphras*, founder of the church in Colossae (4.12--13; Philem 23).

**[1.9](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0)): Prayer for continued growth** in knowledge (v. 9), moral maturity (v. 10), and endurance (v. 11). **[9](javascript:void(0)):** *Spiritual wisdom and understanding*, a major theme of the letter (1.25--28; 2.2--4,9--15). **[12](javascript:void(0))--[14](javascript:void(0)):** Perhaps a fragment of a baptismal hymn. **[12](javascript:void(0))--[13](javascript:void(0)):** *Light ... darkness*, apocalyptic imagery for the opposing domains within the cosmos (see 1.16n.; 1 Thess 5.5). **[12](javascript:void(0)):** *Inheritance*, a metaphor based on Israel\'s inheritance of the land as a gift of God. **[14](javascript:void(0)):** *Redemption*, release or ransom from slavery.

**[1.15](javascript:void(0))--[20](javascript:void(0)): The supremacy of Christ.** This enduring language of an early Christian hymn, probably based on the Jewish figure Wisdom/Sophia (Prov 8; Sir 24; Wis 6--9; see also Jn 1.1--18; Phil 2.6--11), expresses Christ\'s supremacy over the cosmos (vv. 15--17) and the church (vv. 18--20). **[15](javascript:void(0)):** *Image*, the perfect, visible manifestation of God. *Firstborn* expresses priority and supremacy. **[16](javascript:void(0)):** *Thrones ... powers*, hostile cosmic powers (1.13; 2.15; Eph 6.12). **[17](javascript:void(0)):** *In him all things hold together*, Christ actively maintains the coherence of the cosmos **[18](javascript:void(0)):** *Head*, ruling authority or originator; see Eph 1.22; 5.23. *The body, the church*, both terms stem from ancient political discourse for a community assembly, emphasizing unity and coherence; see Rom 12.4--5; 1 Cor 12.27. See also Eph 1.22--23n. *Firstborn from the dead*, the first of all those to be resurrected from the dead (1 Cor 15.20,23; Acts 26.23; Rev 1.5). **[19](javascript:void(0)):** *Fullness of God*, the power and presence of God (see also 1.29; 2.9--10). **[20](javascript:void(0)):** *Reconcile ... making peace*, the estrangement of creation from the creator is rectified (1.13--14, 21--22, 2.15).

**[1.21](javascript:void(0))--[23](javascript:void(0)): Assurance and warning.** **[21](javascript:void(0)):** *Hostile in mind, doing evil deeds*, interrelated aspects of the former life (Rom 1.18--32). **[22](javascript:void(0)):** *Fleshly body*, an emphatic contrast with Christ\'s heavenly origins (1.20, 2.9; cf. 1.15--17). *To present you ... before him*, reconciliation is completed by Christ\'s approval at the eschatological judgment (v. 28). **[23](javascript:void(0)):** Concern for continued allegiance to Christ is the primary focus of the letter.

**[1.24](javascript:void(0))--[2.5](javascript:void(0)): Paul\'s mission and pastoral commitment.** **[1.24](javascript:void(0)):** *Completing ... afflictions*, not a denigration of Christ\'s death but an acknowledgment that those who preach the gospel will experience *sufferings* (1.29), such as imprisonment (4.3,10,18) and other hardships (2 Cor 4.7--12; 11.23--28). **[26](javascript:void(0))--[28](javascript:void(0)):** *Mystery*, in Paul\'s writings, the term refers to God\'s secret eschatological plan (Rom 11.25; 1 Cor 2.6--7, 15.51; cf. Dan 2.28; Wis 2.22); in Colossians, Christ himself is the mystery (2.2; 4.3; Rom 16.25--26; cf. Eph 1.10; 3.2--6). *Hope of glory ... so that we may present*, the expectation of their eschatological presentation before Christ. **[2.1](javascript:void(0)):** *Laodicea*, see 4.13n. **[5](javascript:void(0)):** *Morale*, *firmness*, terminology evoking military discipline.

**[2.6](javascript:void(0))--[23](javascript:void(0)): Theological Argument.** 2.6--15: Christ and the cross. **[6](javascript:void(0))--[7](javascript:void(0)):** Thematic statement of the letter (see Introduction; 1.21--23; 3.1--4). **[6](javascript:void(0)):** *Received*, a technical term for the reception of oral tradition (1 Cor 15.1,3); here, that Jesus is Lord (Rom 10.9). **[8](javascript:void(0)):** *Philosophy* includes ethical and religious teachings. *Human tradition*, in contrast to God\'s revelation through Paul. *Elemental spirits*, cosmic forces perhaps based on the four primal elements of Greek thought; associated with the Jewish law in Gal 4.1--5,9--10. **[9](javascript:void(0))--[10](javascript:void(0)):** See 1.19n. **[11](javascript:void(0))--[12](javascript:void(0)):** *Circumcision*, a ritual, bodily mark of membership in the people of Israel (Gen 17.9--14). The significance of circumcision is here transferred to Christian baptism where the previous life (*the body of the flesh)* is shed in solidarity with Christ\'s death and the baptized are given new life (*you were also raised*) as was Christ. **[13](javascript:void(0)):** *Uncircumcision of your flesh*, the Colossians were Gentiles. **[14](javascript:void(0)):** *Record ... demands*, a document detailing transgressions, perhaps similar to that in Dan 7.10 and Rev 20.12. *Nailing it to the cross*, ridding it of its power to condemn. **[15](javascript:void(0)):** *Rulers and authorities*, see 1.16n. *Disarmed ... public example*, language evoking a Roman ritual (the "triumph") where the state\'s vanquished enemies were publically displayed in an elaborate parade.

**[2.16](javascript:void(0))--[23](javascript:void(0)): Warnings against ascetic practices.** **[16](javascript:void(0)):** *Matters of food and drink*, observance of Jewish dietary laws. *Festivals, new moons, or sabbaths*, a summary of the Jewish religious calendar (e.g., 2 Chr 8.13; Neh 10.33). **[17](javascript:void(0)):** *Shadow ... substance*, Platonic language contrasting the temporal/inferior with the eternal/perfect (see Heb 8.5n.). **[18](javascript:void(0)):** Ascetic practices (*self-abasement*) used to achieve a mystical ascent to heaven (*dwelling on visions*); *worship of angels* may refer to ecstatic participation in worship of God alongside angels or the showing of reverence to angels. **[19](javascript:void(0)):** *Head, body*, see 1.18n. **[20](javascript:void(0)):** *Died to*, no longer under the authority of (vv. 8--15). *As if ... world*, see 2.11; 3.1--3. **[21](javascript:void(0)):** Jewish purity regulations. **[22](javascript:void(0)):** See Mk 7.7,19. **[23](javascript:void(0)):** The criticism is either that such practices do not address the author\'s moral concerns (3.5,8) or that they inappropriately focus attention on the body (see note *c*).

**[3.1](javascript:void(0))--[4.6](javascript:void(0)): Ethical implications.** **[3.1](javascript:void(0))--[4](javascript:void(0))**: Maintain a heavenly perspective. **[1](javascript:void(0)):** *Raised*, 2.12. *Seated at the right hand of God*, see Eph 1.19--20n. **[1](javascript:void(0))--[2](javascript:void(0)):** *Seek ... set*, commands to orient one\'s life around the heavenly reality of Christ\'s exaltation and authority. **[3](javascript:void(0)):** *Died*, see 2.11--12n. *Hidden with*, expressing an intimate and inseparable connection. **[4](javascript:void(0)):** *Is revealed*, at the eschatological judgment.

**[3.5](javascript:void(0))--[11](javascript:void(0)): Reject sins of the old life.** **[5](javascript:void(0)):** *Put to death*, vehemently refuse to engage in. *Fornication ... evil desire*, inappropriate sexual behavior. *Idolatry*, often linked with sexual sins in Jewish and Christian thought (Hos 4.12--19; Rom 1.23--27; 1 Cor 10.7--8). **[6](javascript:void(0)):** *Wrath*, God\'s eschatological judgment. **[8](javascript:void(0)):** *Anger ... abusive language*, a list of vices commonly condemned in antiquity (cf. 1 Cor 6.9; Gal 5.19--21). **[9](javascript:void(0))--[10](javascript:void(0)):** *Old self ... new self*, another contrast emphasizing the new act of creation (recalling Gen 1.26--27) brought about by baptism (2.12). *Stripped of*f, changing one\'s clothing as a metaphor for adopting a new way of life (3.12--14; Eph 4.22--24). **[11](javascript:void(0)):** An eloquent rejection of privileges based on ethnicity and socioeconomic status; cf. the additional abrogation of a gender hierarchy in Gal 3.28. *Barbarian ... Scythian*, shorthand in antiquity for uncultured peoples.

**[3.12](javascript:void(0))--[17](javascript:void(0)): Adopt virtues of the new life.** **[12](javascript:void(0)):** *Compassion ... patience*, virtues emphasizing a proper attitude toward oneself and genuine concern for others. **[13](javascript:void(0)):** *Forgive*, Eph 4.32; cf. Mt 6.14--15. **[16](javascript:void(0)):** *Word of Christ*, teachings concerning Christ.

**[3.18](javascript:void(0))--[4.1](javascript:void(0)): Household relationships "in the Lord.** " This passage adopts a popular philosophical format of paired commands (wife/husband, etc.) for describing the ancient ideal of the patriarchal family and defends it as appropriate for a community dedicated to Christ as Lord (see the more extensive elaboration in Eph 5.22--6.9). The commands to the male figure somewhat moderate his traditional prerogatives (see 3.19,21; 4.1), although appeal to these rules throughout Christian history has tended to reinforce rather than challenge male authority. **[18](javascript:void(0))--[19](javascript:void(0)):** *Wives*/*husbands*, the first of the three fundamental household relationships. Cf. Eph 5:22--33. **[18](javascript:void(0)):** *Be subject*, accept a position of subordination. The role of Nympha (4.15n) stands in contrast to the idealized subordinate female. **[19](javascript:void(0)):** *Never treat them harshly*, alternatively, "do not be embittered against them." **[20](javascript:void(0))--[21](javascript:void(0)):** C*hildren*/*fathers*, cf. Eph 6.1--4. **[3.22](javascript:void(0))--[4.1](javascript:void(0)):** S*laves*/*masters*, cf. Eph 6.5--9. This relationship is the most fully developed of the three, placing the burden on the slave to act in a way that does not incur the master\'s displeasure.

**[4.2](javascript:void(0))--[6](javascript:void(0)): Final admonitions.** **[3](javascript:void(0)):** *Door for the word*, an opportunity to preach. *Mystery*, see 1.26--27n. *Prison*, see 1.24n. **[5](javascript:void(0)):** *Conduct yourself wisely*, perhaps the motivation for advocating the conservative household ethic above. *Making the most of the time*, recognizing the eschatological urgency. **[6](javascript:void(0)):** *With salt*, with graciousness or perhaps wit (cf. Mt 5.13).

**[4.7](javascript:void(0))--[18](javascript:void(0)): Final greetings and instructions.** **[7](javascript:void(0)):** *Tychicus*, Paul\'s associate (Acts 20.4; 2 Tim 4.12), commended like Epaphras (cf. 1.7). **[9](javascript:void(0)):** *Onesimus*, see Philem 10--21. **[10](javascript:void(0)):** *Aristarchus*, Acts 20.4; 27.2; Philem 24. *Welcome him*, cf. Paul\'s conflict with Mark in Acts 13.13; 15.37--39. **[11](javascript:void(0)):** *Jesus*, a common Jewish name. *The circumcision*, Jewish followers of the Christian movement, here without negative connotations (cf. Gal 2.12). **[12](javascript:void(0)):** *Epaphras*, see 1.7n. **[13](javascript:void(0)):** *Laodicea*, *Hierapolis*, cities located 10 and 15 miles (16 and 24 km), respectively, northwest of Colossae. **[14](javascript:void(0)):** *Luke*, 2 Tim 4.11; Philem 24. Traditionally identified as the author of the Gospel of Luke and Acts (see respective Introductions). *Demas*, 2 Tim 4.10; Philem 24. **[15](javascript:void(0)):** *Brothers and sisters*, see Eph 6.23n. *Nympha*, probably the leader of the church that met in her home (see Philem 1--2). **[16](javascript:void(0)):** *The letter from Laodicea*, no letter is extant, although some scholars identify it with Ephesians. This verse attests to the churches' practice of sharing Paul\'s letters prior to their distribution in a collection. **[17](javascript:void(0)):** *Archippus*, Philem 2. **[18](javascript:void(0)):** A final word in the author\'s handwriting to authenticate the letter (cf. 1 Cor 16.21; Gal 6.11); the rest of the letter would have been dictated to a secretary (see Rom 16.22).
